    • Persistence: A service account with iam.serviceAccountKeys.create creates a key for itself and recreates it whenever defenders delete it.
    • Detection: Alert on google.iam.admin.v1.CreateServiceAccountKey where authenticationInfo.principalEmail equals the account in request.name.
    • Risky roles: roles/editor, roles/owner, roles/iam.serviceAccountKeyAdmin, roles/securitycenter.admin and roles/assuredoss.admin allow key creation.
    • Mitigation: Least privilege, block keys with org policy, and enforce iam.automaticIamGrantsForDefaultServiceAccounts so default accounts lose Editor.
    • Caveats: Google considers it addressed by the May 2024 default-grant change; the author disagrees, and detection was tested in one environment only.
    • Source note: The Red Canary URL now redirects to a Zscaler blog copy of the post.

    Takeaway: Treat a compromised service account as needing disablement, not just key deletion, and alert on any service account creating its own key.

  • Build Go Applications Using Project IDX and the Gemini API
    summary

    TL;DR: Google tutorial (December 2024) for setting up a Go dev environment in the cloud-based Project IDX workspace and starting from Go or Go-plus-Gemini API templates.

    • What it is: Project IDX is Google’s AI-assisted, cloud workspace for full-stack development, launched June 2024.
    • Workspace: Start a blank project, import a GitHub repo, or use a template; each ships a Nix-based .idx/dev.nix.
    • Environment: Add pkgs.go and the golang.go extension to dev.nix, then rebuild the environment.
    • Module: Run Go: Initialize go.mod from the Command Palette or go mod init github.com/myorg/helloWorld.
    • Sample app: main.go serves “Hello, World!” on the PORT env var, defaulting to 3000.
    • Preview: A previews.web block runs go run main.go with PORT = "$PORT" to show a live web preview.
    • Templates: Go backend server templates and a Go plus Gemini template with a “Baking with Gemini” recipe example.
    • Caveats: You must supply your own Gemini API key; no model, pricing, quotas or key-handling guidance is given; config changes require rebuilds.

    Takeaway: Useful only for quick Go prototyping in a browser IDE; pin tools in dev.nix and keep the Gemini API key out of committed config.

  • one: Awesome List of Cybersecurity and AI
    summary

    TL;DR: A CC0 “awesome list” of reading on AI in offensive and defensive cyber, compiled as background for a talk at the 2024 One Conference in The Hague.

    • What it is: A curated link list, not a tool; no code, setup or commands.
    • Hype cycle: Core section with a security-AI hype cycle chart and readings on vector DB security, model stealing, sleeper agents and GCG jailbreaks.
    • Topics: Covers AI Bills of Materials (AIBOMs) and “LLMjacking” abuse of stolen cloud credentials.
    • Policies: EU AI Act, UK NCSC guidelines, an NSA deployment guide and Singapore MAS circular on generative AI risk.
    • Frameworks: MITRE ATLAS, CyberSecEval 2, AVID and the MIT AI Risk Repository.
    • Blue team: AI for incident response, threat intel, malware analysis and threat modelling such as STRIDE GPT.
    • Red team: Supply-chain and Keras model backdoors, AI-assisted bug hunting and automatic tool invocation risks.
    • Caveats: A 2024 snapshot mixing papers, vendor blogs and opinion without marking which is which; links may have rotted.

    Takeaway: Use it as a starting index for AI security threat modelling, especially MITRE ATLAS and LLMjacking, but check each source’s date and credibility.

  • Things We Learned About LLMs in 2024
    summary

    TL;DR: Simon Willison’s year-in-review of LLMs in 2024: GPT-4 was surpassed widely, prices crashed, reasoning models arrived, and agents and prompt injection remained unsolved.

    • GPT-4 beaten: 18 organizations had 70 models ranking above original GPT-4 on Chatbot Arena, starting with Gemini 1.5 Pro.
    • Local models: GPT-4-class Qwen2.5-Coder-32B and Llama 3.3 70B run on a 64GB M2 MacBook Pro.
    • Prices: GPT-4 was $30 per million input tokens in December 2023; GPT-4o mini is $0.15 and Gemini 1.5 Flash 8B $0.0375.
    • Numbers: Describing 68,000 photos with Flash 8B costs about $1.68 total.
    • Reasoning: o1 launched in September; o3 posted strong ARC-AGI results, likely costing over $1,000,000 in compute.
    • DeepSeek v3: 685B parameters trained on 2,788,000 H800 GPU hours (about $5,576,000) versus 30,840,000 hours for Llama 3.1 405B.
    • Agents: Still not real; LLM gullibility and prompt injection, discussed since September 2022, block them.
    • Other: Evals matter, synthetic training data works, Apple Intelligence is weak while MLX excels, and “slop” names unrequested, unreviewed AI content.
    • Caveats: Arena is a vibes-based evaluation; datacenter buildout is worsening environmental impact even as per-prompt cost falls.

    Takeaway: Assume cheap, capable models are everywhere, build evals before shipping LLM features, and treat any agent that reads untrusted input as prompt-injectable.

  • Implementing Security Invariants in an AWS Management Account
    summary

    TL;DR: Chris Farris proposes enforcing security invariants in the AWS Organization management (payer) account, where SCPs and RCPs do not apply, using one universal IAM permission boundary.

    • Problem: SCPs and RCPs skip the management account, yet workloads often live there and can endanger the whole Organization.
    • Approach: Attach one shared permission boundary to every user and role; it grants nothing and only caps maximum permissions.
    • Invariants: Nine rules, covering CloudTrail, member account closure, Organization services, SCP/RCP changes, sts:AssumeRoot, billing, Identity Center, StackSets and Control Tower.
    • Control Tower: Nobody may enable or use it; tagline “Control Tower: Not even Once!”
    • Policy design: A broad Allow with NotAction excludes restricted actions, then conditional allows on aws:PrincipalArn restore them for Cloud Admin, Finance, Identity Center and Terraform roles.
    • Self-protection: Statements deny sts:AssumeRole on OrganizationAccountAccessRole and block edits to the boundary policy itself except by admin and enforcer roles.
    • Enforcement: A Lambda fired by EventBridge on iam:CreateRole, iam:CreateUser and boundary delete/put events reattaches the boundary nearly instantly; a Steampipe query audits coverage.
    • Caveats: A race window exists between principal creation and attachment; AWS-managed Identity Center roles cannot get boundaries; existing boundaries are not handled.
    • Scope: A design pattern with placeholder role names, not a fully tested implementation.

    Takeaway: If workloads run in your payer account, deploy an auto-enforced permission boundary protecting CloudTrail, Organizations, root and billing actions, and move workloads out where possible.

  • Confidential computing at 1Password
    summary

    TL;DR: 1Password explains how it uses AWS Nitro Enclaves to process some decrypted secrets server-side while aiming to keep end-to-end encryption guarantees.

    • Problem: E2EE limits features; enterprise vault-usage reports are too large to decrypt and aggregate on-device.
    • Approach: Confidential computing runs plaintext processing in hardware-isolated enclaves shielded from the OS, cloud provider and 1Password operators.
    • Current use: Powers detailed reporting in 1Password Extended Access Management; other features are under development without a timeline.
    • Attestation: Each Nitro Enclave produces a signed attestation document proving what code it runs.
    • Transparency: Every enclave release is published to Sigstore’s Rekor log so auditors can verify every version that ran.
    • Channel: Clients connect via the Noise Protocol, using a public key trusted through attestation.
    • Client enforcement: Apps refuse enclaves whose code is not signed by 1Password and logged in Rekor.
    • Implementation: Written in Rust, reusing client crypto and safe-logging libraries; an external audit reported zero major vulnerabilities.
    • Caveats: Applies only to certain secrets; trust rests on AWS Nitro and Rekor; auditor unnamed and deeper technical docs promised later.

    Takeaway: When evaluating vendors that process secrets server-side, ask for enclave attestation, a public transparency log and client-side verification rather than trusting policy claims.

  • Avoiding Mistakes with AWS OIDC Integration Conditions
    summary

    TL;DR: Wiz reviews 24 SaaS vendors’ AWS OIDC integration docs and shows that missing aud or sub trust-policy conditions can let any vendor customer assume your role.

    • Root cause: IAM role trust policies for OIDC providers often lack conditions, so anyone authenticating to the same vendor can assume the role.
    • History: In 2023 researchers found GitHub Actions roles without sub; AWS now blocks creating such GitHub policies, but old ones may remain.
    • Spread: The same flaw appeared in Terraform Cloud, Microsoft Defender and GitLab integrations.
    • Shared values: GitHub Actions, Gitpod, Harness, Shisho and Upbound use sts.amazonaws.com as aud, which restricts nothing by itself.
    • Odd vendors: Microsoft Defender relies on sts:RoleSessionName; DoIT uses aws:RequestTag/DoitEnvironment; Env0 adds aws:RequestTag custom claims.
    • Partial guidance: GitLab, Bitbucket, DVC and OpenShift recommend only sub; Teleport, DoIT and sandboxes.cloud recommend only aud.
    • EKS: OIDC providers should also check aud (sts.amazonaws.com) and sub, though aud is often omitted.
    • Tools: IAM Access Analyzer warns about missing condition keys; broad StringLike on sub can still admit every repo and branch.
    • Caveats: Based on public docs only; some vendors publish none, and customer-specific provider URLs reduce risk.

    Takeaway: Audit every OIDC-trusting IAM role for both aud and a tight sub condition, verify which values are truly unique to you, and run Access Analyzer.

  • Securing Grafana on Kubernetes with GCP IAP, Gateway API, and Terraform
    summary

    TL;DR: A Terraform-driven guide to putting Grafana on Kubernetes behind GCP Identity-Aware Proxy with Gateway API, using IAP’s signed JWT as Grafana’s only login path.

    • Why: IAP reduces exposure to Grafana CVEs and adds context-aware access, DDoS protection and audit logging.
    • Architecture: User to IAP to a GCP load balancer from the Gateway to the Grafana service on port 80 in monitoring; PostgreSQL backs Grafana.
    • IAP wiring: A GCPBackendPolicy enables IAP with OAuth secret grafana-oauth-secret; a separate grafana-gateway chart covers limited Helm route support.
    • JWT auth: auth.jwt reads X-Goog-Iap-Jwt-Assertion, verifies against Google JWKs, requires iss of https://cloud.google.com/iap, and maps the email claim.
    • Lockdown: disable_login_form: true, auth.google disabled, sign-up off, new users get Viewer, skip_org_role_sync: true.
    • Terraform: helm_release for chart 8.8.1 (Grafana 11.4.0), google_iap_client, and google_iap_web_backend_service_iam_member granting roles/iap.httpsResourceAccessor to a group.
    • Workaround: The backend service name is GCP-generated, so it is parsed from the networking.gke.io/backend-services annotation matching monitoring-grafana-80.
    • Manual steps: OAuth consent screen (Internal) once per project; re-apply if the annotation is not yet present.
    • Caveats: API and Grafana Terraform provider access must bypass IAP via internal network or port-forward; admin recovery is manual; propagation takes minutes.

    Takeaway: Front internal dashboards with IAP and trust only its verified JWT header, but plan a break-glass admin path and expect the brittle backend-service lookup.

  • Passkeys: They’re Not Perfect but They’re Getting Better
    summary

    TL;DR: The UK NCSC says passkeys are the future of authentication and worth using now, but unresolved usability, recovery and standards gaps block recommending them for mass adoption.

    • Problem: Most cyber harm to citizens involves abuse of legitimate credentials via phishing or weak and reused passwords.
    • Benefits: Passkeys cannot be guessed or phished and are unique per site.
    • Numbers: Microsoft data shows about 8 seconds per passkey sign-in versus 69 seconds for password plus second factor.
    • User issues: Device-bound versus synced passkeys confuse users; device loss, vendor migration and inconsistent terminology remain hard.
    • Recovery risk: Attackers may shift to weak account recovery and reset flows, including phishing recovery keys.
    • Access gaps: Shared devices, people without personal devices and those for whom biometrics fail lack private credential manager access.
    • Relying parties: Multi-domain services may need several passkeys; no consensus on assurance level or whether passkeys count as MFA.
    • NCSC plans: Work with FIDO and vendors, explore passkeys for GOV.UK One Login, review GPG 44, and later push passkeys as default.
    • Caveats: NCSC guidance still defaults to password plus factor; the timing figure is Microsoft’s, not independently tested.

    Takeaway: Offer passkeys as an option now, but harden account recovery first, since it becomes the weakest link once phishing of passwords stops working.

  • mise: Dev Tools, Env Vars and Task Runner
    summary

    TL;DR: mise is a single CLI that installs per-project dev tools, sets environment variables and runs tasks from one committed mise.toml, across shell, editor and CI.

    • Tools: Installs Node.js, Python, Terraform and more from a registry of 1,000+ tools, with different versions per project.
    • Environment: Sets per-project env vars and loads .env files.
    • Tasks: Runs build or test tasks defined in [tasks.*] with the project’s tools and env applied.
    • Bootstrap: mise bootstrap can declare and apply system packages, dotfiles, repositories and services for a whole machine.
    • Install: curl https://mise.run | sh puts the binary in ~/.local/bin; Windows uses winget install jdx.mise.
    • Usage: mise exec node@24 -- node --version runs once without config; mise use node@24 writes mise.toml; mise run hello runs a task.
    • Activation: Optional mise activate hook for bash, zsh or fish updates PATH and env on directory change; mise doctor diagnoses setup.
    • Config: Project mise.toml, global ~/.config/mise/config.toml, and mise.lock for exact versions.
    • Caveats: node = "24" is a series, not an exact pin, so use the lockfile; MIT licensed.

    Takeaway: Commit a mise.toml plus mise.lock so local shells and CI share identical tool versions, and prefer that over the curl | sh install on managed hosts.

  • How AI Enhances Static Application Security Testing (SAST)
    summary

    TL;DR: GitHub explains how it pairs CodeQL with Copilot to model library sources and sinks and auto-generate fixes for SAST alerts directly in pull requests.

    • Problem: Shift-left moved security work onto developers without better tools; roughly one security expert per 100 developers.
    • Survey: In a 2023 GitHub survey, developers ranked fixing vulnerabilities (31%) second only to writing code (32%).
    • Source/sink modeling: GitHub experiments with AI to model open source frameworks for CodeQL, since manual modeling is laborious; no accuracy figures given.
    • Autofix: Code scanning autofix shows an AI fix, codebase-specific explanation and diff in the PR to accept, edit or dismiss.
    • Pipeline: CodeQL taint analysis feeds the alert, query help and data-flow snippets into a constrained prompt producing before/after Markdown.
    • Guardrails: Filters output matching about 150 characters of public code; checks syntax, name resolution and types, and validates dependencies against registries and malware data.
    • Numbers: Fixes for more than 90% of vulnerability types; over two-thirds mergeable with little or no edits.
    • Languages: JavaScript, TypeScript, Python, Java, C# and Go first, with C++ and Ruby planned.
    • Caveats: Vendor-written with no independent evaluation or false-positive data; about a third of fixes still need real edits.

    Takeaway: Enable CodeQL autofix to cut alert-to-fix time, but keep human review on every suggested patch and dependency change.

  • How We Built an AppSec AI That Security Researchers Agree with 96% of the Time
    summary

    TL;DR: Semgrep explains how it benchmarked and tuned its LLM-based Assistant Autotriage until it matched its security researchers on 96% of true-positive SAST findings.

    • Problem: SAST backlogs are huge; 100,000 findings at 15 minutes each would keep 3 people busy around the clock for about a year.
    • How it works: Each finding gets a binary verdict, likely true or false positive, using rule metadata, prior triage, rule examples, Assistant Memories and RAG-supplied dataflow context.
    • Outputs: True positives get a fix and remediation steps as a PR comment or Jira ticket; false positives are auto-tagged and the developer is notified.
    • Benchmark: Over 2,000 researcher-triaged findings, evaluated with promptfoo across gpt-4o, gpt-4o-mini and claude-3-5-sonnet; gpt-4o gave the best balance.
    • Numbers: Initial agreement was about 55% overall (91% true positive, 25% false positive); final was 96% true positive and 41% false positive.
    • Techniques: Prompt refinement and feeding the rule confidence value made Assistant disagree more with low-confidence rules.
    • Design choice: Tuned deliberately to minimize false negatives; improving false-positive detection tended to cost true-positive accuracy.
    • Caveats: Agreement is measured against Semgrep’s own researchers and dataset; Assistant sees only the dataflow trace, not the whole project, and never closes findings.

    Takeaway: When adopting AI triage, benchmark it against your own labelled findings and keep suppressed findings in a backlog that AppSec still reviews.

  • A Commencement Into Real Kubernetes Security
    summary

    (Could not fetch full text.)

    TL;DR: Slide deck for the ShmooCon 2025 talk by Mark Manning and Jay Beale, “A Commencement into Real Kubernetes Security”; slide contents could not be read.

    • Source: The Canva page exposes only the title “SHMOOCON 2025 Presentation - Manning and Beale”; slides render client-side.
    • Talk: The ShmooCon schedule lists “A Commencement into Real Kubernetes Security” by Jay Beale and Mark Manning, Saturday 11 January 2025.
    • Thesis (abstract): Practical demos challenge common assumptions about how Kubernetes security works.
    • Content (abstract): Real-world exploits against a hardened, compliant cluster and new bypasses of runtime security tools.
    • Scale question (abstract): Asks whether Kubernetes security controls can scale.
    • Tools: Covers new features in the open-source KubeHound and Peirates tools; Beale is the architect of Peirates and the Bustakube CTF cluster.
    • Deliverable (abstract): A roadmap for assessing Kubernetes security in an organization and advice on where to prioritize effort.

    Takeaway: Do not treat a compliant cluster as secure; test runtime detections against bypasses and try KubeHound and Peirates in your own assessments.

  • AWS EKS Access Management & Permissions
    summary

    TL;DR: A comparison of the four overlapping EKS auth mechanisms that recommends EKS Pod Identities plus RoleBindings for a platform cluster that manages pods in a separate workload cluster.

    • Problem: AWS permissions (pods changing AWS resources) and Kubernetes permissions (managing K8s objects, even cross-cluster) are separate needs that are often confused.
    • aws-auth (2018): A ConfigMap in kube-system maps IAM principals to RBAC in one cluster only; it is deprecated and gives pods no AWS access.
    • IRSA (2019): OIDC provider plus service account annotations; flexible and cross-cluster, but heavy to configure, with a 100 OIDC providers per account limit and trust policy size limits.
    • Pod Identities (2023): Generic trust on pods.eks.amazonaws.com allowing sts:AssumeRole and sts:TagSession, so one role can be reused across clusters unchanged.
    • Setup: Create role and least-privilege policy, install the pod-identity add-on, then add aws_eks_pod_identity_association with cluster, namespace, service account and role ARN.
    • Gotcha: Pod Identities does not create the service account; you create it and bind its Kubernetes permissions yourself.
    • Cluster Access Management (2023): Access entries and access policies map AWS principals to K8s rights and let you revoke the cluster creator’s cluster-admin.
    • Limits: The 15 AWS-managed access policies such as AmazonEKSClusterAdminPolicy cannot be customized; granular access needs groups on the access entry plus your own RoleBindings.

    Takeaway: For new EKS workloads, use Pod Identities for AWS permissions and explicit RoleBindings for Kubernetes permissions, and plan to retire aws-auth.

  • well-architected-iac-analyzer: Evaluate IaC and Architecture Diagrams Against AWS Well-Architected Best Practices
    summary

    TL;DR: An AWS sample app that uses Amazon Bedrock to review IaC templates and architecture diagrams against Well-Architected best practices and produce prioritized recommendations.

    • Inputs: CloudFormation YAML/JSON, Terraform .tf, CDK in any language, ZIP projects, PNG/JPEG diagrams, and up to 5 PDFs of 4.5MB each.
    • How it works: Best practices from Well-Architected whitepapers sync to a Bedrock Knowledge Base; the default model is global.anthropic.claude-sonnet-5-5.
    • Features: Eisenhower-matrix prioritization of “Not Applied” practices, CSV export, a chatbot, WA Tool integration and IaC generation from diagrams.
    • Lenses: Core framework plus industry and technology lenses such as Serverless, Generative AI and Container Build; custom lenses can be built from PDFs.
    • Architecture: React frontend and backend on ECS Fargate behind an ALB, Cognito or OIDC auth, S3 Vectors (default) or OpenSearch Serverless, DynamoDB and S3.
    • Setup: Deploy iac-analyzer-deployment-stack.yaml via CloudFormation (about 15-20 minutes), or run ./deploy-wa-analyzer.sh -r <region> -c docker.
    • Numbers: Parallel BatchSize 1-30 (default 5); claims up to 80% faster reviews and up to 80% lower vector cost versus OpenSearch Serverless.
    • Limits: Non-production sample, now maintained mainly for security patches; batch sizes above 12 usually need higher Bedrock quotas.
    • Caveats: The ALB is public by default; disabling auth exposes the app, and the global inference profile routes data worldwide.

    Takeaway: Useful for a quick Well-Architected pass over IaC in a sandbox account; keep auth enabled and use a regional inference profile if data residency matters.

  • THE RISK YOU CAN’T AFFORD TO IGNORE: AWS SES AND EMAIL SPOOFING
    summary

    TL;DR: Verifying a whole domain in AWS SES lets anyone with SES send rights spoof any address in that domain, and SES does not log sent mail by default.

    • Root cause: A verified domain identity allows sending from any address on that domain, unlike email identities that allow only confirmed addresses.
    • Who can abuse it: Holders of SES SMTP credentials, or IAM principals with ses:SendEmail or ses:SendRawEmail on the domain identity.
    • Deliverability: Because AWS acts as the domain’s mail server, the author estimates “99.9+%” inbox delivery; the figure is unsourced.
    • Logging gap: SES sends are not logged by default; auditing needs SNS notifications routed to S3, for example via Kinesis Data Firehose, at extra cost.
    • Classification: Sits between CSPM (missing logging) and CIEM (identities can impersonate users); SES is outside benchmarks such as CIS.
    • Mitigation 1: Prefer individually verified email identities; a Custom MAIL FROM domain resolves the DMARC concern that pushed teams to domain verification.
    • Mitigation 2: Attach a Sending Authorization policy that denies ses:SendEmail and ses:SendRawEmail unless ses:FromAddress matches an allowlist.
    • Caveats: No test data is provided, and SPF and DKIM are not discussed.

    Takeaway: Audit SES for verified domain identities, restrict ses:FromAddress with a sending authorization policy, and turn on SES event logging.

  • Advanced Nginx Hardening
    summary

    (Could not fetch full text.)

    TL;DR: A short Medium post by Jens@Fivesec sharing nginx hardening notes; the article body was blocked, so its specific techniques could not be verified.

    • Source: Medium returned HTTP 403 to every fetch, and the post was not in the author’s RSS feed.
    • Author: Published under the Medium handle @js_9757, which the feed names Jens@Fivesec.
    • Context: The author shared it in an r/cybersecurity thread in February 2025 as a few nginx hardening notes.
    • Reader feedback: One commenter suggested adding brotli to the gzip section.
    • Reader feedback: Another point raised was the security trade-offs of TCP Fast Open, implying the post covers it.
    • Unverified: No directives, configs or tools from the post could be confirmed.

    Takeaway: Read the original before reusing any of its config; check compression and TCP Fast Open settings against your own threat model.

  • Connect Your On-Premises Kubernetes Cluster to AWS APIs Using IAM Roles Anywhere
    summary

    TL;DR: AWS walkthrough for giving on-premises Kubernetes pods short-lived AWS credentials via IAM Roles Anywhere, cert-manager and AWS Private CA, with no long-term access keys.

    • Problem: Long-term IAM keys need rotation and tracking, and service account issuer discovery requires a publicly reachable API server.
    • How it works: Pods exchange X.509 certificates for temporary credentials through the IAM Roles Anywhere CreateSession API, signed with SigV4a.
    • CA: AWS Private CA in SHORT_LIVED_CERTIFICATE mode issues certificates valid for 7 days or fewer and backs the trust anchor onprem-k8s-issuer.
    • cert-manager: v1.16.2 with cert-manager-approver-policy, cert-manager-csi-driver for per-pod ephemeral certs, and aws-privateca-issuer providing AWSPCAIssuer.
    • Sidecar: aws_signing_helper serve exposes an IMDSv2-compatible endpoint on port 9911, so application images stay unchanged.
    • Least privilege: Trust policies on rolesanywhere.amazonaws.com are scoped by aws:PrincipalTag/x509Subject/CN and trust anchor ARN; use one role and profile per workload.
    • Bootstrap: The issuer’s first certificate is made manually with openssl, then replaced by a 168h cert renewed 24h before expiry.
    • Caveats: The aws-privateca-issuer Helm chart must be rendered and edited by hand to add the sidecar; not meant for EKS, which should use IRSA or Pod Identity.
    • Hardening: Revocation works through CRL checks, and the post advises a hardened base image instead of plain Alpine.

    Takeaway: For hybrid clusters, replace static AWS keys with short-lived certificate-based credentials, scoped per workload through CN conditions.

  • Four Ways to Grant Cross-Account Access in AWS
    summary

    TL;DR: AWS explains four ways to write resource-based policies for cross-account access and the trade-off each makes between granularity and availability.

    • Baseline: Cross-account access needs both an identity-based policy in the caller’s account and a resource-based policy on the target resource.
    • Method 1, role ARN in Principal: Most granular, but IAM stores the role’s unique ID, so a deleted and recreated role silently loses access.
    • Method 2, account in Principal: Account ID or :root ARN (which does not mean the root user); survives role recreation but delegates decisions to the other account’s admins.
    • Method 3, account plus aws:PrincipalArn: An ArnEquals condition pins one role yet survives recreation, because conditions are not converted to unique IDs.
    • Method 3 caveat: Any future role with the same name in that account will also match.
    • Method 4, organization: Principal "*" plus aws:PrincipalOrgId, since an organization cannot be named as a principal.
    • Owner exclusion: Adding StringNotEquals on aws:PrincipalAccount against ${aws:ResourceAccount} forces same-account principals to also need an identity-based allow.
    • Choosing: Use Method 1 when you own both accounts’ role lifecycles, Method 3 when you do not, and Method 4 for organization-wide sharing.

    Takeaway: Prefer aws:PrincipalArn conditions over role ARNs in Principal when IaC may recreate roles, and audit resource policies regularly.

  • I Want You to Hack AWS: Cloud Penetration Testing for Traditional Hackers | Nick Frichette
    summary

    (Could not fetch full text.)

    TL;DR: Nick Frichette’s roughly 35-minute Black Hills Infosec talk introducing AWS penetration testing to traditional hackers; summary is based on the video description only, no transcript.

    • Talk: “I Want You to Hack AWS: Cloud Penetration Testing for Traditional Hackers”, published 5 March 2025 on the Black Hills Infosec channel.
    • Problem: AWS adds many new attack surfaces, but exploiting them often needs niche knowledge of arcane configurations.
    • Framing: Covers the AWS shared responsibility model and where the pentester fits in it.
    • Fundamentals: Walks through the basics of AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM).
    • Attack surface: Examines important classes of AWS misconfigurations.
    • Tradecraft: Discusses techniques for avoiding detection during engagements.
    • Audience: Aimed at pentesters new to AWS and experienced cloud hackers wanting practical, engagement-ready skills.

    Takeaway: Watch it as an IAM-first primer before an AWS engagement, and use its detection-evasion topics to check what your own monitoring would miss.

  • Ephemeral values in Terraform
    summary

    TL;DR: HashiCorp explains Terraform 1.11 ephemeral values, which let secrets flow through a run without being written to the plan or state file.

    • Problem: Before ephemerality, sensitive values were always persisted to plan and state, so state had to be treated as secret.
    • Ephemeral resources: Temporary resources that read a secret or open a connection; their attributes can be referenced but are never persisted.
    • Lifecycle: Ephemeral resources are opened when needed, renewed if they outlive remote expiry, and closed after dependent work; not every resource implements renew or close.
    • Write-only arguments: Provider-implemented arguments such as password_wo or data_json_wo that are never stored in plan or state.
    • Change detection: Each write-only argument pairs with a stored version argument, such as password_wo_version, which you bump to push a new value.
    • Example: ephemeral "random_password" writes to Vault via data_json_wo, is read back ephemerally, and is fed to aws_db_instance password_wo.
    • Ordering: Ephemeral resources with unknown inputs are deferred to apply; ones that managed resources depend on are opened first.
    • Caveats: They run on every plan and apply; a newly generated ephemeral secret is lost unless written to a secrets manager.

    Takeaway: On Terraform 1.11+, move database passwords and tokens to ephemeral resources and write-only arguments, and manage version arguments to trigger rotations.

  • IssueOps: Automate CI/CD (and more!) with GitHub Issues and Actions
    summary

    TL;DR: GitHub’s guide to IssueOps: driving automation such as approvals and team changes from issue forms, comments and labels, modelled as a state machine in GitHub Actions.

    • Concept: Issues, comments, labels and PRs act as triggers and audit trail for Actions workflows; anything with an API can be automated this way.
    • State machine: Requests move through opened, submitted, approved, denied and closed, with events, guards and actions on each transition.
    • Guards: Comment commands such as .submit, .approve and .deny; approve and deny check that the commenter is in the admins team.
    • Example: A team-membership issue form is parsed to JSON by issue-ops/parser, validated with Octokit teams.getByName, then the user is added on approval.
    • Tools: issue-ops/validator, issue-ops/labeler, actions/github-script, actions/create-github-app-token and peter-evans/create-or-update-comment.
    • Auth: A GitHub App via ISSUEOPS_APP_ID and ISSUEOPS_APP_PRIVATE_KEY reaches resources outside the repo.
    • Safety: Workflows declare minimal permissions, re-validate the body on submit, and reset labels when an issue is reopened.
    • Caveat: One trigger type such as issue_comment serves many events, so every workflow must check comment content.

    Takeaway: IssueOps gives self-service with an audit trail; enforce admin checks in guards, re-validate input at each step, and start with a small workflow.

  • Understanding RCPs and SCPs in AWS: Choosing the Right Policy for your Security Needs
    summary

    TL;DR: Fog Security compares AWS Resource Control Policies and Service Control Policies and explains when to use each, or both layered, across an organization.

    • Core idea: SCPs limit what your principals can do; RCPs limit what can be done to your resources, including by outside principals.
    • History: SCPs date from early 2017; RCPs were released in late 2024.
    • RCP coverage: Only S3, STS, KMS, SQS and Secrets Manager, extending to IAM role trust via sts:AssumeRole and DynamoDB via KMS.
    • Numbers: Both cap documents at 5,120 characters and 5 attachments per entity; 2,000 SCPs and 1,000 RCPs per organization.
    • Use RCPs for: Standardizing resource policies, saving SCP space, and NotResource, which SCPs do not support.
    • Use SCPs for: Services outside the RCP list and NotAction, which RCPs do not support, such as locking admin accounts to iam:* and sts:*.
    • Migration example: Moving an S3 KMS-encryption deny from SCP to RCP needs "Principal": "*" and changes who is covered inside and outside the org.
    • Hardening: Add confused deputy protection with aws:SourceAccount or aws:SourceOrgID.
    • Caveats: NotResource and NotAction logic is easy to get wrong; test organization policies carefully.

    Takeaway: Add RCPs to block external access to S3, KMS, STS, SQS and Secrets Manager, and keep SCPs for principal-side guardrails.

  • A Hard Look at GuardDuty Shortcomings
    summary

    TL;DR: Tracebit tests Amazon GuardDuty and finds narrow service coverage, unpredictable cost, and zero alerts for common data-exfiltration techniques, arguing for canary resources alongside it.

    • Coverage: Covers about ten services such as EC2, EKS, Lambda, RDS and S3, out of nearly 250 AWS services, with 176 finding types.
    • Cost: Billed on CloudTrail, VPC Flow Logs, DNS, EKS audit and S3 data event volume; one S3 Protection bill rose from $2.5k to $6.5k per month.
    • Efficacy: Static severity ignores resource sensitivity, Low findings are noisy, and ML struggles with low-volume, high-impact theft.
    • Stratus Red Team test: Six exfiltration techniques, including Secrets Manager mass reads and shared EBS or RDS snapshots, produced zero alerts.
    • guardduty-tester: 11 of 12 runs worked; Recon:EC2/Portscan, Recon:IAMUser/TorIPCaller and PenTest:S3/KaliLinux never fired.
    • Latency: Median detection took 15 minutes; the best was 5:08 for UnauthorizedAccess:S3/MaliciousIPCaller.Custom.
    • Blast radius: With s5cmd at 316 MB/s and 1,781 deletes/s, an attacker could move about 1.3 TB before the fastest alert.
    • Caveats: Small informal tests by one author; the vendor sells canary infrastructure, so the conclusions favor its product.

    Takeaway: Keep GuardDuty on, but do not rely on it for data exfiltration; add canary credentials and resources and forecast add-on costs during the trial.

  • New Vulnerability in GitHub Copilot and Cursor: How Hackers Can Weaponize Code Agents
    summary

    TL;DR: Pillar Security’s “Rules File Backdoor” hides invisible-Unicode instructions in AI assistant rule files so Cursor and GitHub Copilot silently generate malicious code.

    • Vector: Rule files such as those in .cursor/rules steer code generation, are shared widely, trusted implicitly and rarely reviewed.
    • How it works: Payloads hide in zero-width joiners, bidirectional markers and Unicode tag characters that humans cannot see but models still read.
    • Manipulation: Jailbreak-style storytelling frames the payload as a security requirement and tells the AI not to mention the change.
    • Demo: In Cursor agent mode, “Create a simple HTML only page” produced a script tag loading from an attacker site, with no mention in the reply.
    • Persistence: A poisoned rule file affects every later session for the team, survives forks, and stays invisible in GitHub PR review.
    • Impact: Insecure crypto, auth bypasses, disabled validation, and exfiltration of env vars, credentials and API keys.
    • Vendor response: Cursor (Feb-Mar 2025) and GitHub (Mar 2025) called it user responsibility; GitHub added a hidden-Unicode warning on 1 May 2025.
    • Mitigations: Audit rule files for invisible characters, review AI config like code, and check generated code for unexpected external references.

    Takeaway: Add CI checks that reject hidden Unicode in rule files such as .cursor/rules, and review them as strictly as executable code.

  • MCP (Model Context Protocol): Simply Explained in 5 Minutes
    summary

    TL;DR: Jordan Cutler’s beginner explainer of the Model Context Protocol (MCP): a standard interface that lets LLM clients like Cursor call external tools through adapter servers.

    • Problem: Each third-party API has its own types and patterns, so wiring assistants to Sentry, Slack, JIRA or Gmail is tedious.
    • Core idea: MCP makes providers expose tools through one standard interface; the author frames servers as the adapter pattern.
    • Components: An MCP client (e.g. Cursor) speaks the protocol; MCP servers wrap third-party APIs and translate requests into real API calls.
    • How it works: The Slack server defines tools (name, description, inputSchema), creates the server, and handles CallToolRequestSchema with a switch on tool name.
    • Transport: Client and server talk over standard I/O via StdioServerTransport, not HTTP.
    • Examples: AgentDesk BrowserTools MCP let Cursor read console logs and fix a tooltip bug; Puppeteer MCP let Cursor drive a browser.
    • Setup: Create .cursor/mcp.json, add a command like npx -y @modelcontextprotocol/server-puppeteer, enable it in settings; Slack needs SLACK_BOT_TOKEN and SLACK_TEAM_ID.
    • Limits: Setup grows harder with extra API keys and permissions; the article does not cover security, credential protection or scoping tool access.

    Takeaway: Use this as a mental model of MCP, then separately assess the tokens and permissions each server holds, since the article skips that entirely.

  • Effectively Implementing Resource Control Policies in a Multi-Account Environment
    summary

    TL;DR: AWS Security Blog guide to rolling out Resource Control Policies (RCPs) across an AWS Organization in five phases, with an sts:AssumeRole org-perimeter example and exception patterns.

    • What RCPs are: Coarse-grained, always-on resource boundaries attached to the root, OUs or accounts; not for fine-grained least privilege.
    • Control objectives: Data perimeters, cross-service confused deputy mitigation, and identity-independent rules such as requiring TLS 1.2+ for S3.
    • Five phases: Examine objectives, design guardrails and exceptions, anticipate impact, implement via CI/CD, then monitor continuously.
    • Core policy: Deny sts:AssumeRole for Principal: "*" using StringNotEqualsIfExists on aws:PrincipalOrgID and BoolIfExists on aws:PrincipalIsAWSService false.
    • Exceptions: Exclude accounts with aws:ResourceAccount, tagged roles with aws:ResourceTag/partner-access-exception plus aws:PrincipalAccount, or ARNs via NotResource.
    • Tag governance: A companion SCP restricts who can change the exception tag (aws:TagKeys, aws:PrincipalArn) and blocks passing it as a session tag.
    • Impact analysis: Use IAM Access Analyzer for externally shared roles and query CloudTrail with Athena for STS calls from outside the org.
    • Deployment: CloudFormation AWS::Organizations::Policy in pipelines or Control Tower customizations (rcp deploy method); test in lower OUs, roll out in waves.
    • Caveats: Overly strict RCPs break partner integrations; tag exceptions are only as strong as tag governance; uncovered services need separate controls.

    Takeaway: Analyze external STS access with Access Analyzer and CloudTrail first, then ship an org-perimeter RCP through IaC in waves, locking down exception tags with an SCP.

  • Master Architecture Decision Records (ADRs): Best Practices for Effective Decision-Making
    summary

    TL;DR: AWS ProServe engineers share ten practices for running Architecture Decision Records (ADRs), drawn from 200+ ADRs over 3+ years on teams from under 10 to about 100 people.

    • Problem: Teams lose 20-30% of time coordinating across teams, per the authors’ experience, causing slow delivery and repeated refactoring.
    • Meetings: Keep ADR reviews to 30-45 minutes, readout style: 10-15 minutes silent reading with written comments.
    • Participants: Cross-functional but lean; keep attendees under 10 even on large projects.
    • Scope: One decision per ADR; explore alternatives in a separate design document referenced from the ADR.
    • Feedback: Resolve every comment by editing or reaching consensus; the author owns the document.
    • Timeliness: Expect 1-3 readouts; if more, narrow scope or cut invitees; most decisions are reversible “two-way doors”.
    • Lifecycle: Treat accepted ADRs as “team law”; when superseded, link the new ADR from the old one; store centrally.
    • Adoption: Pilot with one team, use clear templates, track time to decision, rework reduction and team satisfaction.
    • Caveats: Experience-based, no controlled data; irreversible decisions may need more deliberation than suggested.

    Takeaway: Adopt a single-decision ADR template with timeboxed silent-read reviews under 10 people, and keep superseded ADRs linked in one shared repo.

  • Patterns and Techniques for Writing High-Performance Applications with Go
    summary

    TL;DR: The Go Optimization Guide is a free, benchmark-driven series on making production Go services faster, covering memory, concurrency, networking and per-version runtime performance.

    • Approach: Emphasizes measured results over folklore and explains what the runtime does and where costs come from.
    • Memory patterns: Object pooling, preallocation, struct field alignment, avoiding interface boxing, zero-copy, GC behavior, escape analysis and stack allocation.
    • Concurrency patterns: Worker pools, atomics and sync primitives, lazy initialization, immutable data sharing and context management.
    • Nuance: Recommends sync.Pool only “where it actually helps, not everywhere”.
    • Networking: net/http, net.Conn, UDP, 10K+ concurrent connections, GOMAXPROCS with epoll/kqueue tuning, TCP vs HTTP/2 vs gRPC, QUIC with quic-go.
    • Operations: Profiling with pprof, load testing, socket options, DNS and TLS tuning, leak prevention in long-lived connections.
    • Version tracking: 76 benchmarks across Go 1.24-1.27 with an interactive tool comparing deltas by category.
    • Benchmark setup: Linux amd64 (Ice Lake), Linux arm64 (Graviton3) and macOS arm64 on dedicated EC2 with variance retry logic.
    • Source: Personal project in astavonin/go-optimization-guide, built with Material for MkDocs.

    Takeaway: Profile with pprof first, then consult the matching pattern and the version-tracking benchmarks before tuning Go services or upgrading Go versions.

  • awesome-mcp-servers: A Collection of MCP Servers
    summary

    TL;DR: punkpeye/awesome-mcp-servers is a large curated GitHub list of production and experimental Model Context Protocol servers, organized by category and synced with Glama’s web directory.

    • Purpose: Catalogs MCP servers that give AI tools file access, database connections, API integrations and other context.
    • Scale: About 96.8k stars, 18.3k forks and 13,953 commits at capture; README text exceeds 1.5 million characters.
    • Legend: Icons mark official implementations, language (Python, TypeScript, Go, Rust, C#, Java, C/C++, Ruby), scope and OS.
    • Scope icons: Cloud means the server calls remote APIs; local means it talks to software on your machine; embedded is also flagged.
    • Categories: 50+ sections, including Aggregators, Browser Automation, Cloud Platforms, Databases, Developer Tools, Monitoring, Security and Version Control.
    • Examples: 1mcp/agent merges multiple servers into one; ahujasid/blender-mcp connects assistants to Blender.
    • Related lists: awesome-mcp-clients, awesome-remote-mcp-servers, the glama.ai directory, a Discord and r/mcp.
    • Extras: Translated READMEs in several languages, CONTRIBUTING.md, MIT license; sponsored links appear on the page.
    • Caveat: Inclusion is a listing, not a security review; quality and maintenance vary between servers.

    Takeaway: Use it for discovery, prefer official implementations, and vet any server’s code, permissions and credential handling before connecting it to an agent.

  • awscurl: curl-Like Access to AWS Resources with SigV4 Request Signing
    summary

    TL;DR: awscurl is a curl-like CLI that signs HTTP requests with AWS Signature Version 4, letting you call AWS APIs and IAM-protected endpoints without writing signing code.

    • Problem: Raw curl cannot call SigV4-protected AWS endpoints such as API Gateway with IAM auth, S3 or EC2 query APIs.
    • Install: pip install awscurl, brew install awscurl, or Docker images okigan/awscurl and ghcr.io/okigan/awscurl.
    • Usage: awscurl --service execute-api -X POST -d @request.json https://<prefix>.execute-api.us-east-1.amazonaws.com/<resource>.
    • Credentials: Flags override env vars (AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID, AWS_SESSION_TOKEN), which override ~/.aws/credentials with --profile or AWS_PROFILE.
    • Defaults: --service defaults to execute-api and --region to us-east-1; set both for other services or regions.
    • Curl-like flags: -X, -d, --data-binary, -H, -i, -v, -k, -L, -o and --fail-with-body.
    • Docker: Mount ~/.aws into /root/.aws or pass keys; the README offers a shell alias wrapping this.
    • Alternatives: Go ports (allthings/awscurl, legal90/awscurl) and signing proxies like awslabs aws-sigv4-proxy.
    • Caveat: Forgetting --service signs for the wrong service; passing secrets as flags can leak them into shell history.

    Takeaway: Keep awscurl in your toolbox for testing IAM-authorized API Gateway, OpenSearch or raw AWS APIs, using profiles rather than key flags.

  • github-mcp-server: GitHub’s Official MCP Server
    summary

    TL;DR: GitHub’s official MCP server lets AI agents read code, manage issues and PRs, monitor Actions and query security data, with configurable toolsets and a read-only mode.

    • Remote option: Hosted at https://api.githubcopilot.com/mcp/ for hosts supporting remote MCP, such as VS Code 1.101+, Claude Desktop, Cursor and Windsurf.
    • Local option: Docker image ghcr.io/github/github-mcp-server or a Go binary run with the stdio subcommand.
    • Auth: OAuth browser login (token kept in memory, Docker callback on 127.0.0.1:8085) or GITHUB_PERSONAL_ACCESS_TOKEN, which takes precedence.
    • Default toolsets: context, repos, issues, pull_requests, users; select others via --toolsets or GITHUB_TOOLSETS.
    • Other toolsets: actions, code_security, dependabot, secret_protection, orgs, projects, gists and more; all enables everything.
    • Least privilege: --read-only skips write tools even if named in --tools; README suggests minimal PAT scopes like repo, read:packages, read:org.
    • Enterprise: --gh-host or GITHUB_HOST for GHES and ghe.com; HTTPS required; the remote server does not support GHES.
    • Caveats: Invalid names in --tools stop startup; some hosts like Windsurf need hardcoded tokens in config files.
    • Go module: The v2.0.0 tag is unusable as a module; use a pseudo-version until a fixed release.

    Takeaway: Run it with --read-only, a narrow toolset list and a minimally scoped token, and avoid hosts that force plaintext tokens in config.

  • What Do Hackers Know About Your AWS Account?
    summary

    TL;DR: Plerion argues exposed AWS resources are only exploitable if attackers know their identifiers, and launches Awseye, a free OSINT service mapping publicly discoverable AWS account IDs and resources.

    • Thesis: AWS is API-driven, so attacks need account IDs, ARNs, hostnames or names; attackers collect these while defenders mostly do not.
    • CDK example: Asset buckets follow cdk-{qualifier}-assets-{account_id}-{region} with default qualifier hnb659fds, so knowing account IDs enables takeover research.
    • SQS example: Guessing queue URLs from account IDs plus wordlists across billions of candidates found 209 readable and writable queues.
    • Other examples: ECR policies allowing any AWS account to push or pull, and CloudFront distributions pointing to deleted S3 buckets.
    • Awseye: Enter an account ID to see up to 100 discovered resources, activity status and public exposure; opt-in alerts via a temporary deny-all role.
    • Discovery techniques: Scraping GitHub, NuGet and Pastebin; listing public resources like shared EBS snapshots; guessing names; S3 HTTP HEAD checks.
    • Hostnames tracked: amazonaws.com, on.aws, cloudfront.net, awsapps.com, elasticbeanstalk.com, awsapprunner.com, amplifyapp.com.
    • Rationale: Cites Orca’s 2023 honeypot report of leaked keys used within minutes; defenders rarely build such datasets themselves.
    • Caveats: Vendor content; dataset admitted incomplete, mentions include false positives, and no accuracy metrics are given.

    Takeaway: Look up your account IDs in Awseye, change predictable defaults like the CDK qualifier, and fix resource policies or dangling DNS that only obscurity protects.

  • How to use AWS Resource Control Policies
    summary

    TL;DR: Wiz explains AWS Resource Control Policies (RCPs), the org-wide resource-side counterpart to SCPs that also constrains principals outside your Organization, with example perimeter policies and rollout caveats.

    • What RCPs are: AWS Organizations policies that grant nothing and cap who can access resources, overriding even a bucket policy that makes data public.
    • Supported services: Five at writing: S3, STS, SQS, Secrets Manager and KMS.
    • vs SCPs: SCPs only bind principals in your Organization, so an attacker granting an external account via resource policy bypasses them; RCPs do not.
    • Identity perimeter: Deny sts:AssumeRole unless aws:PrincipalOrgID or a listed aws:PrincipalAccount matches, exempting aws:PrincipalIsAWSService.
    • GitHub OIDC fix: Deny sts:AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity when token.actions.githubusercontent.com:sub is null or not repo:<org>/*, closing wildcard trust policies.
    • Other uses: Enforce TLS 1.2+ on all S3 access once, block external sharing, and deny actions like s3:DeleteObject even to compromised admins.
    • Caveats: No dry-run or audit mode; denials return a generic AccessDenied; RCPs do not follow accounts moved to another OU or Organization.
    • Visibility gaps: Access Analyzer shows who has external access but not how; CloudTrail data events are off by default.
    • Rollout: Review logs first, test in a sandbox, promote dev to staging to production in groups, and review logs after.

    Takeaway: Deploy an RCP blocking AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity from GitHub repos outside your org, after checking Access Analyzer and CloudTrail for legitimate external access.

  • Kube-Policies: Guardrails for Apps Running in Kubernetes
    summary

    TL;DR: Square describes Kube-Policies, its in-house OPA-based Kubernetes admission layer that replaced Pod Security Policies with staged, guardrail-style validating and mutating policies.

    • Problem: Kubernetes defaults favor speed over security, and PSPs and Pod Security Admission did not fit Square’s varied platforms.
    • Alternatives rejected: K-Rail, Gatekeeper and Kyverno each missed some of seven requirements, including dry runs, exceptions and observability.
    • How it works: OPA in server mode evaluates Rego policies behind Kubernetes validating and mutating admission webhooks.
    • Staged modes: Validating policies go monitor, warn (HTTP Warnings header), deny; mutating policies go dry run, then patch.
    • Example policies: Deny privilege escalation, hostIPC and hostNetwork; mutate to readOnlyRootFilesystem, drop capabilities and runAsNonRoot.
    • Testing: Rego unit tests, e2e tests on ephemeral kind clusters checking audit logs, plus opa check --strict, regal and CodeQL.
    • Observability: OPA Prometheus metrics, audit-log annotations and apiserver_admission_webhook_rejection_count; denial spikes flag attacks or bugs.
    • Safety nets: Critical allowlist for aws-node and kube-proxy, a breakglass bypass, and an explicit fail-open vs fail-closed choice.
    • Limits: Policies are baked into the image, so changes need staged rollouts; exceptions need a ticket, PR and two-team approval.

    Takeaway: Roll out admission policies as monitor, warn, then deny, prefer safe mutations, and build breakglass plus system-component allowlists before enforcing.

  • How to Harden GitHub Actions: The Unofficial Guide
    summary

    TL;DR: Wiz’s updated GitHub Actions hardening cheat sheet, revised after tj-actions (2025) and the 2026 trivy-action and Axios attacks, covering settings, workflow pitfalls, secrets and runners.

    • Incidents: tj-actions cascaded from a vulnerable workflow to leaked PATs to poisoned actions; attackers force-pushed 75 of 76 trivy-action tags.
    • Axios: Malicious 1.14.1 and 0.30.4 were live about three hours, via an inserted plain-crypto-js dependency.
    • Pwn requests: pull_request_target and workflow_run run with secrets; checking out fork code is dangerous even after GitHub’s December 2025 change.
    • Injection: Interpolating issue titles, branch names or labels into run: enables command injection; writes to GITHUB_ENV or GITHUB_PATH can inject LD_PRELOAD.
    • Credentials: actions/checkout persists tokens in .git/config that can leak via artifacts; set persist-credentials: false.
    • Third-party actions: Only SHA pinning guarantees the same code; transitive weakly pinned actions still expose you; use SHA-pin enforcement.
    • Cooldowns: Wait 7-14 days before adopting new versions, estimated to catch 80-90% of supply chain attacks; pinact --min-age 7 or Renovate minimumReleaseAge.
    • Settings: Read-only default GITHUB_TOKEN, permissions: {} per workflow, no Actions PR approval, avoid toJson(secrets) and secrets: inherit.
    • Runners: Use ephemeral runners grouped by trust, default-deny egress, never self-hosted on public repos; prefer OIDC and GitHub Apps.

    Takeaway: Run zizmor in CI, SHA-pin actions with a 7-day cooldown, set permissions: {}, and audit every pull_request_target workflow now.

05.10.2024

  • Trail of Bits Testing Handbook
    summary

    TL;DR: The Testing Handbook is a free, CC BY 4.0 guide from Trail of Bits on configuring, optimizing and automating static and dynamic analysis tools, including in CI/CD.

    • Static analysis: Chapters on CodeQL and Semgrep; Trail of Bits also publishes its own Semgrep rules and CodeQL queries for C, C++ and Go.
    • Fuzzing: libFuzzer, AFL++, LibAFL for C/C++, cargo-fuzz for Rust, plus Python and Ruby; covers harness writing, coverage analysis, AddressSanitizer, OSS-Fuzz and snapshot fuzzing.
    • Web: A Burp Suite Professional section with a step-by-step guide and tips on telling bugs from features.
    • Crypto: Wycheproof, constant-time testing (dudect, Timecop) and zero-knowledge protocols.
    • Languages: A C/C++ security checklist (multiple OSes, seccomp/BPF) and a Rust section covering memory zeroization, model checking and supply chain analysis.
    • Roadmap: kAFL and formal verification with Tamarin are listed as upcoming.

    Takeaway: A practical starting point when you need to wire Semgrep, CodeQL or a fuzzer into a pipeline without reading every tool’s docs. Use the chapters as setup recipes.

  • GCPwn: Enumeration and Exploitation Framework for GCP
    summary

    TL;DR: GCPwn is a BSD-3 Google Cloud offensive security framework by Scott (@WebbinRoot) at NetSPI for credential management, enumeration, exploitation and attack-path graphing, with limited Google Workspace coverage.

    • Enumeration: Modules such as enum_gcp, enum_all, enum_iam, enum_cloudstorage, enum_google_workspace and enum_drive.
    • Exploitation: Service account token minting, signed JWTs, SA key creation, setIamPolicy abuse, Cloud Scheduler/Cloud Tasks abuse, Workload Identity Federation and OIDC token capture via API Gateway.
    • Unauthenticated: unauth_* modules, e.g. bucket brute-forcing and API key scope checks.
    • Permission discovery: Tracks call success/failure, runs explicit testIamPermissions checks and analyzes IAM bindings.
    • Graphing: Exports BloodHound OpenGraph JSON; process_og_attack_paths does text-based path finding.
    • Setup: pip install gcpwn, release binaries or Docker; data lands in a local SQLite DB with CSV/JSON/Excel export.
    • Limits: Workspace coverage is limited, Drive download is beta, some exploit modules are “coming soon”, and the author notes parts were written with LLM help and should be reviewed.

    Takeaway: A Pacu-style toolkit for GCP assessments. Use it on authorized projects to map what a compromised credential can reach, and review the code before operational use.

  • fwd:cloudsec North America 2024: Opening Session
    summary

    (Could not fetch full text.)

    TL;DR: The 10-minute opening session of fwd:cloudsec North America 2024, given by Aaron Zollman, a long-time organizer of the conference.

    • Event: fwd:cloudsec 2024 ran June 17-18, 2024 in Arlington, Virginia; the welcome was June 17 at 09:00 in Breakout 1.
    • Milestone: The schedule describes it as the fifth fwd:cloudsec and the first run fully independently of any other security conference.
    • Speaker: Zollman helped run the first fwd:cloudsec, has served in several conference roles (listed as Board President in 2023) and leads security and platform at a health-tech company.
    • Channel: Published on the official fwd:cloudsec YouTube channel, which hosts the rest of the 2024 talks in the same playlist.
    • Source caveat: No transcript or description was available; this is based on YouTube oEmbed metadata, the pretalx schedule entry and Datadog’s conference recap.

    Takeaway: Context only. The value is the playlist it opens: the 2024 fwd:cloudsec talks on AWS, GCP and Kubernetes security.

  • The EKS Hacking Playbook: Lessons from 3 Years of Cloud Security Research
    summary

    (Could not fetch full text.)

    TL;DR: A fwd:cloudsec 2024 talk by Hillai Ben-Sasson and Nir Ohfeld that turns three years of cloud security research into a checklist of what they look for when attacking production Amazon EKS clusters.

    • Premise: EKS is both a Kubernetes cluster and an AWS service, so it inherits risks from both and adds some of its own.
    • Scope: Recurring misconfigurations seen in large organizations, from network configuration to RBAC.
    • Format: For each mistake: how an engineer makes it, how a researcher exploits it, and the real research engagement it came from.
    • Defense: Closes with hunting approaches plus remediation and detection built on existing AWS tooling.
    • Date: Presented June 17, 2024, Breakout 1.
    • Source caveat: No transcript was available; this is based on the abstract (Thinkst Citation/pretalx listing) and YouTube oEmbed metadata. Specific techniques in the talk are not covered here.

    Takeaway: Worth watching if you run EKS: use it as an attacker-perspective review list for network exposure, RBAC and the AWS-IAM-to-Kubernetes boundary.

  • Get into AWS Security Research as a n00bcake
    summary

    (Could not fetch full text.)

    TL;DR: Daniel Grzelak (Plerion, previously Atlassian) at fwd:cloudsec 2024 on how newcomers can start doing their own AWS security research.

    • Message: Getting started in cloud security research does not need to be difficult.
    • Tip - docs: Read AWS documentation looking for security issues that are “as designed” behavior.
    • Tip - public code: Search public code for misconfigurations.
    • Tip - errors: Pay attention to error messages, which leak behavior worth exploring.
    • Style: Datadog’s recap calls it down-to-earth advice with a great sense of humor, drawn from his and others’ experience.
    • Source caveat: No transcript was available; this is based on Datadog Security Labs’ fwd:cloudsec 2024 recap, a Tracebit post and YouTube oEmbed metadata.

    Takeaway: A good on-ramp for anyone who wants to find novel AWS issues rather than repeat known ones. Pair it with Grzelak’s “15 ideas for cloud security research” list.

  • The Path to Zero-Touch Production
    summary

    (Could not fetch full text.)

    TL;DR: Rami McCarthy (formerly Figma infrastructure security) at fwd:cloudsec 2024 on a practical framework for moving a cloud-native company toward Google-style zero-touch production.

    • Goal: Reduce routine human access to production; changes go through automation, safe proxies or audited break-glass.
    • AWS access options: Which production-access mechanisms exist in AWS, when to use each, and how to use them safely.
    • Deep dives: Building just-in-time / temporary access and running operational scripts safely.
    • Maturity model: Slides describe stages from Initial through Foundational, Established and Advanced to Zero Touch Production.
    • Background: The concept traces to Google’s 2019 SREcon EMEA “Zero Touch Prod” talk.
    • Source caveat: No transcript was available; this is based on the pretalx abstract, the Speaker Deck slides listing and YouTube oEmbed metadata.

    Takeaway: Useful roadmap for cutting standing prod access in AWS. Start with JIT access and scripted operations before aiming for full zero-touch.

  • Taking a Look at Kubernetes Profiling
    summary

    TL;DR: Rory McCune looks at Go pprof profiling, which Kubernetes enables by default in several control-plane components, and whether exposing it is a real risk (his answer: it depends).

    • Scope: kube-apiserver, kube-scheduler, kube-controller-manager and kubelet expose profiling by default; kube-proxy does not.
    • Endpoints: /debug/pprof/profile returns profiling data; /debug/flags/v accepts PUT to change log verbosity at runtime.
    • Access control: Control-plane endpoints are gated by RBAC non-resource URL rules; kubelet access is gated by the node/proxy resource.
    • Commands: go tool pprof -http=:8080 http://localhost:8001/debug/pprof/profile and curl -X PUT http://127.0.0.1:8001/debug/flags/v -d "10" via kubectl proxy.
    • Risks: On managed clusters, raising API server log level plus log access could enable CVE-2020-8561 (webhook-based probing of the provider network); traces can also cost control-plane resources.
    • Fix: Set --profiling=false on apiserver, controller-manager and scheduler; set enableDebuggingHandlers off in kubelet config; restrict node/proxy.

    Takeaway: Low-severity but cheap to close. Disable profiling in production and audit who holds node/proxy and non-resource endpoint grants.

  • Stop Worrying About allowPrivilegeEscalation
    summary

    TL;DR: Christophe Tafani-Dereeper explains what the Kubernetes allowPrivilegeEscalation field actually does: it sets the Linux no_new_privs flag, a hardening option and nothing more.

    • Mechanism: false makes runc set no_new_privs (kernel 3.5+) on the container process, so setuid/setgid binaries no longer grant elevated rights. Default is true.
    • Demo: A setuid-root binary calling setreuid(0, 0) lets UID 1000 reach root when the field is true; with false the calls fail.
    • Does not stop: Container escape, cluster-level privilege escalation, or kernel exploits such as DirtyCow or CVE-2023-0386.
    • No effect: On workloads already running as root or with CAP_SYS_ADMIN.
    • Unrelated to privileged: The API server rejects allowPrivilegeEscalation: false combined with privileged: true.
    • Verdict: Leaving the default is one missing hardening layer, not a critical finding; the field’s name is misleading.

    Takeaway: Set it to false as cheap defense in depth, but do not rank scanner findings about it above running as non-root, dropping capabilities and avoiding privileged pods.

  • The CloudSec Engineer: A Career Book on Cloud Security Engineering
    summary

    TL;DR: The CloudSec Engineer is a career book by Marco Lancini (CloudSecList author) on entering and progressing in cloud security engineering.

    • Part I: Choosing infosec and cloud security as a career, and career levels.
    • Parts II-IV: Skills, learning tips and expectations for entering the field, establishing yourself as a senior engineer, and thriving toward Staff+.
    • Part V: Choosing companies, finding jobs, interview preparation and managing offers.
    • Bonus: Templates for side projects, a brag document, reverse interview questions and offer tracking.
    • Format: DRM-free PDF and EPUB, 250+ pages, 1,100+ links, lifetime updates; no print edition.
    • Price: $18 book only, $26 complete package (discount codes listed on the page).

    Takeaway: Aimed at people planning a cloud security career path or preparing for interviews; the free newsletter gives a taste of the author’s style.

  • tfprovidercheck: CLI to Prevent Malicious Terraform Providers from Being Executed
    summary

    TL;DR: tfprovidercheck by Shunsuke Suzuki is a CLI that fails when Terraform loads a provider not on your allow list, to stop malicious providers from executing in CI.

    • How it works: Reads terraform version -json after terraform init and compares loaded providers to the allow list.
    • Usage: terraform version -json | tfprovidercheck -c .tfprovidercheck.yaml, run before validate, plan and apply.
    • Config: YAML providers list with exact name (e.g. registry.terraform.io/hashicorp/aws) and optional version constraint such as ">= 3.0.0"; no glob or regex.
    • Config sources: -c flag, TFPROVIDERCHECK_CONFIG_BODY, TFPROVIDERCHECK_CONFIG, then .tfprovidercheck.yaml.
    • Tamper resistance: Recommends pull_request_target and passing config via TFPROVIDERCHECK_CONFIG_BODY in the workflow so a PR cannot edit the allow list.
    • Why not lock files: .terraform.lock.hcl gets new providers added by init, and required_providers is hard to govern across child modules and monorepos.

    Takeaway: Cheap supply-chain control for Terraform pipelines that run plans on untrusted PRs. Keep the allow list outside the PR’s control.

  • Single Sign-On or Single Point of Failure?
    summary

    TL;DR: A June 2024 Doyensec post by Anthony Trummer introducing research on what happens to infrastructure access when the SSO identity provider is compromised, using Teleport as the access platform.

    • Question: Does SSO put “all our eggs in one proverbial basket”? The research models IdP compromise impact on Teleport-protected infrastructure.
    • Range: Impact scales with privilege, from an unprivileged IdP account (“surprising impacts”) to a fully compromised IdP.
    • Detection: The whitepaper includes guidance on which logs to check for each attack type.
    • Hardening: Teleport hardening recommendations to limit damage in worst-case scenarios, plus a short checklist for teams.
    • Source caveat: The blog post is a summary; techniques, log indicators and specific recommendations are in the linked whitepaper and checklist, not in the post itself.

    Takeaway: Treat the IdP as tier-0. If you front infrastructure access with SSO, read the whitepaper and apply the checklist so one IdP account cannot become root everywhere.

  • Understanding the Risks of Long-Lived Kubernetes Service Account Tokens
    summary

    TL;DR: A GitGuardian article on why long-lived Kubernetes service account tokens stored as Secrets are risky and how to replace them with short-lived TokenRequest tokens.

    • Token types: Legacy SA tokens are Secrets that never expire; TokenRequest API tokens are projected into pods, time-bound and invalidated when the pod is deleted.
    • Leak paths: Shared volumes, unencrypted HTTP, commits to repos, verbose logging, insiders and RCE in the pod.
    • Abuse: Cryptomining, malicious workloads, RBAC changes for escalation, backdoor resources and data theft.
    • Mitigation: Set automountServiceAccountToken: false on the ServiceAccount or Pod when the API is not needed.
    • Policy: A Kyverno ClusterPolicy with a CEL expression rejecting Secrets of type kubernetes.io/service-account-token.
    • Trade-offs: Short-lived tokens need renewal logic, CI/CD changes, expiry error handling and add API calls.

    Takeaway: Disable token automount by default and block creation of legacy token Secrets cluster-wide; workloads that need API access should use projected tokens.

  • Wut.Dev AWS Organization Viewer
    summary

    TL;DR: Wut.Dev AWS Organization Viewer (beta, by Matthew Fuller’s wut.dev) is a browser app for browsing AWS resources and Organization structure in filterable, exportable tables.

    • Setup: Paste an Access Key, Secret Key and Session Token, or JSON from aws sts get-session-token --output json.
    • Client-side: The page states credentials are stored in browser local storage and “never sent to a server”; a Delete All Data button clears them.
    • Org mode: Uses the management account to assume roles into member accounts; a standalone single-account mode also exists.
    • Features: Table view with filter, sort and export; configurable service menu; optional LLM integration with your own endpoint and key.
    • Extras: Opt-in anonymous usage stats (off by default) and Pro license features.
    • Caveats: The page does not list required IAM permissions. The URL now redirects to app.wut.dev/org.

    Takeaway: Handy for a quick visual inventory of an AWS Organization. Use short-lived, read-only credentials since you are pasting them into a web page.

  • River: Fast and Reliable Postgres-Backed Background Jobs in Go
    summary

    TL;DR: River is an MPL-2.0 background job queue originally for Go, backed by Postgres (and now SQLite), built around enqueueing jobs in the same transaction as your application data.

    • Transactional enqueue: Jobs are guaranteed enqueued if the transaction commits and vanish on rollback; workers do not see them before commit.
    • Features: Batch insert via Postgres COPY FROM, multiple queues, periodic/cron and scheduled jobs, unique jobs (by args, period, queue, state), snooze and cancel from inside workers.
    • Reliability: Automatic retries, error and panic handling, transactional job completion.
    • Ops: Subscriptions for logging/metrics, test helpers and a web UI for jobs and queues.
    • Driver: The Go example uses riverpgxv5 with a pgx v5 pool.
    • Languages: The current README lists cross-compatible implementations for Go, JS/TS, Ruby and Rust, plus job insertion from Python.

    Takeaway: If you already run Postgres, River avoids a separate broker and the dual-write problem. Good fit for Go services that need reliable async work.

  • SmoothMQ: Self-Hostable Drop-In Replacement for SQS
    summary

    TL;DR: SmoothMQ is an AGPL-3.0, self-hostable drop-in replacement for AWS SQS shipped as a single Go binary.

    • Compatibility: Works with existing SQS clients by changing only the endpoint URL, e.g. http://localhost:3001; Celery works with an sqs://...@localhost:3001 broker URL.
    • Features: Web UI to manage queues and search individual messages, observability, tracing, message scheduling and rate-limiting.
    • Run: go run . server starts the UI on port 3000 and the SQS API on 3001.
    • Storage: The README does not name the backend; the repo has a queue/sqlite directory, suggesting SQLite.
    • Status: About 2.3k stars at fetch time; the README asks for feedback via a survey and does not state production readiness.

    Takeaway: Useful for local development against SQS or running SQS-style queues off AWS. Check maturity and AGPL obligations before production use.

  • doggo: Command-Line DNS Client for Humans
    summary

    TL;DR: doggo by Karan Sharma is a Go command-line DNS client “for humans”, inspired by Rust’s dog, with colored tabular output and modern encrypted DNS protocols.

    • Protocols: UDP, TCP, DNS over HTTPS (with HTTP/3 via --http3), DNS over TLS, DNS over QUIC and DNSCrypt.
    • Output: Human-readable tables or --json for scripting, e.g. doggo example.com --json | jq '.responses[0].answers[].address'.
    • Debugging: --trace follows the delegation chain; response times shown; EDNS options (ECS, NSID, cookies, padding, extended errors).
    • Examples: doggo MX github.com @9.9.9.9, doggo example.com @https://cloudflare-dns.com/dns-query, doggo --reverse 8.8.8.8 --short.
    • Extras: Globalping queries from other countries (--gp-from Germany,Japan), ndots/search support, IDN punycode, TOML config.
    • Install: Homebrew, many distro package managers, go install github.com/mr-karan/doggo/cmd/doggo@latest, or ghcr.io/mr-karan/doggo.

    Takeaway: A friendlier dig that also tests DoH/DoT/DoQ resolvers. Worth installing for DNS troubleshooting.

  • openstatus: Open-Source Synthetic Monitoring and Status Page Platform
    summary

    TL;DR: openstatus is an AGPL-3.0 open-source platform for synthetic uptime monitoring, status pages and incident response, available hosted or self-hosted.

    • Monitoring: Checks from 28 regions across 3 cloud providers, alerting via Slack, Discord, PagerDuty, email and others.
    • Status pages: Custom domains, password protection, maintenance windows, subscriber notifications by email, RSS and webhooks.
    • Incidents: Declare and resolve from dashboard or Slack, with severity, commander and timeline.
    • As code: Monitors, pages and notification channels defined in YAML or Terraform, applied via CLI or CI.
    • Stack: Next.js dashboard, Hono API, Go checker, Turso with Drizzle, Tinybird analytics.
    • Self-host: docker compose up -d (dashboard on 3002, status pages on 3003), Coolify or a Railway template.

    Takeaway: A self-hostable alternative to Statuspage plus Pingdom-style checks. The Terraform support makes it easy to keep monitors in the same repo as infra.

  • How I Built a Digital Forensics and Incident Response Lab in AWS
    summary

    (Could not fetch full text.)

    TL;DR: A Medium post by Adam Messer describing how he built a digital forensics and incident response (DFIR) practice lab on AWS.

    • Topic: Building a personal cybersecurity DFIR lab environment in AWS rather than on local hardware.
    • Author: Adam Messer, per the Medium URL.
    • Related pattern: AWS Prescriptive Guidance has an automated IR and forensics pattern using separate security and forensics accounts, Lambda, EBS snapshots and S3 for artifacts, with phases of containment, acquisition, examination and analysis; it is not confirmed that the post uses it.
    • Source caveat: Medium returned HTTP 403 and web search did not surface the article text; this summary is based only on the title and URL. No architecture, tools or cost figures from the post could be verified.

    Takeaway: Open the post directly for the build steps. For an AWS-native reference design, the AWS Prescriptive Guidance forensics pattern is a solid baseline.

  • dotenvx: Encrypted .env Files from the Creator of dotenv
    summary

    TL;DR: dotenvx, from the creator of dotenv, is a cross-language CLI and library that encrypts .env files so they can be committed to git and decrypted at runtime.

    • Encryption: secp256k1 public-key crypto; each value is encrypted with AES-256 under an ephemeral key (ECIES). DOTENV_PUBLIC_KEY lives in .env, DOTENV_PRIVATE_KEY in a secrets manager or .env.keys.
    • Commands: dotenvx encrypt, decrypt, run -- <cmd>, get, set KEY value, del, keypair.
    • Environments: -f .env.production with matching DOTENV_PRIVATE_KEY_PRODUCTION; multiple -f files, --overload, and --convention=nextjs.
    • Features: Variable expansion, defaults, command substitution, multiline values, op:// and bw:// references, --redact/--mask output.
    • Install: npm i -g @dotenvx/dotenvx, brew install dotenvx, curl -sfS https://dotenvx.sh | sh, winget or Docker.

    Takeaway: A low-friction upgrade from plaintext .env files. You still have to protect and distribute the private keys, which is the real secret now.

  • Bullfrog: GitHub Action to Block Unauthorized Egress in Workflows
    summary

    TL;DR: Bullfrog is a GitHub Action that audits or blocks outbound network traffic from workflow jobs, allowing only listed domains and IPs.

    • Placement: Must be the first step in every job; traffic before it runs is not seen.
    • Modes: egress-policy: audit (default) logs connections to help build an allow list; block enforces it. Results appear in the job summary.
    • Inputs: allowed-domains (wildcards match subdomains only), allowed-ips, dns-policy (allowed-domains-only default or any).
    • Root bypass: enable-sudo: false stops steps gaining root, since root (or Docker’s daemon) could bypass filtering.
    • Control plane: Optional api-token aggregates results across an org; a free tier is mentioned.
    • Limits: GitHub-hosted Ubuntu runners only (ubuntu-22.04, ubuntu-24.04, ARM variants, ubuntu-slim); container jobs unsupported.

    Takeaway: A simple defense against exfiltration from compromised actions or dependencies. Run audit mode first, then switch to block with sudo disabled.

  • BSidesSF 2024 Talks
    summary

    (Could not fetch full text.)

    TL;DR: The official YouTube playlist of recorded talks from BSidesSF 2024, published by the Security BSides San Francisco channel (@BSidesSF).

    • Event: BSidesSF 2024 took place in San Francisco on May 4-5, 2024, per the call for papers.
    • Content: Recordings of the conference talks, grouped in one playlist on the official channel.
    • Context: tl;dr sec issue 238 linked it alongside other BSidesSF 2024 highlights.
    • Source caveat: YouTube redirected to a consent page, so the video list could not be read; this is based on YouTube oEmbed metadata (title “BSidesSF 2024”, channel Security BSides San Francisco) and the BSidesSF 2024 CFP.

    Takeaway: Browse the playlist for talks relevant to your stack; BSidesSF skews toward practical AppSec, cloud and detection engineering content.

  • Security Engineering at Google: My Interview Study Notes
    summary

    TL;DR: Grace Nolan’s widely shared study notes for security engineering interviews (written for a Google role), covering both technical topics and how to prepare.

    • Networking and web: OSI, DNS, DHCP, ARP, TLS; same-origin policy, CORS, cookies, CSRF, XSS, SQLi, SSRF.
    • Systems: Hypervisors, containers, cloud lateral movement, side channels, privilege escalation, Windows and *nix internals.
    • Crypto and identity: Encoding vs hashing vs signing, key exchange, forward secrecy; certificates, OAuth, Kerberos, MFA/FIDO.
