    • Defense: Threat modelling (STRIDE, DREAD), detection (IDS, SIEM, IOCs), forensics and incident management (PICERL, Google IMAG).
    • Offense: Malware and reversing, exploits, ATT&CK-style attack stages.
    • Coding: Data structures, Big O, Python and security coding exercises such as log parsing and port scanners.
    • Study method: Track terms as To learn/Revising/Done, guess before looking up, spaced repetition, mock interviews and talking through reasoning.

    Takeaway: A solid checklist for any security engineering interview loop. Use it to find gaps, then go deep on the areas the target team cares about.

  • k8s-sniff-https: mitmproxy Blueprint to Intercept HTTPS Traffic from Apps on Kubernetes
    summary

    TL;DR: k8s-sniff-https by Ofir Cohen is a minimal blueprint for running mitmproxy (mitmweb) in a cluster to inspect HTTPS calls that a workload makes to external APIs.

    • Components: A one-replica mitmweb Deployment and Service from deploy/; proxy on 8080, web UI on 8081.
    • CA trust: Copy mitmproxy-ca-cert.pem from /root/.mitmproxy/ in the pod with kubectl cp and give it to the client.
    • Test: An ephemeral curlimages/curl pod sends requests with curl --cacert ... -x mitmweb:8080.
    • UI: kubectl port-forward svc/mitmweb 8081:8081 shows flows, headers and bodies.
    • Limits: Only clients configured to use the proxy and trust the CA are captured; the README does not cover configuring arbitrary apps. Debug tool, not production.

    Takeaway: Quick way to see what a pod actually sends to SaaS APIs during debugging. Remove it afterwards, since it captures decrypted traffic.

  • Moving AWS Accounts and OUs Within an Organization: Not So Simple!
    summary

    TL;DR: Matthew Fuller (wut.dev) explains why moving an AWS account or OU within an Organization is a risky one-call change with no dry run, and what can break.

    • SCPs: Old parent policies stop and new ones apply instantly, e.g. a Production SCP denying s3:GetObject causing AccessDenied.
    • OU path conditions: Policies using aws:PrincipalOrgPaths, aws:ResourceOrgPaths or aws:SourceOrgPaths change behavior; include the org ID in paths because OU IDs are only unique within an org.
    • StackSets: OU-targeted auto-deployment can deploy stacks on arrival; with retention off, stacks (including IAM roles) are deleted on exit.
    • RAM and Control Tower: OU-targeted RAM shares gain or lose access; moving under an enrolled OU can trigger Control Tower enrollment and controls.
    • Reverting: Moving back restores most policy effects, but recreated IAM roles get new AROA IDs that some trusts (e.g. KMS) reference.
    • Checklist: Diff SCPs, list affected StackSets, grep policies for the OrgPaths keys, review RAM shares, check Control Tower; monitor CloudTrail for SCP explicit denies afterwards.

    Takeaway: Treat move-account (and Terraform parent_id changes) as a production change with a pre-flight checklist. Prefer account IDs or full org paths in policies.

  • Top Four Ways to Improve Your Security Hub Security Score
    summary

    TL;DR: An AWS Security Blog post (Priyank Ghedia, Megan O’Neil, July 2024) on four ways to raise the Security Hub security score, which is passed controls divided by enabled controls.

    • Remediate: Fix the failing resource; on recheck the finding becomes PASSED and RESOLVED.
    • Suppress: SUPPRESSED findings are ignored in control status; use automation rules so future matching findings are suppressed too.
    • Disable: Turn off controls that do not apply; central configuration lets a delegated admin manage controls per OU.
    • Customize parameters: Some controls accept custom values that define a pass.
    • AutoScaling.3: Requires IMDSv2 in launch configurations; migrate to launch templates since launch configurations cannot be used for EC2 instance types released after Dec 31, 2022.
    • EC2.18: Flags security groups open to unrestricted TCP/UDP except 80/443; adjust allowed ports via parameters and remove unused groups with Firewall Manager usage audit policies.
    • Source caveat: The fetched text was truncated after two of the five controls discussed.

    Takeaway: Use central configuration and automation rules so the score reflects real risk rather than irrelevant controls, then fix the common Critical/High failures.

  • IAM So Lost: A Guide to Identity in Google Cloud
    summary

    TL;DR: A beginner primer from Google (Sita Lakshmi Sangameswaran, Michele Chubirka, July 2024) on Google Cloud IAM concepts, arguing for persona-based, group-driven access.

    • Concepts: Principals (users, service accounts, groups, Workspace and Cloud Identity accounts), roles, policies, least privilege and separation of duties.
    • Personas: Map job functions such as “platform engineer” to groups, then grant roles to groups, not individuals.
    • Example: A software engineer joins web-app-developer and gets the Cloud Run Developer role.
    • Avoid: Broad basic roles like Editor for everyone.
    • Tooling: IAM policy intelligence tools to migrate toward a group-based model; Architecture Framework security pillar for more.
    • Not covered: Workforce and Workload Identity Federation; no code or config samples.

    Takeaway: Introductory but sound. Build GCP access from org-chart personas and groups so onboarding and audits stay simple.

  • exo: Run Your Own AI Cluster at Home with Everyday Devices
    summary

    TL;DR: exo from exo labs is an Apache-2.0 project that pools everyday devices into one local AI cluster to run models too large for a single machine.

    • Discovery: Nodes find each other automatically on the LAN; EXO_ZENOH_NAMESPACE isolates clusters.
    • Partitioning: Splits models based on each device’s resources and link latency/bandwidth; tensor parallelism claimed at up to 1.8x on 2 devices and 3.2x on 4.
    • RDMA: Over Thunderbolt 5 on macOS 26.2+, claimed 99% lower inter-device latency; requires full mesh cabling and rdma_ctl enable from Recovery.
    • Backend: MLX and MLX distributed; models such as Qwen3-235B, DeepSeek v3.1 671B, Kimi K2 and HuggingFace custom models.
    • API: OpenAI Chat Completions, OpenAI Responses, Claude Messages and Ollama-compatible endpoints at localhost:52415.
    • Limits: Linux runs on CPU only (GPU in development); trust_remote_code models are disabled by default. README content reflects the current version, not the 2024 one.

    Takeaway: Interesting if you have several Apple Silicon machines and want to run large open models locally. On Linux, expect CPU-only performance for now.

  • Securing the Container World with Policies: acjs and ctrdac
    summary

    (Could not fetch full text.)

    TL;DR: A Google Bug Hunters blog post introducing two Google open-source projects, acjs and ctrdac, that bring Kubernetes-style admission control (image signatures, provenance, policy) to containers, including ones running outside Kubernetes.

    • acjs: A Kubernetes admission controller where policies are JavaScript snippets; return true to accept, false or a string to reject, nothing to fall through to defaultAction (reject by default).
    • Policy context: Globals such as req, object and ac.User; built-ins cosignVerify, slsaVerify, slsaEnsureComingFrom and forwardToAdmissionController.
    • Modes: Validating or mutating webhook (mutations become a JSON Patch), served over a Unix socket or mTLS.
    • ctrdac: A lightweight proxy in front of containerd that wraps container-create requests as Kubernetes AdmissionReview and sends them to a webhook such as acjs, so Docker/containerd hosts get admission control.
    • Example policy: Rewriting deprecated gitRepo volumes into an init container to avoid a kubelet privilege escalation risk.
    • Status: Both are “not an officially supported Google product”; the acjs repo is now archived.
    • Source caveat: The blog page is JavaScript-rendered and could not be read; this is based on the google/acjs README and ctrdac package docs.

    Takeaway: Interesting design for enforcing image signing on non-Kubernetes container hosts. Since acjs is archived, treat it as a reference implementation rather than something to deploy.

  • Incidental: Open-Source Incident Management Platform Integrated with Slack
    summary

    TL;DR: Incidental is an MIT-licensed, early-stage open-source incident management platform that lets teams declare and run incidents from Slack, with a hosted version at incidental.dev.

    • ChatOps: Declare and manage incidents inside Slack; a web UI also exists.
    • Customization: Custom severities, fields, incident types and roles.
    • Status pages: Public, customizable status pages for stakeholders.
    • Planned: Custom workflow automation is marked “Coming Soon”.
    • Stack: Python backend, React frontend, separate status-page app; dev needs Docker, docker-compose, pnpm and Node 18, started with make run-dev.
    • Setup: Create a Slack app from slack-manifest.yml and set Slack variables in backend/.env.
    • Limits: README covers local development only, no production deployment guide.

    Takeaway: A starting point for a self-hosted incident.io-style workflow. Expect to do your own hardening and deployment work.

  • Attack Paths into VMs in the Cloud
    summary

    TL;DR: Unit 42 (Jay Chen, June 2024) maps how an attacker with cloud API permissions but no VM credentials can log in to or run code on VMs in AWS, Azure and GCP, all through legitimate features.

    • Startup scripts: Modify EC2 user data (ec2:ModifyInstanceAttribute plus stop/start), Azure VMSS custom data, or GCP startup-script metadata (compute.instances.setMetadata).
    • SSH key push: EC2 Instance Connect (ec2-instance-connect:SendSSHPublicKey), Azure VMAccess extension, GCP metadata SSH keys or OS Login roles.
    • Command execution: SSM Run Command (ssm:SendCommand), Azure Run Command and Custom Script Extension, GCP VM Manager patch jobs (osconfig.patchJobs.exec) and OS policies.
    • Shell via middleware: SSM Session Manager (ssm:StartSession); not feasible on Azure/GCP per the article.
    • Serial console: Bypasses network controls but still needs a password or key; AWS needs account-level enablement, Azure is on by default, GCP uses serial-port-enable.
    • Exposure: 11% of internet-exposed cloud hosts had Critical or High vulnerabilities.
    • Mitigation: Restrict the listed permissions, remove unused agents, disable serial console, block metadata SSH keys in GCP, restrict SSM documents and Azure extension types.

    Takeaway: Treat VM-modifying and command-execution permissions as equivalent to shell access, and alert on their use. A compromised VM also hands over its attached identity.

  • Getting Started with Exploit Development
    summary

    TL;DR: dayzerosec’s 2024 roadmap for learning binary exploitation, built almost entirely on free resources.

    • Prerequisites: C (for the memory model), x86-64 assembly and calling conventions, Python with pwntools, Linux; Pwn College Fundamentals covers most of it.
    • Step 1: Pwn College CSE 466 (Fall 2023) through “Program Exploitation”, including shellcoding and sandboxing.
    • Step 2: ROP Emporium, 64-bit x86 first, ARM later.
    • Step 3: Open Security Training Vulnerabilities 1001 for heap, OOB and integer bug theory.
    • Step 4: Pwn College race conditions plus CSE 598 modules: format strings, FILE struct, dynamic allocator misuse, exploitation primitives, Windows crash course.
    • Concepts: Weird machines via LiveOverflow videos and Thomas Dullien’s 2015 paper and 2018 talk.
    • Next: Nightmare, how2heap, Malloc Maleficarum, HeapLAB (paid); Ret2 Fundamentals if you want paid training.

    Takeaway: A clear, ordered path for anyone starting pwn. Follow interest over strict order and expect frustration as part of the process.

  • Thwacking DDoS with AWS WAF
    summary

    TL;DR: Rami McCarthy’s practical guide to mitigating Layer 7 DDoS with AWS WAF, built from public incident write-ups and pricing realities.

    • Match rules first: Look for low-cardinality attack traits: JA3 TLS fingerprints (most powerful), geography, header order, User-Agent, missing or static cookies, ASNs.
    • Managed rules: Only AWSManagedIPDDoSList judged useful; Bot Control and IP reputation lists were too imprecise or costly.
    • Rate limits second: Per-IP, global limits on unauthenticated traffic, per-route; minimum 1-minute window, up to minutes of lag, 10 rate rules per ACL, 10,000 IPs tracked per rule.
    • Actions: Start in Count, Block only high-signal rules; Challenge is billed per challenge served.
    • Costs: Booters about $30/month, botnets about $300/month; Shield Advanced $3,000/month with a one-year commitment, rarely worth it except for high-risk low-traffic endpoints.
    • Cases: Blender peaked at 100,000 RPS, Railway about 250,000 RPS, Basecamp 80,000 RPS.
    • Gotchas: Lock origins to CloudFront, WAF inspects only the first 64 KB of bodies, logs may contain auth material.

    Takeaway: Prepare before an attack: dashboards of top JA3/UA/IP, Count-mode rules ready to flip, and origins that cannot be hit directly. Expect 30-60 seconds of impact at onset.

  • Poor Man’s MFA for AWS Client VPN
    summary

    TL;DR: Ian Mckay shows how to add a cheap second factor to certificate-based AWS Client VPN: a client connect handler Lambda asks the user on Slack to approve with a thumbs-up.

    • Flow: After mutual TLS succeeds, the Lambda DMs the user with the source IP and platform and polls reactions.get every two seconds for +1.
    • Identity mapping: The user’s Slack member ID is embedded in the client certificate CN, e.g. <name>-<slackmemberid>.<domain>, issued with Easy-RSA.
    • Slack app: Scopes chat:write and reactions:read; the xoxb- bot token sits in Secrets Manager.
    • Constraints: Lambda name must start with AWSClientVPN-; the handler has a 30-second limit, so users must approve within it.
    • Code gaps: No explicit deny path; the 30-second timeout ends unapproved attempts.

    Takeaway: A workable stopgap when you cannot federate Client VPN with SAML. Treat it as push-approval MFA and watch for approval fatigue.

  • Using S3 as a Container Registry
    summary

    TL;DR: Adolfo Ochagavía shows that a plain S3-compatible bucket can serve docker pull, and that pushing layers to S3 was much faster than to ECR.

    • Pull path: Docker only issues HTTP HEAD/GET on /v2/<image>/manifests/<tag>, the manifest digest and /v2/<image>/blobs/<digest>; any static server with correct Content-Type works.
    • Push: No docker push; files are uploaded to the expected paths with the S3 SDK. The demo used Cloudflare R2 for free egress.
    • Numbers: A 198 MiB layer uploaded at 24-28 MiB/s to ECR vs 115-190 MiB/s to S3, up to about 8x faster.
    • Why: S3 multipart uploads run in parallel; the OCI Distribution Spec forces sequential layer pushes. Sequential S3 uploads dropped to ECR speed.
    • Limits: Experimental; no validation of pushed images, no scanning, no native per-repo access control; benchmarks ran inside AWS over a VPC.

    Takeaway: A neat hack for read-only or public image distribution and a hint at where registry push speed is lost. Not a replacement for a real registry’s controls.

  • govulncheck: Report Known Vulnerabilities That Affect Go Code
    summary

    TL;DR: govulncheck is the Go team’s official tool that reports known vulnerabilities your Go code can actually reach, using the Go vulnerability database.

    • Reachability: Static analysis of source (or a binary’s symbols) to find calls into vulnerable functions, not just vulnerable modules.
    • Database: Queries vuln.go.dev, sending only module paths; -db points to an alternate DB.
    • Modes: govulncheck ./... (source), -mode binary <path>, -mode extract for a smaller blob.
    • Flags: -tags, -test, -show traces, -show verbose.
    • Output: Text, -json, -format sarif, -format openvex; non-zero exit on findings in text mode, 0 for JSON/SARIF/OpenVEX.
    • Limits: Conservative for interface and function-pointer calls, blind to reflect, binaries give no call graphs, findings cannot be silenced yet, pre-Go 1.18 binaries get stdlib findings only.

    Takeaway: Add govulncheck ./... to Go CI. Its reachability filter cuts the noise that generic SCA tools produce.

  • Secure Guardrails with Semgrep: Free Semgrep Academy Course
    summary

    TL;DR: “Secure Guardrails with Semgrep” is a free Semgrep Academy course on moving AppSec from reactive SAST findings to proactive guardrails that keep developers on secure paths.

    • Size: 45 lessons in 13 sections, about 3.5 hours of video.
    • Concepts: Secure defaults, shift-left and paved roads, and how guardrails differ from reactive SAST.
    • Rule writing: Banned functions, API call order, blocklisting weak ciphers, metavariable operators, an entropy-based secrets analyzer.
    • Autofix: Building remediation into the developer workflow.
    • Taint mode: Dataflow rules for path traversal, command injection and SQL injection.
    • Adoption: Rollout strategy with a Netflix case study.

    Takeaway: Good hands-on route to writing custom Semgrep rules that enforce your own secure patterns, not just generic vulnerability checks.

  • Enabling Security Guardrails: Infrastructure as Code with CDK for Terraform
    summary

    TL;DR: Zip security engineers Ashish Patel and Victor Chen (July 2024) describe moving AWS from click-ops to Python CDK for Terraform with secure-by-default wrapper classes and an SCP that blocks console changes.

    • Problem: Many engineers held AWS admin, peer review was hard to enforce and change visibility was poor.
    • Structure: One stack per environment, a shared secure_templates folder, a dedicated IAM role per stack via GitHub Actions OIDC on separate runners.
    • Secure defaults: Wrapper classes such as DatabaseInstance over DbInstance default to encrypted, non-public storage; public DBs require an allowlist or raise a security exception.
    • Review: CODEOWNERS makes security a required reviewer for secure_templates and production main.py.
    • Anti-click-ops: Resources get a terraform-managed tag; an SCP denies non-read actions on tagged resources except on-call, SSO admin and the Terraform runner role.
    • Results: 100% of IAM, S3, RDS and security group changes code-reviewed; AWS admin count down 95%.

    Takeaway: The pattern to copy is wrapper constructs plus a tag-based SCP; review alone does not stop console drift, the SCP does.

  • Building a Security Platform Engineering Team
    summary

    TL;DR: Kane Narraway (who led a security platform team at Shopify) on what a security platform engineering team is, when to form one and how to staff it.

    • Definition: A team that builds software making security the default, following the “secure paved roads” idea; buy commodity problems like staff SSO.
    • Focus areas: Internal access (IAM, PAM, zero trust), developer tooling (encryption, secrets, auth services), customer support tooling and scaling vuln management and reviews.
    • When: Build only if needs are unique and the team can afford long-term work; rough trigger is a security org near 30 people with at least 3 headcount (1 EM, 2 engineers).
    • Staffing: EM, frontend and backend engineers, PMs; often ex-security engineers; use the company’s existing languages.
    • Anti-pattern: Part-time builders or a single engineer risk burnout, no redundancy and hard handovers.
    • Retire tools: Shopify’s custom zero trust system was eventually overtaken by vendors; treat that as success.

    Takeaway: A clear decision framework for build vs buy in security. Ship guardrails people want to use, “the carrot, not the stick”.

  • IAM So Lost: A Guide to Identity in Google Cloud
    summary

    TL;DR: A beginner primer from Google (Sita Lakshmi Sangameswaran, Michele Chubirka, July 2024) on Google Cloud IAM concepts, arguing for persona-based, group-driven access.

    • Concepts: Principals (users, service accounts, groups, Workspace and Cloud Identity accounts), roles, policies, least privilege and separation of duties.
    • Personas: Map job functions such as “platform engineer” to groups, then grant roles to groups, not individuals.
    • Example: A software engineer joins web-app-developer and gets the Cloud Run Developer role.
    • Avoid: Broad basic roles like Editor for everyone.
    • Tooling: IAM policy intelligence tools to migrate toward a group-based model; Architecture Framework security pillar for more.
    • Not covered: Workforce and Workload Identity Federation; no code or config samples.

    Takeaway: Introductory but sound. Build GCP access from org-chart personas and groups so onboarding and audits stay simple.

  • Moving AWS Accounts and OUs Within an Organization: Not So Simple!
    summary

    TL;DR: Matthew Fuller (wut.dev) explains why moving an AWS account or OU within an Organization is a risky one-call change with no dry run, and what can break.

    • SCPs: Old parent policies stop and new ones apply instantly, e.g. a Production SCP denying s3:GetObject causing AccessDenied.
    • OU path conditions: Policies using aws:PrincipalOrgPaths, aws:ResourceOrgPaths or aws:SourceOrgPaths change behavior; include the org ID in paths because OU IDs are only unique within an org.
    • StackSets: OU-targeted auto-deployment can deploy stacks on arrival; with retention off, stacks (including IAM roles) are deleted on exit.
    • RAM and Control Tower: OU-targeted RAM shares gain or lose access; moving under an enrolled OU can trigger Control Tower enrollment and controls.
    • Reverting: Moving back restores most policy effects, but recreated IAM roles get new AROA IDs that some trusts (e.g. KMS) reference.
    • Checklist: Diff SCPs, list affected StackSets, grep policies for the OrgPaths keys, review RAM shares, check Control Tower; monitor CloudTrail for SCP explicit denies afterwards.

    Takeaway: Treat move-account (and Terraform parent_id changes) as a production change with a pre-flight checklist. Prefer account IDs or full org paths in policies.

  • A Hard Look at GuardDuty Shortcomings
    summary

    TL;DR: Rami McCarthy at Tracebit (a canary vendor) tests and critiques Amazon GuardDuty on coverage, cost, efficacy and detection latency.

    • Coverage: Supports about ten AWS services out of nearly 250, with 176 finding types; new protections are paid add-ons with slow regional rollout.
    • Cost: Usage-based and hard to forecast; examples include S3 Protection rising from about $2.5k to $6.5k/month and EKS Protection costing more than the cluster.
    • Bypass: Stratus Red Team exfiltration techniques (bulk Secrets Manager reads, SSM parameter decryption, sharing EBS/RDS snapshots, S3 batch deletion) raised zero alerts.
    • Tester results: With amazon-guardduty-tester, 11 of 12 findings ran and 8 fired; median detection 15 minutes, fastest 5m08s.
    • Ransomware math: At measured throughput, an attacker could exfiltrate roughly 100 GB to 1.3 TB of S3 data before the fastest alert.
    • Caveats: Small informal test, three findings failed for unknown reasons, and the author’s employer sells a competing approach.

    Takeaway: Keep GuardDuty as a compliance baseline, but do not assume it covers exfiltration of secrets or snapshots. Run your own adversary simulations and add detections for the gaps.

  • Red Team Interview Questions
    summary

    TL;DR: A HADESS (HadessCS) GitHub repo of red team interview questions, organized by topic with a table of contents of about 60 sections, focused heavily on Windows and Active Directory tradecraft.

    • Structure: A single README; the readable part held about 200 questions across 41 sections, roughly five or six per section.
    • Access and AD: Initial Access, Windows Network, Active Directory, Kerberoasting and Kerberos, NTLM, LDAP, RDP.
    • Credentials: Mimikatz, SAM file, Shadow file, LSA, LSASS, WDIGEST, CredSSP, MSV, breaking hashes.
    • Internals: Windows internals, Windows API vs DLL, NTDLL, Native API, Windows drivers, system and kernel programming.
    • Ops: Privilege escalation, post-exploitation and lateral movement, persistence, C2, tunneling, evasion, EDR vs antivirus, malware development, YARA.
    • Sample: “When would a developer choose the Native API over the Win32 API?”

    Takeaway: Useful as a self-quiz before red team or offensive interviews. It lists questions, so you still need to research the answers.

  • Anyone Can Access Deleted and Private Repository Data on GitHub
    summary

    TL;DR: Joe Leon at Truffle Security (July 2024) shows that commits from deleted forks, deleted repositories and pre-public private forks stay reachable on GitHub, naming it Cross Fork Object Reference (CFOR).

    • Deleted fork: Commits remain reachable through the upstream repo by hash; the author found about 40 valid API keys in deleted forks of three popular repos from a large AI company.
    • Deleted repo: When the upstream is deleted, a fork becomes the network root and post-fork commits remain accessible.
    • Private to public: Commits in a private fork made before the upstream was open-sourced can be viewed via the public repo.
    • Access: github.com/<owner>/<repo>/commit/<hash> works for unreferenced commits; short SHAs (min 4 hex chars, 65,536 options) can be brute forced; hashes also leak via the events API and GH Archive.
    • GitHub response: Working as designed and documented.
    • Fix: Rotate any secret ever pushed; deletion is not remediation. Scan whole repository networks.

    Takeaway: Assume anything pushed to a repo network with a public member is public forever. Rotate keys on exposure and scan forks, not just your own history.

  • terraform-pr-commenter: GitHub Action That Comments Terraform fmt/init/plan Output on PRs
    summary

    TL;DR: terraform-pr-commenter by Rob Burger is a Docker-based GitHub Action that posts Terraform fmt, init, plan and validate output as PR comments, deleting its older comments to keep the thread clean.

    • Inputs: commenter_type (fmt/init/plan/validate), commenter_input (stdout+stderr), commenter_exitcode.
    • Dependency: Needs hashicorp/setup-terraform with its wrapper enabled to capture output and exit codes.
    • Env vars: GITHUB_TOKEN (required), TF_WORKSPACE for matrix runs, EXPAND_SUMMARY_DETAILS, HIGHLIGHT_CHANGES (turns ~ into ! in diffs).
    • Usage: uses: robburger/terraform-pr-commenter@v1 in a step with if: always() after the Terraform step.
    • Limits: Linux runners only; examples pin old versions (actions/checkout@v2, Terraform 0.15.0) and the repo shows 19 open issues, so maintenance is unclear.

    Takeaway: Quick way to surface plans in PR review. Check maintenance status and pin by commit SHA, or consider maintained forks.

  • An Opinionated Ramp-Up Guide to AWS Pentesting
    summary

    TL;DR: Lizzie Moratti’s staged roadmap (AWS Security Digest, July 2024) for experienced pentesters moving into AWS customer-side pentesting.

    • Stage 1: Keep a glossary, solve pwnedlabs.io labs with official and pro write-ups (e.g. Tyler Ramsbey), and proxy tools through Burp to see raw AWS API calls.
    • Stage 2: Read hackingthe.cloud, AWS in Plain English, og-aws, Cloudonaut; redo labs without walkthroughs; do the Wiz Big IAM Challenge.
    • Stage 3: Solve labs with only the CLI/console, then write your own boto3 scripts and get them reviewed.
    • Hygiene: Vet all code in a test account and run aws sts get-caller-identity before state-changing calls.
    • Stages 4-7: Rich Mogull’s SLAW labs, Cloud Resume Challenge, Scott Piper’s maturity roadmap, SCP best practices, her AWS pentest methodology, then ongoing community learning.
    • Hot takes: Breadth before depth, skip paid AWS pentest certs for now, do not learn three clouds at once, beware scan-and-rebrand vendors.

    Takeaway: A concrete, mostly free curriculum. The proxy-the-tools and write-your-own-boto3 steps are what build real understanding.

  • Automate Monitoring for Your Amazon EKS Cluster Using CloudWatch Container Insights
    summary

    TL;DR: An AWS blog post (Manish Garg, Navdeep Pareek, Sushant Jagdale, July 2024) with an event-driven solution that keeps CloudWatch Container Insights alarms in sync as EKS worker nodes scale.

    • Static alarms: Cluster- and pod-level alarms created once with Terraform (v1.7.5) from terraform.tfvars, notifying via SNS email.
    • Dynamic alarms: EventBridge catches EC2 Auto Scaling events and a Lambda creates or deletes per-node alarms defined in alarm_list_inputs.json in S3.
    • Collection: The CloudWatch Observability EKS add-on runs the CloudWatch agent as a DaemonSet.
    • Infra: CloudFormation deploys the VPC, EKS cluster and add-on via ./scripts/deploy.sh -o apply in us-east-1.
    • Testing: Change NUM_WORKER_NODES and reapply to see alarms created and removed.
    • Cleanup: ./scripts/deploy.sh -o destroy, then manually delete leftover dynamic alarms.

    Takeaway: Reasonable pattern if you rely on per-node CloudWatch alarms in autoscaling clusters; aggregated metrics or Prometheus-style alerting may avoid the alarm churn altogether.

  • Kubernetes Security Fundamentals: Introduction
    summary

    (Could not fetch full text.)

    TL;DR: The introduction video of Datadog’s “Kubernetes Security Fundamentals” series, published on Datadog’s YouTube channel, matching the Datadog Security Labs blog series by Rory McCune.

    • Premise: Kubernetes leaves much of security to third-party software: runtime security, vulnerability management, log analysis and user authentication.
    • Delegation: Networking, storage and runtimes come from CNI, CSI and CRI projects, so cluster security includes all of that software.
    • Managed vs unmanaged: Managed services run the control plane for you; unmanaged distributions need more hardening but allow more customization.
    • Series topics: Component API security, authentication, authorization, admission control, network security, PKI, secrets, image security, runtime security, monitoring and auditing, across vanilla Kubernetes, EKS, AKS and GKE.
    • Source caveat: No transcript was available; the channel comes from YouTube oEmbed metadata and the content is inferred from the matching Datadog Security Labs introduction article. It is not confirmed that the video presenter is Rory McCune.

    Takeaway: A good structured entry point to Kubernetes security. Pair the videos with the written Datadog Security Labs articles, which include the details.

  • Kubernetes Security Fundamentals: Authorization
    summary

    TL;DR: Part 4 of Rory McCune’s Datadog Security Labs series (July 2024) explains how Kubernetes authorization works across its modules and where the risky gaps are.

    • Evaluation: Modules run in flag order and return allow, deny or no opinion; all no-opinion means deny. No central store, so auditing means checking every module.
    • Bypass: system:masters skips all authorization, including webhooks; reserve it for break-glass.
    • Modes: AlwaysAllow (microk8s default), Node authorizer with NodeRestriction, ABAC (file-based, not on EKS/GKE/AKS), RBAC, and webhook.
    • RBAC: Role/ClusterRole with RoleBinding/ClusterRoleBinding; ClusterRole + RoleBinding scopes reuse to a namespace. Verbs are free strings, so custom ones like impersonate escape tools such as kubectl auth can-i.
    • Non-resource URLs: system:public-info-viewer exposes /healthz, /livez, /readyz, /version unauthenticated.
    • Kubelet: Uses webhook authz via SubjectAccessReview; nodes/proxy allows exec in containers, and direct kubelet access bypasses audit logging and admission control.

    Takeaway: Audit for system:masters members, impersonate, wildcards and nodes/proxy grants. These are the RBAC rights that quietly equal cluster admin.

  • Why You Should Disable Unauthenticated Read-Only Ports on GKE Kubelet Servers
    summary

    TL;DR: Orca Security (Yonatan Broder, August 2024) explains why the deprecated, unauthenticated kubelet read-only port 10255 on GKE nodes should be disabled, and how to find and close it.

    • Exposure: Port 10255 is plain HTTP with no authentication and exposes node and pod status and metrics. Google binds it to localhost, but local processes and pods with hostNetwork: true can still reach it.
    • Risk: An attacker with local node access can use the data for reconnaissance or privilege escalation. The author rates exploitation as difficult and the reward as low.
    • Numbers: 87% of organizations running GKE that Orca scanned had at least one open 10255 port.
    • Vendor timeline: Google emailed GKE customers on July 26. New clusters on GKE 1.32+ have the port disabled by default; existing clusters are not changed. Future versions will remove the option to re-enable it.
    • Mitigation: Inventory open 10255 ports, move consumers to the authenticated secure port 10250, disable 10255 per Google’s guide, then add a custom organization policy blocking it on new and existing clusters.
    • Coverage: Orca alerts on enabled kubelet read-only ports on GKE, EKS and AKS.

    Takeaway: Low severity but cheap to fix. Migrate any metrics scrapers off 10255, disable it everywhere, and enforce that with an org policy rather than waiting for the forced phase-out.

  • Announcing Karpenter 1.0
    summary

    TL;DR: AWS announced Karpenter v1.0.0 on August 14, 2024: the node autoscaler’s APIs graduate from beta to stable, with a promise of no breaking changes across 1.0 minor versions.

    • Maturity: APIs moved alpha to beta in October 2023 and now beta to stable. All APIs stay available through future 1.0 minors.
    • Platform: Works on Amazon EKS or any conformant Kubernetes cluster.
    • Disruption budgets by reason: Budgets can be scoped to specific disruption reasons such as underutilization, emptiness and drift.
    • Forceful disruption mode: Lets operators favour urgent node replacement (for example for security) over application availability.
    • consolidateAfter: Expanded to give finer control over when consolidation happens, trading cost against availability.
    • Not covered here: The announcement gives no v1 resource names, YAML or migration steps; those are in the Karpenter launch blog and karpenter.sh docs.

    Takeaway: 1.0 is the point where Karpenter APIs are safe to standardize on. Read the upgrade guide before moving from v0.x, and use reason-scoped budgets to stop drift or consolidation from churning critical nodes.

  • Understanding AWS Networking: A Guide for Network Engineers
    summary

    TL;DR: Robert de Meyer, a former network engineer, maps AWS VPC networking onto familiar constructs (routers, VRFs, NAT, route reflectors) for traditional network engineers. Published August 13, 2024.

    • VPC model: A VPC is regional; subnets live in one AZ. The author models the VPC as a router and each subnet as an L3 VRF with its own route table; the VPC CIDR is always present in every subnet. There is no real L2 or broadcast.
    • Addressing: Each subnet reserves the first address (gateway), second (DNS resolver), third (future) and last (broadcast, which AWS does not support). Overlapping CIDRs across VPCs are allowed, so plan before interconnecting.
    • Traffic control: NACLs are stateless and per subnet; Security Groups are stateful, bound to ENIs, can reference other SGs, and several can attach to one ENI. Source/destination check must be disabled for routing or firewall appliances.
    • Edge and services: Internet Gateway, NAT Gateway, Elastic IPs (1:1 NAT on the IGW); NLB (L4), ALB (L7), GWLB (L3). Gateway endpoints (S3, DynamoDB) use prefix lists; interface endpoints create per-AZ ENIs and rely on Route 53 private hosted zones.
    • Transit Gateway: A regional hub likened to a route reflector, with association and propagation per route table for segmentation, BGP with partly fixed attributes, and route quotas that can drop a BGP session. Connect attachments (GRE) reach 5 Gbps versus 1.25 Gbps for VPN.
    • Under the hood: The author’s reading of re:Invent material covers the mapping service, HyperPlane nodes (NAT Gateway, NLB, EFS) and Blackfoot edge devices.

    Takeaway: A good translation layer for anyone coming from on-prem networking. The practical lessons are non-overlapping CIDR planning, DNS for interface endpoints, and watching TGW route-table and BGP quotas.

  • Using AI for Offensive Security
    summary

    TL;DR: A Cloud Security Alliance paper (AI Technology and Risk Working Group, released August 6, 2024) on how LLM-powered AI and agents fit into vulnerability assessment, penetration testing and red teaming.

    • Scope: Offensive security use cases for LLMs and AI agents: vulnerability assessment, pentesting and red teaming.
    • Phases: Frames AI assistance across five phases: reconnaissance, scanning, vulnerability analysis, exploitation and reporting.
    • Other topics: Overview of LLMs and agents, how threat actors use AI, expected near-term advances, and governance, risk and compliance considerations.
    • Limits: The paper discusses current limitations of AI in offensive security; the landing page lists this but gives no detail.
    • Format: A downloadable CSA artifact; the landing page names no individual authors and gives no page count.

    Takeaway: Useful as a structured map of where AI can speed up an offensive engagement and the governance questions it raises. Read the full PDF for specifics; the landing page is only an outline.

  • Kubernetes Testing Environment: An Open-Source Resilience Platform for EKS, GKE and AKS
    summary

    TL;DR: KTE (Kubernetes Testing Environment) is an Apache 2.0 open-source project from Orca Security’s Research Pod that stands up EKS, GKE or AKS clusters and runs open-source Kubernetes security tools against them, as a free, vendor-agnostic KSPM-style setup.

    • Repo: github.com/orcasecurity-research/kte.
    • Clouds: AWS EKS, Google GKE and Azure AKS, each with its own Terraform project under deployment/clusters that creates the cluster and deploys a generic Helm chart.
    • Tools: kubesec, kube-score, Polaris, kor, Trivy Operator and Checkov. Dynamic tools run in the cluster; static tools (kubesec, kube-score) scan the Helm chart YAML and write HTML reports.
    • CLI: kte.sh with apply, state, destroy and tunnel; config.yaml selects tools per cloud. Results link from dashboards/index.html.
    • Access: Dashboards are ClusterIP-only; you reach them through the included SSH tunnel Terraform projects and a browser dynamic proxy.
    • Limits: The default Helm chart is generic, so swap in your own to test realistically. Dashboard experience varies by tool. No cost, version support or maintenance scope is stated.

    Takeaway: Handy for comparing free Kubernetes posture scanners side by side or rehearsing attack scenarios in a throwaway cluster. Replace the sample chart with your real workloads and tear the clusters down to control cost.

  • GitHub Actions Attack Diagram
    summary

    TL;DR: An SVG attack diagram by John Stawinski and Adnan Khan that walks through finding and exploiting GitHub Actions misconfigurations, starting from read-only or write access to an org or repository.

    • Paths covered: From self-hosted runner takeover, to pwn requests, to secrets exfiltration; the README says the paths were used on red team engagements and public research and are not exhaustive.
    • Format: One file, GitHub Actions Attack Diagram.svg, plus README and CONTRIBUTORS; new or outdated TTPs are reported through Issues.
    • Talks: Built alongside Black Hat USA 2024 ‘Continuous Integration, Continuous Destruction’ and DEF CON 32 ‘Grand Theft Actions’ (slides linked).
    • Case studies: Links write-ups on PyTorch, CodeQL, Microsoft, Puppet (RoguePuppet) and TensorFlow supply chain attacks.
    • Numbers: 24 commits, 194 stars and 13 forks at fetch time.

    Takeaway: Use it as a decision tree when assessing your own Actions setup: check for self-hosted runners on public repos, pull_request_target patterns and secret exposure, and follow the linked write-ups for real exploitation detail.

  • 3.7 Million Fake GitHub Stars: A Growing Threat Linked to Scams and Malware
    summary

    TL;DR: Socket research led by Hao He (Socket intern, CMU PhD student), published August 27, 2024, found about 3.7 million suspected fake GitHub stars from July 2019 to July 2024, many tied to scam and malware repositories.

    • Numbers: 3,746,538 suspected fake stars across 10,155 repositories; about 89% of those repos have since been deleted, but only 18.12% of the starring accounts. Stars can cost as little as $0.10 each.
    • Content: Malware (VirusTotal flags 28 repos still online), piracy and game cheats, crypto sniping bots, and low-quality awesome lists. Example: Solmonster/PhantomSniper-Solana-Sniper-Bot steals crypto via a hidden spawn() call.
    • Data: GH Archive in BigQuery, about 20 TiB over five years.
    • Detection: A low-activity heuristic (accounts that star and go inactive the same day) plus CopyCatch-style clustering of N users starring M repos within a short window; both produce false positives.
    • Effect: Early modelling suggests a short-term bump in real stars but a negative effect over time, with no significant effect on downloads.
    • Response: Socket added a High-severity ‘Suspicious Stars on GitHub’ alert.

    Takeaway: Star counts are not a trust signal. Check whether issues, PRs and contributors match the stars before adopting a package, especially for crypto tools and cracks.

  • Kubernetes Is Evolving, the CKA Exam Too!
    summary

    TL;DR: A CNCF post (September 5, 2024) announcing that the Certified Kubernetes Administrator exam competencies will change no sooner than November 25, 2024, while the domains stay the same.

    • Timing: The update will not take place before November 25, 2024; the exact date was not set in the post.
    • Domains: Unchanged (for example Storage, Troubleshooting), but competencies within them change.
    • Added: ‘Use the Gateway API to manage Ingress traffic.’
    • Removed: ‘Provision underlying infrastructure to deploy a Kubernetes cluster’, reflecting the shift to managed platforms.
    • Details: The full competency list is in the linked Linux Foundation announcement; weights and other topics are not covered in the post.

    Takeaway: If you are preparing for the CKA, study Gateway API and check the Linux Foundation curriculum for the current competency list rather than older prep material.

  • Achieving Zero Trust Security on Amazon EKS with Istio
    summary

    TL;DR: Part four of the AWS ‘Istio on EKS’ series (Praseeda Sathaye et al., September 3, 2024) applies zero trust principles to an EKS sample app using Istio mTLS, JWT validation, ingress TLS and OPA external authorization.

    • mTLS: Moves the mesh from permissive to STRICT PeerAuthentication, with certificates from cert-manager, istio-csr and aws-privateca-issuer backed by AWS Private CA.
    • End-user auth: RequestAuthentication validates JWTs from Keycloak. Requests with no JWT pass by default, so it is paired with an AuthorizationPolicy requiring authenticated claims.
    • External authz: A CUSTOM AuthorizationPolicy in the workshop namespace forwards decisions to an OPA sidecar on port 9191, injected with Gatekeeper mutations; rules live in policy.rego.
    • Ingress: istio-ingress sits behind an NLB with an ACM certificate (a self-signed cert imported to ACM in the demo); traffic is checked with siege and visualized in Kiali.
    • Code: github.com/aws-samples/istio-on-eks, modules/04-security, marked demo-only, not production.

    Takeaway: A concrete recipe for the common pitfall that RequestAuthentication alone does not block anonymous requests. Copy the STRICT mTLS plus AuthorizationPolicy pattern, and treat the sample’s self-signed certs as demo-only.

  • Using Go Instead of Bash for Scripts
    summary

    TL;DR: Krzysztof Kowalczyk (kjk) describes replacing per-platform .sh and .bat project scripts with one multipurpose Go program, because bash is hard to remember and write and Go runs everywhere.

    • Layout: A single do directory holds one Go program; commands are chosen by flags like -run, -test, -deploy, and running with no args prints them.
    • Wrappers: do/do.sh and do/do.bat just cd do and go run .; a doit shell function finds and runs do.sh from anywhere in the project.
    • Setup: main calls cdToTopDir() so paths are relative to the repo root, then dispatches on flags.
    • Helpers: must(err) panics on error, runCmd logs and captures command output, checkGitClean blocks deploys on a dirty tree, plus logf, openBrowser, zip and file helpers, and a composable line counter.
    • Trade-offs: More lines than shell, which the author considers immaterial; panic-on-error is fine for scripts but not production code.

    Takeaway: A practical pattern if your team already writes Go: one typed, cross-platform task runner instead of fragile shell. It requires a Go toolchain on every dev machine.

  • How to 10X Your Cloud Security (Without the Series D)
    summary

    TL;DR: A Rami McCarthy slide deck (posted September 11, 2024) on scaling a cloud security program without a big budget, using guardrails, secure defaults and invariants instead of gatekeeping.

    • Principles: Do things manually first, then automate; prefer high-signal, low-noise tooling; guardrails not gatekeepers; build tools developers can use; aim for desirable rather than absolute security.
    • Invariants: Identify scope, measure adherence, document exceptions, prevent regressions; set a baseline, meet it, enforce it, raise it.
    • What does not scale: Absolute least privilege, centralized security review and authorship; security champions described as crutches for processes that do not scale.
    • Program areas: Account architecture and allowlists, asset inventory and secrets scanning, zero-access-by-default IAM with crown-jewel carve-outs, detection engineering and canaries, secure-by-default IaC modules, Kubernetes hardening.
    • Tools named: Steampipe, AWS Access Advisor, Semgrep, gitleaks, cartography, terraform-aws-secure-baseline, org-kickstart, SigmaHQ and other detection rule repos.
    • 30-60-90 plan: Assess and baseline, fix one thing well with invariants, then build a reproducible process and kill a class of risk.

    Takeaway: A strong checklist for a small security team. Pick one area, define an invariant, enforce it automatically, and only then expand.

  • Beyond the AWS Security Maturity Roadmap
    summary

    TL;DR: Rami McCarthy’s fwd:cloudsec talk (June 12, 2023) on what to do after Scott Piper’s AWS Security Maturity Roadmap, organized around build-versus-adopt-versus-buy decisions for each control area.

    • Framework: Build only if the problem or scale is unique to you, integration costs more than building, or license costs outweigh it.
    • Secrets and inventory: Standardize secrets early with a thin wrapper over cloud services; adopt inventory before controls and do not write your own cloud API collectors.
    • CSPM and remediation: Do not build an open-source CSPM; use auto-remediation only when IaC or a change chokepoint is not available.
    • IaC: Secure modules once there is a real need; write environment-specific scanning rules, surface them at PR time, and roll out block mode gradually.
    • Access and infra: Incremental JIT access for step-up and break-glass; move from SSH to SSM early; egress filtering starts in monitor mode; data perimeter and SCPs rolled out carefully.
    • Tools named: Vault, sops, Steampipe, CloudQuery, prowler, cloud-custodian, tfsec, Semgrep, checkov, Canarytokens, iamlive, granted, stratus-red-team, smokescreen, Teleport, Falco, Tetragon and more.

    Takeaway: Use it as a menu for the next stage of an AWS program once basics are done. The tool lists per area save a lot of market research.

  • revive: Fast, Configurable, Extensible Drop-In Replacement for golint
    summary

    TL;DR: revive by Minko Gechev is an MIT-licensed, configurable Go linter and drop-in replacement for golint, with a framework for custom rules.

    • Speed: About 2x faster than golint on the same rules and over 6x with typed rules off. On Kubernetes: golint about 55 s, revive about 8.5 s without type checking, about 26 s with it.
    • Rules: Roughly 105 rules, marked by golint origin and whether they need type info.
    • Config: TOML via -config; enable or disable rules, set severity and arguments, for example [rule.cyclomatic] with arguments = [10].
    • Output: Nine formatters including friendly, stylish, json, ndjson, checkstyle and sarif.
    • Install: go install github.com/mgechev/revive@latest, Homebrew, Docker or binaries.
    • golangci-lint: Available as the revive linter, configured under linters.settings.revive in YAML or JSON.

    Takeaway: If you still run golint (deprecated), revive is the direct replacement. Most teams will use it via golangci-lint and tune rules there.

  • Hacking Kia: Remotely Controlling Cars with Just a License Plate
    summary

    TL;DR: Sam Curry, Neiko Rivera, Justin Rhinehart, Ian Carroll and Kenneth Lugo found that Kia’s dealer portal let anyone take remote control of most Kia vehicles from just a license plate, in about 30 seconds, with or without a Kia Connect subscription.

    • Entry point: The employee dealer portal on kiaconnect.kdealer.com allowed self-registration, which yielded a valid token for dealer-only API endpoints.
    • Chain: License plate to VIN via a third-party service; dealer VIN lookup returned the owner’s name, email and phone; dealer endpoints then demoted the owner and added the attacker as primary owner.
    • Impact: Geolocation, lock/unlock, start/stop, horn and lights; camera access on some models. The victim got no notification.
    • Scope: Vehicle table covers 2014 to 2025 model years, varying by model and trim.
    • Disclosure: Reported June 11, 2024; Kia said it remediated August 14; publicly disclosed after validation. The PoC tool was never released, and Kia said the flaw was not exploited maliciously.

    Takeaway: A textbook broken-access-control chain: an internal portal with open signup trusted by privileged APIs. Audit partner and employee portals for self-registration and check that their tokens cannot reach owner-level actions.

  • Cloud Logging Tips and Tricks
    summary

    TL;DR: Alice Klimovitsky (Wiz, September 17, 2024) covers practical gaps and defaults in AWS, Azure, GCP and Google Workspace logging, arguing control plane logs are the best starting point because they cover the most attack stages.

    • Categories: Identity, data, network, compute and control plane log sources.
    • AWS: Use an organization trail so new accounts are not left unlogged; console history is 90 days; the first trail’s management events to S3 are free; S3 exfiltration needs data events enabled.
    • Azure: Activity logs keep 90 days and Entra audit/sign-in logs 7 to 30 days by license, so set diagnostic settings. Most control plane reads (listing resources, users, policies) are not logged. Sign-in logs carry a location object.
    • GCP: Admin Activity logs on by default, kept 400 days, but writes only; enable Data Access ADMIN_READ for reads. Config changes show in DATA_WRITE, off by default.
    • Workspace: Admin, Login, SAML, OAuth and Groups logs on by default for 6 months; streaming to GCP is free. Only the Login category includes error logs.
    • Detections: Unusual sign-in locations, brute force, persistence via new users, roles or VMs, enumeration, and data destruction.

    Takeaway: Check each default against what you would need in an incident: turn on GCP ADMIN_READ, S3 data events where it matters, and longer Azure retention before you need them.

  • Mitigating Attack Vectors in GitHub Workflows
    summary

    TL;DR: Joyce Brum of Google’s Open Source Security Team (OpenSSF blog, August 12, 2024) lists the main GitHub Actions attack vectors and concrete mitigations for each.

    • pull_request_target: Checking out and running PR head code with secrets lets an attacker print them; base32 encoding bypasses log redaction.
    • workflow_run artifacts: A privileged workflow that downloads artifacts from an unprivileged PR run can be fed attacker-controlled code.
    • Script injection: ${{ github.event.comment.body }} or issue titles in run: execute as shell; writing untrusted data to $GITHUB_ENV injects variables.
    • Cache and Actions: Untrusted code in the default-branch context can poison caches; tag pins can be moved; imposter commits from forks can look legitimate.
    • Mitigations: permissions: {} or contents: read by default; pass untrusted data via env:; split unprivileged and privileged workflows; pin Actions to full SHAs and check for the fork warning; no caching in release workflows.
    • Tools: OpenSSF Scorecard CLI and Scorecard Action, plus Dependabot or Renovate (monthly suggested).

    Takeaway: A compact hardening checklist for any repo with Actions. Run Scorecard and grep your workflows for pull_request_target and inline ${{ }} in run steps first.

  • AWS: VPC Flow Logs, NAT Gateways, and Kubernetes Pods, a Detailed Overview
    summary

    TL;DR: Arseny Zinchenko (RTFM, May 2024) uses VPC Flow Logs with a custom format and CloudWatch Logs Insights to find which EKS pods drive NAT Gateway data-processing costs.

    • Cost: NAT Gateway is $0.045/hour (about $32/month) plus $0.045/GB processed in both directions.
    • Log format: Custom fields including pkt-srcaddr, pkt-dstaddr, pkt-src-aws-service, flow-direction, traffic-path, interface-id; srcaddr/dstaddr are the hop, pkt-* the original endpoints.
    • Terraform: terraform-aws-modules/vpc ~> 5.5.2 with flow_log_max_aggregation_interval = 60 and flow_log_log_format (escape ${...} as $${...}).
    • Queries: Logs Insights parse @message over 19 fields, then sum(bytes) by NAT ENI, source EC2 or pod IP.
    • Pod visibility: By default the VPC CNI SNATs pod IPs to the node IP, hiding pods. Setting AWS_VPC_K8S_CNI_EXTERNALSNAT=true on aws-node makes pkt_srcaddr show the pod IP. hostNetwork: true also works but is discouraged.
    • Findings: One outbound flow via NAT yields three records (EC2 ENI egress, NAT ENI ingress and egress); NAT ENI records have an empty instance-id. CloudWatch storage of flow logs got expensive even for a small VPC.
    • Source caveat: The itnext.io page returned 403; summary is based on the author’s identical post on setevoy.substack.com.

    Takeaway: If NAT costs are high on EKS, enable custom-format flow logs and external SNAT temporarily to attribute traffic to pods, then fix the top talkers (often S3 or DynamoDB that should use VPC endpoints).

  • How to Build a Secure Recon Network Using Tailscale
    summary

    TL;DR: Rami Tawil (Bugcrowd, September 17, 2024) shows bug bounty hunters how to put a recon VPS behind Tailscale, with no public inbound access, an exit node, Taildrive file sharing and Tailscale SSH.

    • Architecture: Ubuntu 24.04 VPS running Amass, a Windows 11 PC and an Android phone joined in one tailnet.
    • Lockdown: sudo ufw default deny incoming, sudo ufw allow in on tailscale0, then reconnect via the Tailscale hostname.
    • Exit node: Enable IP forwarding in /etc/sysctl.d/99-tailscale.conf, sudo tailscale up --advertise-exit-node, approve in the admin console.
    • Taildrive: ACL nodeAttrs granting drive:share and drive:access, a tailscale.com/cap/drive grant, tailscale drive share reconbox ~/, mapped on Windows at http://100.100.100.100:8080.
    • SSH: sudo tailscale up --ssh --advertise-exit-node (add --accept-risk=lose-ssh if warned), then browser SSH from the admin console.
    • Caveat: The example Taildrive grant uses * sources and destinations with read-write access.

    Takeaway: A cheap way to keep recon infrastructure and its data off the internet. Tighten the example ACLs to specific users and devices before relying on it.

  • AWS and Kubecost Collaborate to Deliver Kubecost 2.0 for Amazon EKS Users
    summary

    TL;DR: An AWS Containers blog post (September 30, 2024) announcing Kubecost 2.0 features for EKS users at no cost, in the EKS-optimized bundle that has been free since August 2022.

    • Network costs: Near real-time network cost by pod, namespace, cluster and cloud service, including cross-AZ and cross-region traffic.
    • Actions: Automated request right-sizing and scheduled cluster or namespace turndown (nights, weekends), configured in UI or YAML.
    • Forecasting: ML forecasts in Allocations, Assets and Cloud Cost dashboards, plus anomaly detection.
    • Performance: New API backend claims 100x faster at scale, 3x better resource efficiency, and up to three years of history.
    • Install: Helm from oci://public.ecr.aws/kubecost/cost-analyzer with the EKS values file (example pins 2.4.1), the EKS add-on, or AWS Marketplace. Bundles Prometheus and kube-state-metrics by default.
    • Prereqs: Helm 3.9+; EBS CSI driver on 1.23+; configure a StorageClass on 1.30+, which has none by default. Do not expose the UI without an auth layer.

    Takeaway: A free way to get per-pod and network cost visibility on EKS. Port-forward the UI for a quick look and use the network view to find cross-AZ chatter.

  • Managing AWS EKS Access Entries with Terraform and OpenTofu
    summary

    TL;DR: Saifeddine Rajhi (AWS Community Builders, October 14, 2024) explains EKS access entries as the replacement for the aws-auth ConfigMap and shows how to manage them with the terraform-aws-modules/eks module in Terraform or OpenTofu.

    • Why: aws-auth is a manual, hard-to-audit YAML map where one mistake can lock users out. Access entries go through the EKS API and also remove the hidden default cluster creator.
    • Modes: CONFIG_MAP, API_AND_CONFIG_MAP, API. Switching is one-way: aws eks update-cluster-config --access-config authenticationMode=API.
    • Terraform: Module ~> 20.0 with enable_cluster_creator_admin_permissions = true and access_entries taking principal_arn, kubernetes_groups and policy_associations (each a policy_arn and access_scope of cluster or namespace).
    • Policies: AmazonEKSClusterAdminPolicy, AmazonEKSAdminPolicy, AmazonEKSEditPolicy, AmazonEKSViewPolicy; the example scopes View to the default namespace.
    • RBAC mix: Map entries to kubernetes_groups such as eks-admins and bind them with a ClusterRoleBinding.
    • Verify: aws eks list-access-entries --cluster-name <name>.

    Takeaway: Move to API_AND_CONFIG_MAP first, recreate aws-auth mappings as access entries in code, verify, then switch to API. Remember there is no way back.

  • Cloud-Native Incident Response in AWS: Part II
    summary

    TL;DR: Part II of Invictus Incident Response’s AWS cloud-native IR series (October 4, 2024) is a practical guide to using Amazon Athena to query logs during an investigation.

    • Model: Athena does not index data; it queries it in place in S3, with Glue holding the schema. The post warns against treating it as a SIEM.
    • Partitioning: Partition by region, year, month, day and hour to reduce scanned data, cost and query time.
    • Log sources: CloudTrail, VPC Flow Logs, ELB, S3 access and CloudFront logs.
    • Loading: You need the S3 location and a DDL statement; the example creates an elb_logs table by changing LOCATION.
    • Query tips: Use LIMIT to cap cost; result reuse (60 minutes to 7 days) misses recent events; use dot notation for STRUCT fields and json_extract_scalar for STRING JSON, for example roleSessionName from AssumeRole events.
    • Extra: A downloadable Athena cheatsheet on GitHub.

    Takeaway: Pre-create partitioned Athena tables for CloudTrail and flow logs before an incident, so responders can query in minutes instead of writing DDL under pressure.

  • s3cme: Template Go Repo with Supply Chain Security Pipelines (ko SBOM, cosign, SLSA Provenance)
    summary

    TL;DR: s3cme by Mark Chmarny is an Apache-2.0 template Go repo with GitHub Actions pipelines built for software supply chain security: scan, build with ko, sign with cosign, and attach SLSA provenance.

    • On push: Trivy code vulnerability scan and CodeQL SARIF results into repo security alerts.
    • On tag: ko image build and push with SBOM, Trivy image scan with a max-severity gate, cosign signing and attestation, SLSA provenance via slsa-github-generator, verified with slsa-verifier and a CUE policy.
    • Schedule: CodeQL analysis every 4 hours.
    • Release: Version lives in .version; make tag tags and pushes; images go to ghcr.io with .sig, .att and SPDX 2.3 .sbom artifacts.
    • Verify: cosign verify-attestation --type slsaprovenance with a certificate identity regexp, GitHub OIDC issuer and policy/provenance.cue.
    • Cluster enforcement: Sigstore policy-controller with policy/slsa.yaml and namespace label policy.sigstore.dev/include=true.

    Takeaway: A working reference for wiring SBOM, signing and SLSA provenance into a Go release pipeline. Copy the workflows and admission policy rather than designing from scratch.

  • Terraform Stacks Part 1: An Introduction
    summary

    TL;DR: Mike Guy (October 23, 2024) introduces HCP Terraform Stacks, a public-preview feature for deploying the same set of modules across many environments without custom pipelines, with an Azure walkthrough.

    • Files: .tfstack.hcl for components, providers, variables and outputs; .tfdeploy.hcl for deployments, identity and orchestration.
    • Components: component blocks reference modules; providers get labels such as provider "azurerm" "this".
    • Deployments: Instances of the stack, for example dev, stg, prd, each with its own subscription and inputs.
    • Orchestration: orchestrate blocks with check conditions; the example auto-approves only dev when the plan is applyable. Other actions (deferral_replan, replan, converged) listed but not explored.
    • Limits: Public preview, not for production; 20 deployments per stack, 500 stack resources per org; VCS integration required; the demo needed Terraform 1.10.0-alpha20240926 and the tfstacks CLI. An identity_token variable had to be ephemeral.

    Takeaway: Worth tracking if you maintain workspace-per-environment sprawl in HCP Terraform, but it is HCP-only and preview, so do not migrate production yet.

  • zizmor: Static Analysis Tool for GitHub Actions
    summary

    TL;DR: zizmor is an MIT-licensed static analysis tool for GitHub Actions (and Dependabot and pre-commit configs) that finds security issues in CI/CD definitions. The repo now lives at github.com/zizmorcore/zizmor.

    • Audits: Template injection leading to code execution, accidental credential persistence and leakage, excessive permission scopes, imposter commits and confusable git refs; the full list is at docs.zizmor.sh/audits/.
    • Scope: GitHub Actions workflows and actions, Dependabot and pre-commit configurations.
    • Build: Repo contains Cargo.toml and pyproject.toml, indicating Rust with Python packaging (inference from files, not stated).
    • Docs: Install, quickstart and usage recipes are at docs.zizmor.sh, not in the README.
    • Maintainer: Sponsor links point to woodruffw (William Woodruff).

    Takeaway: Run zizmor in CI over .github/workflows to catch injection and over-permissioned tokens before attackers do. It pairs well with OpenSSF Scorecard.

  • AWS Security Guardrails and Terraform
    summary

    TL;DR: Naman Sogani built two Python scripts that use Claude 3.5 Sonnet on AWS Bedrock to generate AWS security requirements and secure-by-default Terraform modules per service.

    • Requirements Generator: requirements-generator.py merges and enhances requirements from Checkov and Prowler into JSON (ID, name, description, provider, domain).
    • Terraform Creator: terraform-creator.py writes main.tf, variables.tf and notes.md per service, with requirement traceability and coverage notes.
    • Assumptions: Hub-and-spoke via Transit Gateway, Identity Center SSO, no IAM user keys, CloudTrail and flow logs on, private-only resources.
    • Prompt rules: Do not create supporting resources (KMS keys, buckets, SGs); one resource block per resource; most secure defaults.
    • Services: Examples include S3, SageMaker, MSK, RDS, ALB, ECS, EKS, API Gateway, Kinesis, MWAA and KMS.
    • Repo: github.com/naman16/AWS-Security-Guardrails-TF.
    • Limits: AI output needs review; no measured accuracy given, only ‘a few hours’ with ‘reasonable accuracy’; some requirements cannot be expressed in Terraform.

    Takeaway: A useful starting point for a secure module library, not a finished one. Review each generated module against your own environment before use.

  • safer-scps: Safer AWS SCP Deployments via Real-Time Monitoring
    summary

    TL;DR: safer-scps by Matthew Fuller is a pair of CloudFormation stacks that stream SCP-caused AccessDenied events from every member account to a central place in near real time, so you can watch for breakage while rolling out a Service Control Policy.

    • Problem: SCPs have no dry-run mode and CloudTrail delivery can lag more than 15 minutes.
    • Flow: In each member account, an EventBridge rule matches AccessDenied events whose message ends in ‘deny in a service control policy’ and forwards them to a management-account event bus, then CloudWatch Logs.
    • Metrics: A metric filter splits by Account and Action for an ‘ScpErrors’ dashboard (30 s period) or Live Tail.
    • Deploy: bus.yml in the management account with your Org ID; rules.yml via StackSets with the EventBusArn output.
    • Cost: Cross-account events about $1 per million, logs about $0.50/GB; near zero unless error volume is high. Stop Live Tail when done.
    • Limits: Per-region deployment, relies on exact AWS error text, data events untested; log group name is inconsistent in the README.

    Takeaway: Deploy it before your next SCP change and keep the dashboard open during rollout, so a bad deny shows up in seconds instead of in a support ticket.

  • How AWS Enforcement Code Logic Evaluates Requests to Allow or Deny Access
    summary

    TL;DR: The AWS IAM User Guide page describing the order in which AWS enforcement code evaluates policies to reach Allow or Deny.

    • Defaults: Everything is implicitly denied except the root user; an explicit deny anywhere overrides any allow.
    • Order: Explicit deny across all policies, then RCPs, then SCPs, then resource-based policies, identity-based policies, permissions boundaries, and session policies.
    • RCPs and SCPs: Each must contain an applicable Allow or the request is denied. RCPFullAWSAccess is attached automatically and cannot be detached.
    • Resource policies: Within one account, an Allow to an IAM user, role session or federated user ARN can grant access despite an implicit deny in identity policies, boundaries or session policies. An Allow to a role ARN is still limited by boundaries and session policies.
    • Exceptions: IAM role trust policies and KMS key policies must explicitly allow the principal.
    • Sessions: Non-session principals end at Allow; if a session policy is passed and does not allow the action, the request is denied.

    Takeaway: Keep this page open when debugging AccessDenied. The subtle bit is same-account resource policies granting directly to sessions, which can bypass permission boundaries.

  • aws-gate: Better AWS SSM Session Manager CLI Client
    summary

    TL;DR: aws-gate by xen0l is a BSD-licensed Python CLI wrapper around AWS SSM Session Manager that lets you connect to EC2 instances by name, tag, IP, DNS or ASG instead of only instance ID, and adds SSH over SSM.

    • Lookup: Instance ID, DNS or private DNS, IP, Name:value tag, instance name, or asg:name.
    • Config: Host aliases with profile and region in ~/.aws-gate/config and ~/.aws-gate/config.d.
    • Commands: aws-gate session <id>, aws-gate ssh <id> [command] with local port forwarding (for example to RDS), aws-gate ssh-config to generate ~/.ssh/config, and ssh-proxy used as ProxyCommand.
    • SSH keys: Ephemeral keys pushed via EC2 Instance Connect; scp works but can be slow.
    • Requirements: Python 3.5+, session-manager-plugin, SSM Agent 2.3.68.0+, suitable instance profile IAM.
    • Install: pip install aws-gate, Homebrew tap xen0l/homebrew-taps, or Docker. Debug with GATE_DEBUG.

    Takeaway: Makes SSM a practical SSH replacement so you can close port 22. Check recent commit activity before standardizing, since maintenance status is not stated.

  • Pinniped: The Easy, Secure Way to Log in to Your Kubernetes Clusters
    summary

    TL;DR: Pinniped is an Apache 2.0 project from VMware Tanzu that provides identity services for Kubernetes: it plugs external identity providers into clusters for one login experience across on-prem and managed cloud clusters.

    • Purpose: Authentication for Kubernetes using externally managed identities instead of shared credentials.
    • Single sign-on: Users log in once to reach all their clusters.
    • Tooling: Works with native tools such as kubectl.
    • Install: Described as easy to install on almost any Kubernetes cluster, including managed cloud environments.
    • IdPs: Repo topics list OIDC, LDAP and Active Directory; integrates with an enterprise IdP over standard protocols.
    • Numbers: About 742 stars and 5,000+ commits at fetch time.

    Takeaway: A self-hosted option for replacing static kubeconfigs and cloud-specific auth with one SSO flow across mixed clusters. See pinniped.dev for the component architecture before deploying.

  • The Dark Side of Domain-Specific Languages: Uncovering New Attack Techniques in OPA and Terraform
    summary

    TL;DR: Shelly Raban (Tenable, November 18, 2024, from her fwd:cloudsec Europe talk) shows how OPA Rego policies and Terraform code can be abused to execute code and exfiltrate secrets in pipelines.

    • OPA setup: An attacker with write access to the bucket OPA loads policies from uploads malicious Rego that runs at evaluation.
    • OPA exfil: opa.runtime().env plus http.send leaks environment variables; a Rego chain queries IMDSv2 for instance role credentials; net.lookup_ip_addr tunnels data via DNS even when http.send is blocked.
    • Terraform plan-time: PR pipelines running terraform plan (for example setup-terraform) execute data sources, so any PR author can run code on the runner.
    • Data sources: external runs a local program; http leaks secrets in URLs (IMDSv2 unreachable since it needs PUT); dns_a_record_set exfiltrates a Secrets Manager value via DNS.
    • Provisioners: local-exec (example pipes /etc/passwd to netcat) and remote-exec (coin miner on new EC2).
    • Mitigations: Separate plan and apply roles, vetted modules and providers, OPA capabilities.json allow_net, logging, and custom scanning before plan.

    Takeaway: Treat terraform plan on untrusted PRs as code execution. Give plan jobs minimal credentials and restrict network egress for OPA and Terraform runners.

  • AWS Application Load Balancer Announces CloudFront Integration with Built-In WAF
    summary

    TL;DR: AWS (November 15, 2024) added a one-click option in the ALB console that puts a CloudFront distribution with a preconfigured AWS WAF web ACL in front of an Application Load Balancer.

    • What it does: Creates and configures ALB, CloudFront and WAF together, replacing a manual multi-service setup.
    • Protection: Preconfigured WAF web ACL with basic protections against common web threats.
    • Origin lock-down: Optional security group allowing only CloudFront IPs; if it is the only inbound rule, all requests pass through CloudFront and WAF.
    • Caching: CloudFront caches HTML, CSS/JS and images per the app’s Cache-Control headers.
    • Pricing and regions: Standard ALB, CloudFront and WAF pricing; all commercial regions; new and existing ALBs.

    Takeaway: The fastest way to get edge WAF and origin lock-down for an ALB app. Review the default WAF rules and make sure the ALB is not still reachable directly.

  • Updated Whitepaper: Architecting for PCI DSS Segmentation and Scoping on AWS
    summary

    TL;DR: AWS Security Assurance Services (Abdul Javid, Padmakar Bhosale, Ted Tanner, November 15, 2024) announce an updated whitepaper on PCI DSS 4.0 segmentation and scoping on AWS.

    • Alignment: Follows the PCI Council’s information supplement on scoping and network segmentation, updated for PCI DSS 4.0.
    • New content: Reference architectures for account structure with AWS Organizations OUs, network-layer design patterns, firewall rule examples mapped to PCI requirements, and more hands-on segmentation scenarios.
    • Topics: Defining boundaries between in-scope and out-of-scope resources, east-west and north-south traffic flows, and account and network structure as the base of segmentation.
    • Key point: Software-defined networking and service choice can shrink the cardholder data environment compared with on-prem.
    • Audience: Engineers, QSAs and internal security assessors.

    Takeaway: If you run card data on AWS, use the whitepaper’s account and OU patterns to isolate the CDE early; account-level separation is the cheapest scope reduction.

  • Amazon EKS Now Supports Amazon Application Recovery Controller (ARC)
    summary

    TL;DR: Since October 22, 2024, Amazon EKS supports Amazon Application Recovery Controller (ARC) zonal shift and zonal autoshift to move in-cluster traffic away from an impaired Availability Zone.

    • Zonal shift: You trigger moving in-cluster network traffic for multi-AZ apps from an impaired AZ to healthy ones.
    • Zonal autoshift: AWS performs the shift for you when it detects AZ impairment.
    • Practice runs: Configurable tests to confirm the cluster runs with one less AZ.
    • Enable: EKS console, AWS CLI, CloudFormation or eksctl; then manage shifts via the ARC console, CLI or Zonal Shift APIs.
    • Regions: All commercial regions except GovCloud (US). Pricing is not mentioned.

    Takeaway: Enable it on multi-AZ clusters and run a practice shift; it exposes workloads that cannot survive losing an AZ (single replicas, zonal volumes, tight PDBs).

  • Hands-On Security Tips for Centralized Root Access in AWS (AssumeRoot)
    summary

    (Could not fetch full text.)

    TL;DR: A Medium post by oraspir with hands-on tips for AWS Organizations centralized root access and sts:AssumeRoot, including notes for CSPM and CDR tooling.

    • Feature: Centralized root access lets the management account (or a delegated admin) manage member account root credentials and run task-scoped root sessions instead of logging in as root.
    • Enable: Two features from the management account: root sessions (enables sts:AssumeRoot) and root credentials management (remove member root credentials).
    • AssumeRoot rules: Must be called with management or delegated-admin credentials, not root, and against a regional STS endpoint; the global endpoint is not supported. Sessions are visible in CloudTrail.
    • Hardening: Delegate to a dedicated security account, limit sts:AssumeRoot to who needs it, and narrow tasks with the sts:TaskPolicyArn condition key.
    • Source caveat: Medium returned 403; this summary is based on the post title, search snippets and AWS documentation, not the article’s specific tips.

    Takeaway: Enable centralized root access, delete member root credentials, and alert on AssumeRoot events in CloudTrail. Read the original post for its specific detection tips.

  • AWS Application Load Balancer Introduces Header Modification for Traffic Control and Security
    summary

    TL;DR: Since November 21, 2024, AWS Application Load Balancer can rename its TLS headers, insert response headers, and drop its Server header.

    • Rename: All ALB-generated TLS headers: the six mTLS headers and the two TLS version and cipher headers, so existing backends can keep their expected names.
    • Insert: Custom response headers such as CORS and security headers like HSTS (Strict-Transport-Security).
    • Remove: Disable the ALB-generated Server response header to reduce fingerprinting.
    • Regions: All commercial, GovCloud (US) and China regions. Pricing not mentioned.

    Takeaway: Set HSTS and strip the Server header at the ALB instead of in every app, and use header renaming to ease migrating mTLS backends.

  • Secure Root User Access for Member Accounts in AWS Organizations
    summary

    TL;DR: An AWS Security Blog post (Jonathan VanKim, Sowjanya Rajavaram, November 22, 2024) on centrally managing root access for AWS Organizations member accounts: removing root credentials and running short, task-scoped root sessions.

    • Root credentials management: Centrally view, delete and block recovery of member root passwords, access keys, signing certs and MFA.
    • Privileged root actions: Task-scoped root sessions of up to 15 minutes, started only from the management or delegated admin account with sts:AssumeRoot.
    • Enable (CLI): aws organizations enable-aws-service-access --service-principal iam.amazonaws.com, register-delegated-administrator, aws iam enable-organizations-root-sessions, aws iam enable-organizations-root-credentials-management.
    • Task policies: IAMDeleteRootUserCredentials, IAMCreateRootUserPassword, IAMAuditRootUserCredentials, S3UnlockBucketPolicy, SQSUnlockQueuePolicy under arn:aws:iam::aws:policy/root-task/.
    • Example: aws sts assume-root --target-principal <acct> --task-policy-arn arn=arn:aws:iam::aws:policy/root-task/S3UnlockBucketPolicy, then aws s3api delete-bucket-policy.
    • Caveats: New accounts get no root password; SCPs and VPC endpoint policies still apply to root sessions; restrict with sts:TaskPolicyArn.

    Takeaway: Turn this on, delegate to a security account, and delete member root credentials. It removes the need to vault dozens of root passwords and MFA devices.

  • How to Use AWS Resource Control Policies
    summary

    TL;DR: Scott Piper (Wiz, November 28, 2024) explains AWS Resource Control Policies (RCPs), the resource-side counterpart to SCPs, with practical example policies.

    • What: Org-wide guardrails on who can access your resources, including principals outside the Organization; they only restrict and never grant.
    • Services: S3, STS, SQS, Secrets Manager and KMS at launch.
    • Examples: Enforce TLS (1.3) on S3 org-wide; data perimeter statements; deny sts:AssumeRole unless aws:PrincipalOrgID matches or the caller is an approved vendor; restrict sts:AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity to a GitHub sub like repo:octo-org/*; block S3 deletes even from external accounts.
    • vs SCPs: SCPs do not apply to external principals, RCPs do; RCPs do not travel with an account that moves OU or Org.
    • Pain points: Denials return a generic AccessDenied that does not name the RCP; no dry-run, so review with Access Analyzer and CloudTrail and roll out sandbox-first.

    Takeaway: RCPs make data perimeter and OIDC trust restrictions enforceable in one place. Start with the GitHub OIDC and org-only AssumeRole examples, rolled out gradually.

  • Securely Share AWS Resources Across VPC and Account Boundaries with PrivateLink, VPC Lattice, EventBridge, and Step Functions
    summary

    TL;DR: Jeff Barr (AWS News Blog, December 1, 2024) introduces Resource Gateways and Resource Configurations, built on VPC Lattice and PrivateLink, to share private resources across VPCs and accounts and call them from EventBridge and Step Functions.
