    • CLI: The linked reference is aws logs start-live-tail. The announcement shows no syntax.
    • Filtering: Fine-grained filter and highlight controls. Specific syntax is not listed in the post.
    • Use: Brings the console experience to the terminal and to custom dashboards inside or outside AWS.
    • Regions: All commercial regions where CloudWatch Logs is available.
    • Pricing: Not stated. See the CloudWatch pricing page.

    Takeaway: Replace console tab-watching with aws logs start-live-tail during deploys. Check Live Tail pricing before leaving sessions open.

  • On Fire Drills and Phishing Tests
    summary

    TL;DR: Matt Linton (Google, “Chaos Specialist”) argues on the Google Security Blog (22 May 2024) that surprise phishing tests resemble early surprise fire evacuation tests and should be replaced by announced “phishing fire drills”.

    • Analogy: Early surprise fire tests caused injuries without improving survival. Engineering (wider doors, push bars, sprinklers) did, and drills became announced training.
    • Mandate: FedRAMP requires annual phishing tests and asks companies to bypass systemic anti-phishing controls during them.
    • Harms: No evidence tests reduce successful phishing; a cited 14,000-participant study found counterproductive effects and persistent repeat clickers. Tests flood D&R teams with reports, leave risky allowlists behind, and erode employee trust.
    • Drill design: Send an email that announces itself as a drill and asks staff to report it via the normal channel.
    • Metrics: Completion of the reporting exercise, time from open to first report, time to first escalation, report counts at 1, 4, 8 and 24 hours.
    • Real fix: Unphishable credentials such as passkeys and multi-party approval; Google says it has not seriously worried about password phishing in nearly a decade.

    Takeaway: Measure and train reporting, not click rates, and spend the effort on phishing-resistant auth.

  • Glasskube: The Next Generation Package Manager for Kubernetes
    summary

    TL;DR: Glasskube is an Apache 2.0 Kubernetes package manager with a GUI and CLI, offering dependency-aware, GitOps-ready packages from a central repository. The repo was archived (read-only) on 17 June 2026.

    • Features: Browser UI and CLI install, typed package configuration (UI or interactive CLI questionnaire), dependency resolution into correct namespaces, update preview and apply, multiple and private repositories.
    • Setup: brew install glasskube/tap/glasskube, glasskube bootstrap, glasskube serve (UI on http://localhost:8580), glasskube install [package].
    • GitOps: Every package is a Kubernetes custom resource, so it can live in Git. Renovate integration was in progress.
    • Claims: Says it is faster than Helm or Kustomize but gives no benchmark.
    • Status: Quick start labelled Beta; about 3.5k stars, 1,177 commits at archive time.

    Takeaway: Interesting take on CRD-based package management, but archived. Do not adopt for new clusters; stick with Helm/Flux/Argo.

  • Netfetch: Scan Kubernetes Clusters for Network Policies and Unprotected Workloads
    summary

    TL;DR: Netfetch is an MIT-licensed Go tool by deggja that scans Kubernetes clusters for network policies and flags workloads no policy targets, with a CLI and a Vue/D3 dashboard.

    • Scanning: Whole cluster or one namespace, save results to file, scan a specific policy to see which pods it selects.
    • Remediation: Can generate default-deny policies where missing; dashboard suggests editable policies from existing workloads.
    • Scoring: Each scan gives a 1-100 score that drops as more workloads lack a policy.
    • Commands: netfetch scan --dryrun, netfetch scan <namespace>, netfetch scan --target <policy-name>, netfetch dash --port 8081 (default 8080).
    • Install: Homebrew tap deggja/netfetch or a Helm chart for the in-cluster dashboard. Needs a kubectl context with rights to read and create network policies.
    • Policy support: Kubernetes NetworkPolicy and Cilium, including cluster-wide Cilium with --cilium.

    Takeaway: Quick way to find pods with no network isolation. Run --dryrun first and review generated default-deny policies before applying.

  • Centrally Manage Member Account Root Email Addresses Across Your AWS Organization
    summary

    TL;DR: AWS announcement (7 June 2024) that the Organizations management account or a delegated admin can now change member accounts’ root email addresses centrally, without signing in as root.

    • Interfaces: AWS CLI, SDKs and the Organizations console, via the Accounts API that already handled contacts and Region opt-in.
    • Verification: The new address must confirm a one-time password. The root email does not change until it is verified.
    • Cost and regions: No extra charge; all commercial and China regions.
    • Prerequisites: Not listed in the announcement; see the linked documentation.
    • Security angle: Removes a reason to log in as root and lets you move root emails off personal or stale mailboxes.

    Takeaway: Audit member account root emails and move them to controlled distribution lists centrally.

  • AWS Adds Passkey Multi-Factor Authentication (MFA) for Root and IAM Users
    summary

    TL;DR: Sébastien Stormacq on the AWS News Blog (11 June 2024): AWS adds FIDO2 passkeys as an MFA option for root and IAM users and begins enforcing MFA for root users.

    • Passkeys: Used as a second factor alongside the password, not a replacement. Domain-bound, so phishing-resistant. Synced passkeys (iCloud Keychain, Google, 1Password) and hardware keys both work.
    • Enforcement: Starts with root users of Organizations management accounts, rolled out a few thousand accounts at a time with a sign-in prompt and grace period. No per-stage dates given.
    • Exclusions: China (Beijing, Ningxia) and GovCloud (US) accounts, which have no root user.
    • Register: IAM console, user, Multi-factor authentication, Assign MFA device, choose passkey or security key, follow browser prompts.
    • Recovery: Multiple MFA devices per user are allowed.
    • Availability: All regions except China.

    Takeaway: Register at least two passkeys or keys on every root user now. Move humans to IAM Identity Center rather than IAM users.

  • How to Safeguard Your SSH Environment with Identity-Aware Proxy and Security Command Center
    summary

    TL;DR: Google Cloud post (14 June 2024, Rahul Ramachandran and Joakim Nydrén) using the XZ Utils backdoor (CVE-2024-3094) as a prompt to front SSH with Identity-Aware Proxy and prioritise exposure with Security Command Center.

    • Context: Google’s public Compute Engine images were not affected. Custom images should follow bulletin GCP-2024-021.
    • IAP controls: Access decided by user group, device context (managed device, disk encryption, OS version, mTLS certs) and network context (IP ranges, geolocation).
    • Attack surface: IAP removes the need for public IPs on VMs.
    • SCC Risk Engine: Attack path simulation, e.g. exposed instance to lateral movement to a high-value database.
    • Example: Cites Wayfair’s use of IAP device posture checks.
    • Limits: Mostly conceptual. No gcloud commands, firewall ranges or IAM roles; it links to the IAP TCP forwarding docs.

    Takeaway: Drop public IPs and SSH via IAP TCP forwarding with device-aware policies. Read the linked docs for the actual setup.

  • Introducing GKE Compliance: Maintain Clusters and Workloads Against Industry Standards
    summary

    TL;DR: Google (Poonam Lamba, 7 June 2024) introduces GKE Compliance, a managed part of GKE posture management that checks clusters and workloads against industry standards with no in-cluster install.

    • Standards: CIS Benchmark for GKE, and Pod Security Standards baseline and restricted profiles.
    • UI: Compliance tab in GKE posture management; fleet-wide or per-cluster view refreshed every 30 minutes.
    • Drill-down: Per-constraint details, non-compliant resources and remediation steps.
    • Pricing: Originally included in GKE Enterprise at no extra cost. A later note says GKE was consolidated into a single paid offering in September 2025.
    • Status: The post does not say preview or GA.

    Takeaway: If you run GKE, enable it for a free continuous CIS/PSS view before buying a third-party KSPM tool.

  • Mastering Go: Challenging Quiz on Advanced Concepts for Go Programmers
    summary

    TL;DR: A 12-question multiple-choice quiz on idyllic.app testing intermediate-to-advanced Go knowledge, by creator @martialdouble-t.

    • Format: Four options per question, one correct; score, share and retake at the end.
    • Topics: reflect package purpose, goroutines, buffered channels, the scheduler, select, sync.WaitGroup, closing channels, context for timeouts and cancellation, garbage collection, deadlock detection.
    • Popularity: About 3.5k plays, rated 3.9 from 5 ratings.
    • Depth: Concept-level questions, not code puzzles.

    Takeaway: A five-minute self-check on Go concurrency basics. Not a substitute for real practice.

  • Common Anti-Patterns in Go Web Applications
    summary

    TL;DR: Miłosz Smółka (Three Dots Labs, 2021) argues most Go web apps decay through tight coupling, and lists anti-patterns with fixes built on separate models and an application layer.

    • Single model: One struct for JSON, DB and validation couples everything. Use separate HTTP, storage and app models with plain mapping functions.
    • Overapplied DRY: Premature abstraction creates coupling; some repetition is fine.
    • Magic tags: ORM permission tags and cross-field validation tags lose compile-time safety. Prefer code generation (oapi-codegen, sqlboiler) and always set explicit tags.
    • Logic in handlers: Move rules into an application layer. Use types valid by construction instead of raw strings for IDs.
    • Schema-first / CRUD-first: Model domain behaviour (e.g. create team with owner in one call), not tables.
    • Distributed monolith: Do not split into microservices before boundaries are clear.
    • Numbers: Four implementations of one domain: 292 lines (strong coupling), 345 (medium), 298 + 2,154 generated (medium), 408 (weak coupling).

    Takeaway: Decoupling costs a bit more code up front. Start by splitting API and DB models; it pays off as the app grows.

  • Neosync: Open-Source Data Anonymization and Synthetic Data Orchestration
    summary

    TL;DR: Neosync is an MIT-licensed platform for anonymising production data, generating synthetic data and syncing it across environments. Acquired by Grow Therapy and archived on 30 August 2025; no longer maintained.

    • Features: Synthetic data from schema, PII anonymisation, SQL-based subsetting, referential integrity preserved.
    • Pipeline: Async jobs with retries using an event-sourcing model.
    • Transformers: Pre-built for common data types, plus custom JavaScript or LLM-based ones.
    • Integrations: PostgreSQL, MySQL, S3.
    • Deploy: Docker Compose (make compose/up, UI on localhost:3000) or Helm chart charts/neosync.
    • Config: Declarative, GitOps-style for CI.

    Takeaway: Good reference design for test-data anonymisation, but unmaintained. Choose a maintained alternative for new work.

  • Three Ways to Think About Channels
    summary

    TL;DR: Max Hoffman (DoltHub, June 2024) explains Go channels from three angles: as locked queues, as part of a set of concurrency primitives, and as CSP message passing.

    • Queue view: A fixed-size, lock-protected queue. Senders block when full; receivers drain after close. Writing to a closed channel or closing a nil/closed one is a bug.
    • Patterns: select with default for non-blocking trySend; a done channel as escape hatch.
    • Primitives: WaitGroup for known work where errors do not matter; errgroup for unbounded work, shutdown and context cancellation.
    • CSP view: Based on Hoare’s CSP. Sending pointers still shares memory; the main gain is cheap concurrency.
    • Real example: Dolt’s fetcher refactor uses about a dozen channel contexts to coordinate table downloads.
    • Caveat: Mutexes or atomics can be faster in some cases.

    Takeaway: When channel code confuses you, ask what a queue would do, and pair channels with errgroup for real shutdown handling.

  • A Pragmatic Guide to Go Module Updates
    summary

    TL;DR: Carlos Becker (GoReleaser maintainer, June 2024) explains Go module versioning in practice: tagging, moving to v2+, monorepo tags and retractions.

    • Initial versions: Untagged modules get pseudo-versions v0.0.0-{timestamp}-{commithash}. Tagging v0.1.0 is just a git tag.
    • Major versions: v2+ needs a /v2 module path suffix, e.g. module github.com/fake/mod/v2; users run go get github.com/fake/mod/v2@v2.0.0.
    • Import rewrite: Update imports before tagging or v2 depends on v1. His gomod-rename script runs go mod edit -module and sed over .go files.
    • Monorepos: Prefix tags with the directory, e.g. git tag ansi/v0.1.0.
    • Retraction: Add retract v11.0.1 with a reason to go.mod; users get a warning.

    Takeaway: Handy checklist for a v2 bump. Rewrite imports and verify the build before you push the tag.

  • Shameless Green: TDD in Go
    summary

    TL;DR: John Arundel (Bitfield Consulting), in an excerpt from The Power of Go: Tests, shows “shameless green” TDD: write the simplest code that passes the failing test, then tidy up.

    • Origin: Term from Sandi Metz and Katrina Owen’s 99 Bottles of OOP.
    • Example: A ListItems function for a text adventure, e.g. “You can see here a battery, a key, and a tourist map.”
    • Steps: Failing test, ugly passing code, cmp.Diff for clear failure output, refactor into a table test with a testCase struct, add one case at a time.
    • Rule: “New behaviour, new test”, so you know when you are done.
    • Advice: Correctness first, beauty second; shameless green code can ship if needed.

    Takeaway: Use cmp.Diff and table tests from the start, and resist designing before the tests force it.

  • Consistently Prepared: Year-Round Strategies for Career Growth
    summary

    TL;DR: Leif, a Senior Engineering Manager at Semgrep (ex-Segment, Twilio), gives software and security ICs year-round habits so review and promotion season is not a scramble, with tips for managers.

    • Hype list: A spreadsheet with Month, What, Impact, Notes columns, one tab per year. “If it isn’t recorded, it didn’t happen.”
    • Impact: Describe business or customer effect with metrics, not just what was built.
    • Artifacts: Design docs, project retros, quarterly team retros, and weekly notes on a recurring reminder.
    • Visibility: Demos, team-channel updates, recognising teammates, public writing or talks, documenting and training others.
    • Career ladders: IC and manager each rate a deconstructed ladder before reviews, then compare. Near promotion, fill in both current and next level.
    • Manager tips: Write reviews a successor could use, prepare calibration cheat sheets, line up other managers to vouch for reports.

    Takeaway: Start a hype list today and update it monthly; it turns self-reviews and promo cases into copy-paste work.

  • 6 Questions to Ask When Interviewing for an AppSec Role
    summary

    TL;DR: Louis Nyffenegger (PentesterLab founder) lists six questions AppSec candidates should ask at the end of an interview to judge whether the role fits (June 2024).

    • Build or buy: Shows whether the job is engineering-heavy or tool deployment and management.
    • Training: Conference and platform budget signals whether skills stay current.
    • Dev/DevOps relationship: Collaborative vs siloed or adversarial; does AppSec take part in adopting new tech.
    • Typical day: Meetings vs design reviews, code review or pentesting.
    • Next three problems: Gauges maturity and strategy vs constant firefighting.
    • Recent win: Shows what the team values and whether its strategy works.
    • Advice: Pick one or two that matter most; the interview is two-way.

    Takeaway: Keep these in your back pocket for AppSec interviews, especially “next three problems” to detect a reactive team.

  • The Path to Zero Touch Production (Slides)
    summary

    TL;DR: Rami McCarthy’s deck (June 2024) on moving toward Zero Touch Production, where humans do not touch prod directly and every change is automated, software-validated or made through audited break-glass.

    • Why: Human access brings risk from attackers and mistakes; the deck cites Google attributing 13% of incidents to human interaction.
    • Maturity stages: Initial (everyone admin, SSH), Foundational (standing RBAC, ~50 engineers), Established (granular RBAC, JIT, ~500), Advanced (shell phased out, guardrailed tools), Zero Touch.
    • Shell options compared: SSH, EC2 Instance Connect (and Endpoint), WireGuard, SSM Session Manager, ECS Exec, Verified Access, VDI, Cloud9. Recommends SSM by stage 3, ECS Exec for ECS.
    • Replacement capabilities: SSM RunCommand scripts, async jobs, internal tool platforms (Clutch, Retool, Django Admin), SSM Automation, read-only analytics, JIT and break-glass.
    • Metrics: Active shell access and incident MTTR.
    • Caveat: Zero touch is a north star, rarely the highest-ROI security investment.

    Takeaway: Use the stages to place your org, then invest in JIT access and a smooth access UX before trying to remove shells.

  • Stop Worrying About allowPrivilegeEscalation
    summary

    TL;DR: Christophe Tafani-Dereeper explains that Kubernetes allowPrivilegeEscalation only controls the Linux no_new_privs flag, so leaving it at the default true is far less dangerous than scanners suggest.

    • What it does: Sets no_new_privs on the container process so children cannot gain privileges via setuid/setgid binaries. runc applies it.
    • What it does not do: It does not let a process become root, escape the container or escalate in the cluster by itself, and does not block kernel exploits such as DirtyCow-style bugs.
    • Experiment: An Alpine image with a root-owned setuid binary calling setreuid/setregid got root with the option on; with it off the calls failed. A C program setting no_new_privs before a shell gave the same block.
    • Irrelevant cases: No practical effect for workloads already running as root; cannot be combined with privileged mode.
    • Verdict: Setting it to false is sound hardening, but its absence is not a critical finding.

    Takeaway: Set allowPrivilegeEscalation: false in baseline templates, but prioritise fixing privileged containers and root workloads first.

  • How We Hacked Multi-Billion Dollar Companies in 30 Minutes Using a Fake VSCode Extension
    summary

    (Could not fetch full text.)

    TL;DR: Part 1 of a series by Amit Assaraf, Itay Kruk and Idan Dardikman (later Koi Security) on publishing a fake “Darcula” copy of the Dracula Official VS Code theme to show how weak Marketplace trust signals are.

    • Setup: Built in about 30 minutes from the real theme’s source plus a collection script. Registered darculatheme.com to get a verified publisher badge via DNS verification alone, and linked the real Dracula repo.
    • Data collected: Hostname, domain, OS platform and installed extension count sent to their server.
    • Reach: 100+ installs within a day, including a machine at a company worth $483 billion, large security vendors and a national court network.
    • Weaknesses: 45,000 publishers but only 1,800 verified; package.json repo URLs are not checked; no extension permission model; auto-update on by default. A 2018 permissions request (microsoft/vscode #52116) got no response.
    • Follow-up: Their ExtensionTotal scanner reported 1,283 extensions with known malicious code (229M installs), 8,161 talking to hardcoded IPs, 2,304 using another publisher’s repo.
    • Source caveat: Medium returned 403. Based on the GIGAZINE write-up and BleepingComputer/BankInfoSecurity coverage found via search.

    Takeaway: Treat VS Code extensions as unsandboxed code. Allowlist extensions on developer machines and do not trust the verified badge.

  • Taking a Look at Kubernetes Profiling
    summary

    TL;DR: Rory McCune (raesene, June 2024) looks at the Go pprof profiling endpoints Kubernetes components expose by default and what someone with access can do with them.

    • Exposure: /debug/pprof/profile is on by default in kube-apiserver, kube-scheduler, kube-controller-manager and the Kubelet; kube-proxy is the exception.
    • AuthZ: Control-plane endpoints use RBAC non-resource URLs (usually cluster-admin). Kubelet profiling sits under node/proxy.
    • Log level change: curl -X PUT http://127.0.0.1:8001/debug/flags/v -d "10" sets debug verbosity remotely.
    • Profiling: go tool pprof -http=:8080 http://localhost:8001/debug/pprof/profile.
    • Risks: In managed clusters, raised log levels could enable CVE-2020-8561-style leaks or DoS; traces might contain sensitive data (not observed).
    • Disable: --profiling=false for apiserver, controller-manager, scheduler; enableDebuggingHandlers for Kubelet.

    Takeaway: Turn profiling off in production and audit who holds node/proxy, which is more powerful than it looks.

  • GCPwn: Enumeration and Exploitation Framework for GCP, Modeled Like Pacu for AWS
    summary

    TL;DR: GCPwn is a BSD-3 Python framework from NetSPI, by Scott (@WebbinRoot), for enumerating, testing permissions on and exploiting GCP and Google Workspace, modelled on Pacu for AWS.

    • Coverage: About 44 Google Cloud client libraries, including Storage, IAM, GKE, Cloud Run, Secret Manager, Functions, Compute, BigQuery, Artifact Registry. Limited Workspace (users, groups, roles, OUs, devices, OAuth grants).
    • Permission checks: testIamPermissions calls plus IAM binding analysis.
    • Loot: Optional download of bucket contents and secret values; experimental Drive download.
    • Exploit modules: E.g. service account impersonation and Workload Identity Federation exchange.
    • Output: JSON, CSV, Excel and BloodHound CE OpenGraph JSON for attack paths.
    • Install: pip3 install gcpwn (extras gcpwn[table,excel]), or clone and python -m gcpwn, binary or Docker.

    Takeaway: The GCP equivalent of Pacu for authorised assessments. Run it with a leaked-credential scenario to see real blast radius.

  • How to Create a Pipeline for Hardening Amazon EKS Nodes and Automate Updates
    summary

    TL;DR: AWS Security Blog post by Nima Fotouhi (June 2024) building a pipeline that applies CIS benchmarks to EKS-optimised AMIs and rolls hardened images out to managed node groups automatically.

    • Benchmarks: CIS Amazon Linux 2 v2.0.0 and Amazon Linux 2023 v1.0.0 via Ansible Lockdown roles.
    • Build: EC2 Image Builder applies the roles, publishes the AMI, stores benchmark results in S3 and triggers an Amazon Inspector scan.
    • Rollout: SNS and Lambda start a state machine that creates new launch template versions and updates EKS managed node groups.
    • Freshness: A weekly EventBridge rule runs a Lambda that checks for a newer EKS-optimised parent AMI and notifies subscribers.
    • Deploy: CloudFormation template from a GitHub repo; parameters include Ansible args and ClusterTags to select clusters.
    • Prerequisites: EKS cluster with custom-launch-template node groups, AWS CLI, Inspector enabled.
    • Caveat: Do a threat analysis and review each CIS control for workload compatibility first.

    Takeaway: A ready template if you must ship CIS-hardened nodes. Test controls in a non-prod cluster since some break kubelet or workloads.

  • Cloud Security Posture and Contextualization Across Cloud Boundaries from a Single Dashboard
    summary

    (Could not fetch full text.)

    TL;DR: A Microsoft Defender for Cloud blog post on the Microsoft Community Hub (2024) about viewing cloud security posture and context across clouds from one dashboard.

    • Scope: Per Microsoft docs on the same feature set, the Defender for Cloud overview covers Azure, AWS, GCP, on-prem and connected DevOps tools in one place.
    • Posture score: Findings roll into a single secure score; higher means less identified risk.
    • Context: Attack path analysis and risk-based prioritisation by exploitability and business impact.
    • Scoping: Tenant-level or scoped views with unified RBAC per persona.
    • Source caveat: The page is JS-rendered and returned only its title. Points are based on Microsoft Learn docs for the Defender for Cloud overview dashboard found via search, not the post itself.

    Takeaway: Relevant if you run Defender CSPM across multiple clouds. Read the Microsoft Learn overview page for current details.

13.05.2024

  • Detecting Manual AWS Actions: An Update!
    summary

    TL;DR: Arkadiy Tetelman (Feb 2024) updates his 2019 method for alerting on manual (non-IaC) AWS changes, replacing user-agent matching with an identity invariant from Okta SAML session names.

    • Old approach: Matched console user-agent strings; brittle and missed CLI/API activity.
    • Invariant: Humans reach AWS only through Okta and AssumeRoleWithSAML, and Okta sets the role session name to the employee’s email.
    • Rule: Alert when the session name ends in the company domain, CloudTrail readOnly is false, and the event is not on an exception list.
    • Exceptions: A hardcoded list fixes AWS events mislabelled as read/write; some mutating events are excluded for operational reasons.
    • Bypass detection: A second alert on AssumeRole where the original session name ends in the company domain and the new one differs.
    • Caveats: The exception list is tailored to his services; events like ConsoleLogin may deserve dedicated alerts.

    Takeaway: If humans federate through one IdP, key detections on session name plus readOnly instead of user agents. Add the session-rename alert or it is trivially bypassed.

  • Popular Git Config Options
    summary

    TL;DR: Julia Evans (Feb 2024) compiles the most popular git config options from a Mastodon poll, with what each does.

    • Pull: pull.ff only or pull.rebase true to avoid accidental merge commits.
    • Conflicts: merge.conflictstyle zdiff3 shows the original code; rerere.enabled true reuses resolutions.
    • Rebase: rebase.autosquash true, rebase.autostash true.
    • Push: push.default simple/current, push.autoSetupRemote true.
    • Diffs: diff.algorithm histogram, diff.colorMoved default, core.pager delta, commit.verbose true.
    • Misc: init.defaultBranch main, help.autocorrect, core.excludesfile, includeIf for work/personal configs, url."git@github.com:".insteadOf, fsckobjects true, branch.sort -committerdate.
    • Caveat: Many defaults have changed, so some options are now redundant.

    Takeaway: Worth a skim to steal three or four settings, zdiff3, histogram and autoSetupRemote being the usual wins.

  • Security Centralization for AWS Multi-Account Using Native Services
    summary

    TL;DR: Nitesh Saini (InfraCloud, March 2024) walks through centralising security, logging and access across AWS accounts with Organizations and native services run from delegated admin accounts.

    • Structure: OUs by environment or project; management account at the top; dedicated security and logging accounts as delegated administrators.
    • Baseline: IAM Identity Center (federation, permission sets), org CloudTrail (KMS, log file validation, Insights), GuardDuty with auto-enable, Security Hub (needs Config recording), Config aggregator, Inspector for EC2/ECR/Lambda.
    • Advanced: IAM Access Analyzer, Detective, Macie, Systems Manager, S3 Storage Lens, CloudFormation StackSets, Trusted Advisor.
    • Steps: Enable trusted access, delegate admins, convert trail to org trail, enable GuardDuty, Config then Security Hub, aggregator, Inspector.
    • IaC: Only CloudFormation StackSets is mentioned; mostly console steps.
    • Source caveat: The InfraCloud URL now redirects to improving.com; summary based on the identical DEV Community cross-post.

    Takeaway: A solid checklist for a native multi-account security baseline. Codify it in Terraform or Control Tower rather than clicking through.

  • How to Develop an Amazon Security Lake POC
    summary

    TL;DR: AWS Security Blog guide (Feb 2024, Anna McAbee, Marc Luescher, Marshall Jones) on planning and running an Amazon Security Lake proof of concept.

    • Six steps: Understand the service, set success criteria, define configuration, prepare, enable, validate.
    • Success criteria examples: Centralise org logs, cheaper VPC Flow Logs into a SIEM, augment on-prem SIEM with OpenSearch, feed SageMaker, QuickSight dashboard of Security Hub findings.
    • Sources: CloudTrail, VPC Flow Logs, Route 53 Resolver logs, partner and custom sources; EKS and WAF logs added in a Sept 2024 update.
    • Format: Normalised to OCSF and stored as compressed Parquet.
    • Subscribers: Athena and other AWS services, or partner SIEMs.
    • Cost: 15-day free trial per account from enablement; enable all accounts during the trial to get a realistic estimate.
    • Timeline: Third-party sources usually take longer; consider a second phase.

    Takeaway: Use the trial window deliberately: turn on every account and source you plan to keep, then read the usage page before committing.

  • How I Keep Myself Alive Using Golang
    summary

    TL;DR: Matt Boyle (Cloudflare engineering manager, Type 1 diabetic) describes a Go system on Encore that monitors his blood glucose and treats lows as incidents with escalation (ByteSizeGo, March 2024).

    • Ingest: A Miao Miao reader scans his Libre sensor every two minutes; the Tomato app posts readings to his endpoint (he used an echo server to learn the payload).
    • Metrics: Each reading updates a gauge shown in Grafana; also stored in Postgres best-effort, logging errors rather than failing.
    • Annotations: A Telegram bot logs food, exercise and insulin as Grafana annotations.
    • Alerting: A 5-minute cron opens an incident.io incident when glucose is below 4; texting “i need help” also opens one.
    • Escalation: Unresolved incidents page family members after 20 minutes.
    • Stack: Encore for APIs, cron, metrics and logs; Go stdlib net/http, encoding/json.

    Takeaway: A neat example of applying on-call tooling to a personal problem, and of how little code Encore needs for cron plus metrics.

  • Auditing AWS EKS Pod Permissions
    summary

    TL;DR: Eric Johnson (Puma Security, Feb 2024) explains the three ways EKS pods get AWS permissions and gives scripts to map each pod to its IAM policies.

    • Node role via IMDS: Pods reach IMDS by default and inherit the node role, which mixes kubelet and workload permissions and enables cross-namespace escalation.
    • IRSA: Service account annotation eks.amazonaws.com/role-arn, webhook-injected env vars, sts:AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity via the cluster OIDC provider.
    • EKS Pod Identity: Associations defined at cluster level, credentials from a link-local endpoint with a token file.
    • Mitigation: IMDSv2 with hop limit 1, or a Calico NetworkPolicy denying egress to 169.254.169.254/32.
    • Audit: IRSA: kubectl get serviceaccounts -A then aws iam list-attached-role-policies. Pod Identity: aws eks list-pod-identity-associations and describe-pod-identity-association.
    • Tools: jq, Terraform metadata_options, Datadog’s Managed Kubernetes Auditing Toolkit (MKAT).

    Takeaway: Block IMDS from pods first, then use the scripts or MKAT to inventory which service accounts carry which IAM rights.

  • GitHub Enables Push Protection by Default to Stop Secrets Leaks
    summary

    TL;DR: BleepingComputer (Sergiu Gatlan, 29 Feb 2024): GitHub turned on secret scanning push protection by default for all public repositories.

    • What it does: Scans pushes and blocks commits containing secrets before they land.
    • Coverage: Over 200 token types and patterns from more than 180 providers (API keys, private keys, access tokens).
    • History: Beta April 2022, GA for public repos May 2023.
    • Rollout: Could take a week or two to reach each account.
    • Bypass: Remove the secret or mark it safe and bypass; can be disabled in settings (not recommended).
    • Numbers: Over 1 million secrets leaked in public repos in the first eight weeks of 2024, “more than a dozen accidental leaks every minute”.
    • Private repos: Need GitHub Advanced Security on Enterprise.

    Takeaway: Free safety net for public repos. Also enable it for private repos where licensed and still run your own pre-commit scanner.

  • GopherCon 2023 Talks
    summary

    TL;DR: Gopher Academy’s official YouTube playlist of GopherCon 2023 talks, about 23 videos.

    • Language and stdlib: “Go Changes” (Russ Cox), “Everything You Always Wanted to Know About Type Inference” (Robert Griesemer), “Structured Logging for the Standard Library” (Jonathan Amsterdam), “The Future of JSON in Go” (Joe Tsai).
    • Security: “High-Assurance Go Cryptography” (Filippo Valsorda), “Vulnerability Management for Go” (Julie Qiu), “Understanding Supply Chain Threats with Static Analysis” (Jess McClintock).
    • Performance: “Building a Highly Concurrent Cache in Go” (Konrad Reiche), “Balanced GC: A Copying Garbage Collector” (Yifei Zhang), “Blazing Fast Merge with Loser Trees” (Bryan Boreham).
    • Practice: “Idiomatic Go Tells a Story” (Kaylyn Gibilterra), “Clean Up Your GOOOP” (Dylan Bourque), “Reliably Absorbing a Go Release” (Madhav Jivrajani).
    • Tools and fun: Bubble Tea TUIs (Andy Haskell), Orchestrion auto-instrumentation (Jon Bodner), distributed systems (Philip O’Toole), a pinball machine revival (Jeremy Fleitz).

    Takeaway: For security-minded Go devs, start with Valsorda, Qiu and McClintock, then Russ Cox’s “Go Changes”.

  • Arcjet JS SDKs: Rate Limiting, Bot Protection and Attack Defense for Next.js and Node.js
    summary

    TL;DR: Arcjet JS is an Apache 2.0 monorepo of runtime security SDKs for JavaScript/TypeScript apps and AI agents, adding rate limiting, bot protection, WAF-style shielding and more inside your code.

    • Rules: Rate limiting (token bucket, fixed and sliding window, per-user AI token budgets), bot detection by category, Shield against OWASP Top 10, email validation (disposable, invalid), prompt injection and sensitive info detection, IP analysis (VPN, proxy, Tor, hosting), filters and custom rules.
    • Entry points: Request SDKs for HTTP routes; @arcjet/guard for agent tool calls, MCP handlers, queues and jobs.
    • Frameworks: Next.js, Node.js, Bun, Deno, Express, Fastify, Hono, NestJS, Nuxt, Remix, React Router, SvelteKit, Astro.
    • Local analysis: WebAssembly packages (analyze-wasm, redact-wasm); sensitive info detection runs on-device.
    • Setup: npx @arcjet/cli auth login, then e.g. npm i @arcjet/next. Needs an ARCJET_KEY.
    • Caveat: Requires the Arcjet hosted service and key; the README does not fully state which checks are local.

    Takeaway: A quick way to add rate limits and bot blocking in code for JS apps. Weigh the SaaS dependency against a WAF or self-hosted limiter.

  • Hot Takes Episode 1: Protect Your Infrastructure from Yourself
    summary

    (Could not fetch full text.)

    TL;DR: Episode 1 of Teleport’s “Hot Takes” panel series (Nov 2023, about 30 minutes), arguing that human error, not hackers or ransomware, is the biggest threat to infrastructure security.

    • Panel: Kubernetes community figures Kat Cosgrove, Divya Mohan, Frederick Kautz, Chris Short and Kunal Kushwaha.
    • Thesis: “Protect your infrastructure from yourself”: mistakes by operators outweigh external attackers.
    • Publisher: Teleport, an infrastructure access vendor, so expect framing toward access controls.
    • Length: 1,781 seconds (about 30 minutes), published 17 Nov 2023.
    • Source caveat: No transcript available. Based only on the YouTube title, channel and description.

    Takeaway: Background viewing on the case for guardrails and least privilege against operator error. Pair with zero-touch-prod material for concrete steps.

  • haiti: Hash Type Identifier CLI and Library
    summary

    TL;DR: Haiti is an MIT-licensed Ruby CLI and library by Alexandre Zanni (noraj) that identifies hash types and gives the matching Hashcat and John the Ripper formats.

    • Coverage: 675+ hash types, including modern ones such as SHA3, Keccak and Blake2.
    • Cracking refs: Shows Hashcat mode and John format for each candidate.
    • Install: gem install haiti-hash; also Docker, Debian and openSUSE packages.
    • Origin: Forked from Orange-Cyberdefense/haiti; about 1k stars.

    Takeaway: A modern replacement for hashid/hash-identifier that saves looking up Hashcat mode numbers.

  • ServerlessHorrors: Stories of Surprise Serverless Bills
    summary

    TL;DR: ServerlessHorrors is a blog by Andras (Coolify, coolLabs) collecting stories of surprise cloud and serverless bills from bandwidth spikes, DoS, runaway loops and confusing pricing.

    • Providers featured: Vercel, Cloudflare, AWS, Google Firebase and Cloud Run, BigQuery, Netlify, Mailgun, PostHog, Webflow, Framer, Mintlify.
    • Largest bills listed: Cloudflare about $120,000, Netlify about $104,500, Firebase about $100,000, Vercel about $96,280, Firebase/Cloud Run about $72,000.
    • Smaller ones: AWS $103 and $4,241, Vercel $620 to $46,485, PostHog $530 and $1,273.
    • Format: Short posts with tags and RSS; submissions by email or GitHub PR.
    • Caveat: The author builds Coolify, a self-hosted PaaS, so the site has an obvious angle.

    Takeaway: Set billing alerts, spend caps and rate limits before launch; usage-priced platforms bill attacks too.

  • From Lighthouse to Loran: Navigating GCP Security Auditing Tools
    summary

    TL;DR: Alex Morgan surveys native and open-source tools for auditing GCP security, organised around access control, visibility and misconfiguration.

    • Native: Security Command Center standard tier (free, fewer detectors, project-level visibility), Policy Analyzer and IAM Recommender (some features moved to SCC premium after 29 April 2024), gcloud, and the unofficial GCP Scanner for credential-leak impact.
    • Open source: Prowler (CIS, NIST, PCI-DSS; HTML/JSON/CSV), ScoutSuite (multi-cloud, customisable rules), CloudSploit, Cloud Custodian (enforcement, careful with termination actions), Steampipe (SQL over APIs), Purple Panda (privilege escalation paths).
    • Other: HackTricks, Cloud Vuln DB, Chronicle, GCPBucketBrute, Awesome Cloud Security.
    • Archived: Forseti and Security Monkey, since GCP built-ins cover their goals.
    • Verdict: Prowler and ScoutSuite give the best overview; Steampipe extends visibility.

    Takeaway: For a first GCP audit run Prowler or ScoutSuite plus free SCC, then Steampipe for custom queries.

  • Check Out the Shiny New Cloud Security Maturity Model 2.0!
    summary

    TL;DR: Rich Mogull (Securosis, 27 Feb 2024) announces Cloud Security Maturity Model 2.0, built with IANS Research and peer-reviewed by the Cloud Security Alliance.

    • Change: A cloud-native framework rather than existing frameworks stretched to cloud, after about nine months of research.
    • Structure: Nearly 100 control objectives usable as KPIs, in 12 categories across 3 domains, with maturity levels up to 5.
    • Mappings: Objectives map to assessable technical controls for AWS; Azure and GCP planned.
    • Usage: Start with the IANS self-assessment diagnostic (no technical access), then track with the FireMon Cloud Defense CSMM dashboard or the spreadsheet.
    • Cost: Model, diagnostic and dashboard are free; download needs no registration.
    • Disclosure: The author is IANS faculty and manages the Cloud Defense product.
    • Quote: “We don’t lack tools, but we do lack priorities.”

    Takeaway: Useful for setting a prioritised cloud security roadmap. Not every org should target level 5.

  • Ludus: Build Easy-to-Use Cyber Ranges for Testing and Development
    summary

    TL;DR: Ludus, from Bad Sector Labs, is an AGPLv3 system on Proxmox for building cyber ranges (test and lab environments) such as Active Directory networks from a few commands.

    • Automation: From a Debian 12 install to a deployed virtual AD network with a few commands.
    • Networks: Up to 254 arbitrary /24 networks with controllable traffic flow.
    • OPSEC testing mode: Snapshots VMs and cuts internet, with selective allow of domains or IPs to test live C2 without leaking telemetry.
    • Ansible and Packer: Deploy any Ansible role (Galaxy, URL, local); build templates with Packer HCL/JSON, 13 included.
    • Multi-user: Shared or private ranges; all commands support JSON output.
    • Install: Copy the ludus-server binary to a clean Debian 12 host and run it; docs at docs.ludus.cloud.

    Takeaway: A fast way to stand up repeatable AD labs for red-team tooling or detection testing on your own Proxmox box.

  • Persistence: Visual Studio Code Extensions
    summary

    TL;DR: Penetration Testing Lab (March 2024) shows how a red team can persist on a developer machine with a custom VS Code extension that runs code every time the editor starts. Technique first described by Secarma.

    • Scaffold: npm install -g yo generator-code, then yo code creates package.json and extension.ts.
    • Trigger: Activation event "*" in package.json runs the extension on every VS Code start.
    • Payload: activate() registers and immediately executes a command that uses child_process.exec to run whoami or a local implant binary that calls back to C2.
    • Packaging: npm install -g @vscode/vsce, vsce package --allow-missing-repository --allow-star-activation.
    • Install: code --install-extension persistence-pentestlab-0.0.1.vsix.
    • Blend-in: Developers and detection engineers often run VS Code, so the process tree looks normal.

    Takeaway: Defenders should inventory installed extensions, alert on "*" activation and on code --install-extension of local .vsix files, and watch VS Code spawning unexpected children.

  • Banish OEM Self-Signed Certs Forever and Roll Your Own Private LetsEncrypt
    summary

    TL;DR: Lee Hutchinson (Ars Technica, 15 March 2024) walks homelab admins through running Smallstep’s step-ca as a private ACME CA so LAN services get trusted, auto-renewing certificates instead of self-signed ones.

    • Why: Self-signed certs train you to ignore TLS warnings and give encryption without identity verification.
    • Host: An Ubuntu 22.04 LXC container with 512 MB RAM and 8 GB disk; ARM builds exist for a Raspberry Pi.
    • Install: step-cli and step-ca .deb packages via dpkg -i, then step ca init (standalone) and step ca provisioner add acme --type ACME.
    • Service: Move config to /etc/step-ca, run as a step system user, setcap CAP_NET_BIND_SERVICE, systemd unit, systemctl enable --now step-ca.
    • Trust: Copy root_ca.crt and intermediate_ca.crt to /usr/local/share/ca-certificates/ and run update-ca-certificates on clients.
    • Clients: acme.sh (certbot or others work) using DNS-01 with nsupdate against the bind server from part one, authenticated with rndc.key.

    Takeaway: A clear recipe to run your own LetsEncrypt on the LAN. Protect the CA key and password file, since anyone holding them can mint trusted certs for your network.

  • CISA and NSA Release Cybersecurity Information Sheets on Cloud Security Best Practices
    summary

    TL;DR: CISA alert (7 March 2024) announcing five joint CISA/NSA Cybersecurity Information Sheets with cloud security best practices and mitigations.

    • IAM: Secure cloud identity and access management practices.
    • Key management: Secure handling of cryptographic keys in the cloud.
    • Network: Network segmentation and encryption in cloud environments.
    • Data: Securing data stored and processed in the cloud.
    • MSPs: Reducing risk when managed service providers run your cloud.
    • Related: Points to CISA’s SCuBA project and Trusted Internet Connections guidance.
    • Context: These are five of NSA’s ten-part “Top Ten Cloud Security Mitigation Strategies” series released the same day.

    Takeaway: Short, vendor-neutral checklists useful for policy baselines or audit evidence. Start with the IAM and key management sheets.

  • NSA Releases Top Ten Cloud Security Mitigation Strategies
    summary

    (Could not fetch full text.)

    TL;DR: NSA press release (7 March 2024) announcing “Top Ten Cloud Security Mitigation Strategies”, ten Cybersecurity Information Sheets, six co-authored with CISA.

    • 1-3: Uphold the shared responsibility model; secure cloud IAM; secure key management.
    • 4-5: Network segmentation and encryption; secure data in the cloud.
    • 6-7: Defend CI/CD environments; enforce secure automated deployment through infrastructure as code.
    • 8-9: Account for hybrid and multi-cloud complexity; mitigate risks from managed service providers.
    • 10: Manage cloud logs for effective threat hunting.
    • Premise: The accompanying PDF notes many cloud breaches stem from tenant misconfigurations.
    • Source caveat: nsa.gov returned 403. Based on search results (Infosecurity Magazine, CSIAC) and the linked CSI PDF listing.

    Takeaway: Use the ten sheets as a gap-analysis checklist; CI/CD, IaC and logging are the ones most teams under-invest in.

  • The Missing Guide to AWS API Gateway Access Logs
    summary

    TL;DR: Alex DeBrie’s long-form guide (January 2021) to configuring, formatting and querying AWS API Gateway access logs, the one-line-per-request logs you want for debugging things like 500 spikes.

    • Access vs execution logs: Access logs write one line per request. Execution logs produced 32 lines for a single request in his test, so he keeps them off normally.
    • Formats: CLF, CSV, JSON or XML. He prefers JSON for readability; a sample JSON line was about 250 bytes versus 103 for CLF.
    • IAM role gotcha: The CloudWatch log role is a per-region singleton set via AWS::ApiGateway::Account. Deleting the stack that owns it can silently stop logging for every API in the region; use DeletionPolicy: Retain or a standalone stack.
    • Useful fields: requestId, status, responseLatency, integration.requestId. Keep numbers unquoted but quote - placeholders so the JSON stays valid.
    • Tooling: Serverless Framework (provider.logs), SAM (AccessLogSetting for REST, AccessLogSettings for HTTP APIs), CDK (AccessLogFormat.custom).
    • Querying: CloudWatch filter { $.status >= 500 } and Logs Insights aggregations grouped by resourcePath.
    • Limits: HTTP APIs lack X-Ray and resourcePath (use routeKey); authorize.latency always showed 0; CDK’s built-in JSON format omits useful fields.

    Takeaway: Turn on JSON access logs with a custom field set, and keep the account-level CloudWatch role out of any stack you might delete.

  • CloudGrappler: Query High-Fidelity Threat Actor Detections in AWS and Azure
    summary

    TL;DR: CloudGrappler is an Apache 2.0 Python tool from Permiso that runs high-fidelity, single-event threat-actor detections against cloud logs stored in AWS S3, Azure containers and GCP buckets.

    • Engine: Built on cloudgrep, which searches log objects directly in storage rather than in a SIEM.
    • Scope config: data_sources.json lists AWS buckets/prefixes and Azure accounts/containers; a query source of * scans both AWS and Azure.
    • Usage: python3 main.py runs default queries, -p adds Permiso threat-intel use cases, -jo writes JSON reports to reports/json.
    • Filtering: -sd 2024-02-15 -ed 2024-02-16 for a date range, -q "UpdateAccessKey" -s '*' for an ad-hoc query, -f new_file.json for a custom query file.
    • Auth: AWS CLI config or instance profile, az login, and GOOGLE_APPLICATION_CREDENTIALS for GCP.
    • Limits: README recommends short time ranges for speed; no benchmarks or volume limits documented.

    Takeaway: Handy for quick IOC sweeps over raw CloudTrail/Azure logs in storage when you have no SIEM or need a second look during an incident.

  • How We Sped Up AWS CloudFormation Deployments with Optimistic Stabilization
    summary

    TL;DR: AWS DevOps blog post (March 2024, Bhavani Kanneganti and Idriss Laouali Abdou) explaining CloudFormation’s new optimistic stabilization strategy, which AWS says cuts deployment time by up to 40%.

    • Time breakdown: Provisioning = engine time + resource creation time + resource stabilization time.
    • Stabilization: Post-create checks that a resource is actually usable before it is marked CREATE_COMPLETE; failure within the timeout gives CREATE_FAILED and a rollback.
    • Example: aws ecs create-service returns ACTIVE while tasks are still pending, so CloudFormation polls DescribeServices until the service is steady.
    • Old behavior: Dependent resources waited for dependencies to fully stabilize.
    • New behavior: Dependents start as soon as dependencies are created; if a dependent fails, CloudFormation waits for the dependency to stabilize and retries.
    • Visibility: New CONFIGURATION_COMPLETE event status.
    • Caveat: The 40% is an “up to” figure from AWS, not a guarantee.

    Takeaway: No action needed to benefit, but expect CONFIGURATION_COMPLETE events in stack timelines and faster large-stack deploys.

  • Introducing Security Command Center Enterprise: Multicloud Risk Management with AI-Powered SecOps
    summary

    TL;DR: Google Cloud’s March 2024 announcement (Sunil Potti) of Security Command Center Enterprise, combining cloud posture/risk management with Chronicle-style SIEM/SOAR, Mandiant threat intel and generative AI across Google Cloud, AWS and Azure.

    • Risk engine: Builds a “digital twin” of the environment, simulates attacker paths, and provides attack-path visualization and risk scoring.
    • Coverage: Vulnerability and posture management, threat detection, CIEM, DSPM, AI workload protection and IaC/CI/CD scanning.
    • SecOps: Findings flow into cases with out-of-the-box response playbooks.
    • Mandiant Hunt: Optional on-demand human threat hunting.
    • Availability: GA “in the coming weeks” at announcement, subscription with workload-based pricing; existing SCC Premium customers could upgrade at no extra cost.
    • Caveats: Marketing post; no technical configuration, commands or performance data.

    Takeaway: Relevant if you are evaluating CNAPP plus SIEM from one vendor on GCP; treat the claims as vendor positioning until you trial it.

  • Now Available: Free Data Transfer Out to Internet When Leaving Azure
    summary

    (Could not fetch full text.)

    TL;DR: Microsoft’s March 13, 2024 Azure Update announcing free internet egress for customers moving their data out of Azure, following Google (January 2024) and AWS (March 5, 2024).

    • Offer: Exiting customers can transfer data over the internet to another cloud or on-premises at no charge, from any Azure region, on top of the standard 100 GB/month free egress.
    • Process: Contact Azure Support with the planned start date and data volume, finish within 60 days, and cancel all subscriptions. The credit is applied only after transfer completes and all subscriptions on the account are cancelled.
    • Exclusions: Per press coverage, specialized services such as ExpressRoute, VPN, Azure Front Door and Azure CDN are still charged.
    • Driver: Coverage links it to the EU Data Act switching provisions.
    • Criticism: Only applies when fully leaving Azure, not to multicloud egress.
    • Source caveat: The original update URL now lands on the generic Azure Updates feed; summary is based on search results (The Register, TechCrunch, CIO Dive, SDxCentral).

    Takeaway: Useful leverage in exit planning or vendor negotiation, but it does nothing for ongoing multicloud egress costs.

  • M365Documentation: Automatic Microsoft 365 Tenant Documentation
    summary

    TL;DR: M365Documentation by Thomas Kurth is a PowerShell 7 module that generates documentation of a Microsoft 365 tenant’s configuration; it succeeds his IntuneDocumentation module.

    • Coverage: Intune, Entra ID (Azure AD), Cloud Print, Microsoft Information Protection and Windows 365 Cloud PC.
    • Outputs: JSON (good for backups and diffing configs over time), CSV, Markdown, HTML and Word (DOCX).
    • Workflow: Connect-M365Doc, Get-M365DocValidSection, Get-M365Doc, then Write-M365DocWord.
    • Dependencies: Installs from the PowerShell Gallery; uses MSAL.PS for certificate or secret auth and PSWriteOffice 1.0.2+ for Word export (start a new session after updating).
    • Limits: Only assigned Intune apps are documented; component coverage is still growing; custom app registration is in a separate doc.

    Takeaway: A cheap way to snapshot M365/Intune config as JSON for change tracking or handover docs; schedule it with an app registration and diff the output.

  • More Powerful Go Execution Traces
    summary

    TL;DR: Go blog post (March 2024, Michael Knyszek) on the overhauled runtime/trace execution tracer: much lower overhead, scalable traces, flight recording and a programmatic reader.

    • Overhead: Before Go 1.21 tracing cost about 10-20% CPU; frame-pointer unwinding and other work brought it to roughly 1-2% for many apps.
    • Scalability: Go 1.22 rewrote traces so they can be split into self-contained segments.
    • Flight recording: Experimental FlightRecorder in golang.org/x/exp/trace keeps a rolling buffer and snapshots when something slow happens, e.g. an HTTP request over 300 ms.
    • Reader API: Experimental trace.NewReader / ReadEvent for analyzing traces in code, e.g. how often goroutines block on network I/O.
    • Viewing: go tool trace or the open-source gotraceui.
    • Limits: Flight recorder and reader are experimental; go tool trace still loads the whole trace into memory.

    Takeaway: Tracing is now cheap enough to leave on in production; a flight recorder triggered on slow requests is a practical way to catch tail-latency issues.

  • Measuring Your System’s Performance Using Software (Go Edition)
    summary

    TL;DR: Daniel Lemire (March 2024) shows how small Go benchmarks can reveal hardware and runtime behavior: allocations, inlining, cache lines, latency and branch prediction.

    • Benchmarks: BenchmarkXxx(b *testing.B) run with go test -bench .; b.N grows until a run lasts at least one second.
    • Allocations: b.ReportAllocs(); a 100,001-element slice allocated 802,816 bytes/op while small data stayed on the stack.
    • Inlining: -gcflags=-m reports it, //go:noinline disables it; inlined loop about 295 ns/op vs 865 ns/op.
    • Cache: A strided copy suggests a 128-byte cache line; a shuffle test suggests about 16 MB of cache.
    • Dependencies: Prefix sum 142.8 ns/op vs 30.04 ns/op for successive differences; linked lists are latency-bound.
    • Branches: Random data: branchy copy 19,518 ns/op vs branchless 7,124 ns/op.
    • Caveats: Results vary by hardware and are noisy; microbenchmarks alone do not justify optimizations; branchless can lose when branches are predictable.

    Takeaway: Good template for writing your own probes; measure on your target hardware before trusting any of these numbers.

  • For Loops and More in Go
    summary

    TL;DR: Miki Tebeka (Ardan Labs, March 2024) surveys Go loop forms and the bugs each can introduce, including Go 1.22 additions.

    • Assembly: go build -gcflags=-S shows a loop as jumps (JMP, INCQ, CMPQ, JLT); lensm for visual reading.
    • Multiple variables: Init/post clauses can update several vars, but i++, j-- is invalid Go; use i, j = i+1, j-1.
    • Labeled break: A plain break inside switch exits only the switch and can cause an infinite loop; use break loop. goto also shown.
    • Range copies: for _, a := range iterates over copies, so edits are lost; index or read/modify/write (acts[i] = a). Map values need read/modify/write too.
    • Go 1.22: for i := range 3 over integers and for range b.N in benchmarks.
    • Trivia: About 657 goto uses in the Go 1.22 standard library (rough count).
    • Limits: Range-over-func deferred to a later post; no performance data.

    Takeaway: Quick refresher on the range-copy and break-in-switch traps that still catch experienced Go developers.

  • How to Write a 4000 Stars GitHub README for Your Project
    summary

    TL;DR: Daytona CEO Ivan Burazin (March 2024) describes the README structure Daytona used at its open-source launch, when the repo reached nearly 4,000 stars in its first week.

    • Header: Logo, health badges, one-line pitch plus subtitle, visuals (GIFs via LiceCap), feature highlights, and a quickstart with as few commands as possible.
    • Body: Purpose, backstory, detailed getting-started steps; keep it concise and move depth into a docs folder.
    • Hygiene: Contributing guide, license, code of conduct (Contributor Covenant), advising git add <file1> <file2> over git add ..
    • Checklist: Remove empty sections, fix broken links, open labeled issues for missing content.
    • Beyond README: SECURITY.md, a filled About section, Releases, custom labels, “good first issue” tags, issue templates.
    • Caveats: Based on one project’s experience; no data linking README quality to stars.

    Takeaway: A reasonable checklist for launching an internal or open-source tool; the quickstart and SECURITY.md items are the cheapest wins.

  • Using GitHub Actions to Add Go Binaries to a Release
    summary

    TL;DR: Rob Allen (February 2024) shows the GitHub Actions workflow that builds Go binaries for his Flickr uploader Rodeo and attaches them to a GitHub Release automatically.

    • Trigger: on: release with type created.
    • Job: Single build job on ubuntu-latest, actions/checkout@v2, actions/setup-go@v1 with Go 1.20.
    • Build: build-executables.sh <tag> cross-compiles all platforms into ./release.
    • Upload: svenstaro/upload-release-action@v2 with GITHUB_TOKEN, file_glob: true and rodeo-* to upload everything in one step.
    • Design choice: No matrix, since one Go container can cross-compile every target instead of spinning up a runner per platform.
    • Limits: Build script is covered in a separate post; a commenter suggests GoReleaser, not evaluated.

    Takeaway: Fine for small tools; pin action versions to SHAs and consider GoReleaser if you need checksums, SBOMs or signing.

  • How I Built My Own Go Package Index
    summary

    TL;DR: Ozan Sazak (March 2024) explains how he built go.sazak.io, a vanity import path index for his Go packages, from a GitHub sync tool plus a static Next.js site.

    • Mechanism: go get fetches HTML go-import meta tags (import path, VCS, repo URL); optional go-source links source.
    • Sync tool: sync-github-repos lists public repos via the GitHub API, keeps those whose go.mod starts with module go.sazak.io/, and writes metadata (stars, latest tag, packages) to JSON.
    • Flags: HasCLIApp from a cli topic tag; AlphaRelease for pre-releases or versions below v1.0.0.
    • Frontend: Next.js, Shadcn UI, deployed on Vercel.
    • Automation: Pre-commit hook runs --username ozansz --hostname go.sazak.io --out ui/src/repos.json --force-authenticated; each push redeploys.
    • Limits: Single static page; data refreshes only at commit time.

    Takeaway: Vanity import paths decouple your module names from GitHub; this is a small, copyable pattern if you want that for a personal or company namespace.

  • Retina: eBPF Distributed Networking Observability Tool for Kubernetes
    summary

    TL;DR: Retina is Microsoft’s MIT-licensed, cloud-agnostic eBPF network observability platform for Kubernetes, providing Prometheus metrics and on-demand packet captures.

    • Metrics: Prometheus format, exportable to Prometheus or Azure Monitor, visualized in Grafana or Log Analytics.
    • Plugins: dropreason, packetforward, linuxutil, dns; packetparser for advanced metrics and CRD captures.
    • Captures: kubectl krew install retina then kubectl retina capture create --pod-selectors <app=my-app>.
    • Platforms: Linux, Windows and Azure Linux nodes; Windows Server 2019 no longer supported, use 2022.
    • Supply chain: Images verifiable with cosign against the GitHub OIDC issuer.
    • Limits: packetparser advanced mode may perform poorly on 32+ core nodes under heavy load; use basic mode there.

    Takeaway: Worth trying for packet drops and DNS issues in clusters without a full service mesh; start in basic mode on large nodes.

  • Keep Hackers Out of Your Cluster with These 5 Simple Tricks
    summary

    (Could not fetch full text.)

    TL;DR: KubeCon EU 2024 talk by Datadog’s Christophe Tafani-Dereeper and Frederic Baguelin giving a threat-informed, data-driven list of Kubernetes controls, based on honeypots and real container-escape exploitation.

    • Data: Public honeypots imitating the Docker API, Kubernetes API server and Kubelet API, plus a review of exploited container-escape CVEs; attacker goals grouped as deploy malicious workloads, backdoor the cluster, escape containers.
    • Control plane: Use managed Kubernetes, never disable API server auth, keep the API server off the internet (e.g. IAP for private GKE).
    • IMDS: GKE Workload Identity; on EKS/AKS block metadata with NetworkPolicy. On EKS, IMDSv2 alone is not enough; set hop limit to 1 on worker nodes.
    • Cloud privileges: Map pods to cloud roles with Datadog’s Managed Kubernetes Auditing Toolkit (MKAT).
    • Admission control: Kyverno, OPA Gatekeeper or Pod Security Admission; allow only vetted registries, block privileged pods and host mounts; audit first, then enforce.
    • Exploit resistance: securityContext.readOnlyRootFilesystem: true breaks many automated payloads.
    • Source caveat: No video transcript retrieved; based on the Datadog Security Labs abstract and the companion tl;dr sec guest post.

    Takeaway: A short, prioritized EKS/GKE hardening list; the IMDS hop-limit and read-only root FS items are cheap and high value.

  • Introducing TrailDiscover: Simplifying Access to Security Insights About CloudTrail Events
    summary

    (Could not fetch full text.)

    TL;DR: Adan Alvarez introduces TrailDiscover, an open catalog of AWS CloudTrail events documenting which ones attackers have abused, what they enable and what logs they produce, with a searchable site at traildiscover.cloud.

    • Structure: One JSON file per event grouped by AWS service, with event name, source, description, MITRE ATT&CK tactics/techniques, real-world-use evidence links, related research and security implications.
    • Site: Searchable Events pages and an Insights page breaking down incident sources, ATT&CK mappings and services.
    • Extras: The repo now also offers an MCP server for AI assistants and a Datadog dashboard generator.
    • Contributing: PRs for new events; run build.py in tools to regenerate site output; reuse the same URL/title when one report covers several events.
    • Caveats: Author says it is early and may contain mistakes; ATT&CK mappings are best guesses; some implications were AI-generated then reviewed.
    • Source caveat: Medium returned 403; summary based on the project’s GitHub README (adanalvarez/TrailDiscover).

    Takeaway: Good reference when writing CloudTrail detections or triaging an unfamiliar event name during an incident.

  • NamespaceHound: Protecting Multi-Tenant Kubernetes Clusters
    summary

    TL;DR: Wiz (Shay Berkovich, Megan Moore, March 2024) releases NamespaceHound, an open-source Python CLI that assesses namespace-crossing and anonymous-access risk in multi-tenant Kubernetes clusters.

    • Checks: 22 crossing types, e.g. RBAC_SECRETS_STEALING and RBAC_WORKLOAD_CREATION (both High), plus anonymous access.
    • Usage: -n NAMESPACE to scope, -c to include kube-system, -o table/json/csv/html, --kubeconfig, -v.
    • Permissions: Needs read on all resource types (admin, cluster-admin or system:masters also works).
    • Design: Stores no cluster data locally and builds no graph.
    • Framework: Extends Wiz’s PEACH tenant-isolation model to Kubernetes, with hardening advice on RBAC, storage reclaim policies and disabling token automount.
    • Limits: Risk assessment only, not enforcement; Kubernetes has no native way to monitor namespace crossing.

    Takeaway: Run it against any cluster where namespaces are your tenant boundary; findings usually point at over-broad RBAC.

  • bincapz (malcontent): Enumerate Binary Capabilities, Including Malicious Behaviors
    summary

    TL;DR: bincapz, now renamed malcontent, is Chainguard’s Apache 2.0 Go tool that enumerates program capabilities with YARA to detect supply-chain compromises, especially by diffing versions.

    • Rules: YARA-X with over 14,500 rules; third-party sets (Elastic, Mandiant, etc.) only with --third-party.
    • Targets: ELF, Mach-O and PE binaries, scripts in many languages, archives and OCI images.
    • Modes: analyze lists all capabilities, diff compares versions by risk, scan filters by threshold (default HIGH).
    • Settings: --min-risk (default low), --jobs 12, --max-depth 32, --sensitivity 5; registry auth via --oci-auth and MALCONTENT_REGISTRY_* env vars.
    • Run: cgr.dev/chainguard/malcontent:latest or make install-yara-x and make out/mal.
    • Limits: Best on Linux, weaker on macOS, weakest on Windows; analyze is noisy by design; AV may flag it due to embedded YARA strings.

    Takeaway: The diff mode is the useful part: run it between dependency or image versions in CI to spot newly added network, exec or persistence behavior.

  • Fixing Security Vulnerabilities with AI
    summary

    TL;DR: GitHub engineering post (Tiferet Gazit, February 2024) on how code scanning autofix, now Copilot Autofix, uses an LLM to propose fixes for CodeQL alerts and how they evaluated it.

    • Prompt: CodeQL query help, the alert message and line-numbered snippets along the data flow; asks for instructions, before/after code blocks and any new dependencies, without changing functionality.
    • No raw diffs: Models struggle with line-number arithmetic, so edits are expressed as code blocks.
    • Post-processing: Fuzzy matching, syntax parsing, name/type checks; suggested packages verified against registries and screened for vulnerabilities or malware.
    • Evaluation: Harness over 1,400+ JS/TS alerts from 63 CodeQL queries; success means alert gone, no new alerts, no syntax errors, test results unchanged.
    • Numbers: Iteration tripled success rate and cut LLM compute by a factor of six.
    • Limits: Initial release JS/TS only; prompt size limited visible files; edits confined to included code.

    Takeaway: The evaluation criteria are a good model for any AI-fix pipeline: re-run the scanner and tests, never trust the patch alone.

  • OPA 1.0 Is Coming: Here’s What You Need to Know
    summary

    TL;DR: Anders Eknert’s March 2024 OPA blog post on preparing Rego policies for OPA 1.0’s backward-incompatible changes.

    • Keywords: import future.keywords becomes a no-op; if and contains become mandatory in rule heads.
    • Strictness: Several strict-mode checks become default, e.g. duplicate imports and deprecated built-ins are rejected.
    • Reserved names: input and data can no longer be used as identifiers.
    • Server binding: Defaults to localhost instead of all interfaces; use opa run --server --addr 0.0.0.0:8181 to expose it.
    • Migration (v0.59.0+): Add import rego.v1, rewrite with opa fmt --rego-v1, verify with opa check --rego-v1, run with --v1-compatible.
    • Caveat: Change list described as non-comprehensive and subject to change.

    Takeaway: Run opa fmt --rego-v1 and opa check --rego-v1 across your policy repos and check any deployments that relied on OPA listening on all interfaces.

  • weAudit: Collaborative Code Auditing Extension for VS Code
    summary

    TL;DR: weAudit is Trail of Bits’ free VS Code extension for collaborative code review: bookmark findings and notes, track which files are reviewed, and export results.

    • Findings/notes: Create from a selection (default cmd+3 finding, cmd+4 note); shown in a sidebar list and highlighted inline; can span multiple regions.
    • Review tracking: Mark files reviewed (cmd+7) or regions partially reviewed (cmd+shift+7); cmd+0 jumps between partial regions.
    • Export: Markdown export, GitHub/GitLab issue creation and permalinks.
    • Sharing: Each auditor’s data lives in .vscode/$USERNAME.weaudit, which teammates can share and toggle per user.
    • Settings: Tree view mode, GitHub org, username, permalink separator, highlight colors.
    • Limits: Sharing is file-based, not real-time sync.

    Takeaway: Useful for security reviews or large PR audits where you need to prove coverage; commit or share the .weaudit files to coordinate.

  • Learning Go in 2024: From Beginner to Senior
    summary

    TL;DR: Matt Boyle’s ByteSizeGo guide (March 2024) organizes Go learning resources into Beginner, Junior, Mid-level and Senior tiers, each with books, talks, podcasts and a suggested project.

    • Beginner: Standard-library-only CLI that reads a birth date and prints age, run with go run.
    • Junior: HTTP exchange-rate server (/exchange/GBP/USD) with a naive buy signal vs the 7-day average, using table-driven tests.
    • Mid-level: Web scraper with pagination, DB storage and email alerts; concurrency primitives, pipelines, execution traces.
    • Senior: Distributed-systems framework (service discovery, load balancing, fault tolerance, consistent hashing) inspired by go-kit; Go memory model, Kubernetes memory limits.
    • Caveats: Non-exhaustive; many resources paid; some books from 2015-2016; promotes the author’s own products; a newer edition exists.

    Takeaway: The project ladder is the useful part for structuring your own or a team’s Go upskilling.

  • The Case of a Leaky Goroutine
    summary

    TL;DR: Wouter Groeneveld (Brain Baking, March 2024) walks through finding a goroutine leak that caused OOM restarts of Kubernetes pods in a Go service.

    • Detection: Grafana showed goroutine memory climbing; Pyroscope (docker run -it -p 4040:4040 grafana/pyroscope) showed goroutines parked in runtime.gopark inside pipeline functions.
    • Profiling: _ "net/http/pprof" exposes /debug/pprof/; go tool pprof with diff_base compares dumps against a baseline.
    • Root cause: A helper ToDoneInterface closed the wrong channel in defer, and the context was not derived (e.g. WithCancel), so goroutines in a long-running job never exited.
    • Testing: defer goleak.VerifyNone(t) from Uber’s goleak catches leftover goroutines.
    • Production: Uber’s LeakProf mentioned as the systematic option.
    • Fix: Do not convert channels; use derived contexts.

    Takeaway: Add goleak to tests of any code that spawns goroutines, and expose pprof so leaks can be diffed in a running pod.

  • threatcl: Threat Modeling as Code with HCL
    summary

    TL;DR: threatcl (formerly hcltm) is an MIT-licensed CLI for writing threat models as HCL files so they can live in version control and be validated in CI.

    • Format: HCL2 spec (separate repo); JSON also accepted but without imports and variables.
    • Validate: validate, with -invariants to enforce org-wide rules.
    • Outputs: export to JSON, OTM or HCL; dashboard to Markdown with custom templates; dfd renders data flow diagrams as PNG or DOT.
    • Terraform: terraform converts terraform show -json output into information_asset blocks.
    • Extras: server/query for GraphQL, beta mcp, and lsp.
    • Install: Release binaries, Homebrew, ghcr.io/threatcl/threatcl; releases have SLSA provenance verifiable with gh attestation verify.

    Takeaway: Good fit for threat-modeling-as-code: keep models next to the service, validate in PRs, and generate DFDs from the same source.

  • IAMGraph: Mapping Cross-Account Attack Paths in AWS Environments
    summary

    TL;DR: IAMGraph from WithSecure Labs (now under ReversecLabs) models AWS IAM role trust and assume-role paths across many accounts in Neo4j to find cross-account attack paths.

    • Input: Output of aws iam get-account-authorization-details for each account; permissions evaluated with WithSecure’s IAMSpy.
    • Run: iamgraph --db-uri bolt://localhost:7687 run --input-dir ./input/; model and analyse stages can run separately.
    • Database: Neo4j in Docker/Podman; NEO4J_AUTH=none for local use, else --db-user with password prompt.
    • Graph: Account, IAMUser, IAMRole, IdentityProvider, IAMPrincipal nodes with IN, TRUSTS and CAN_ASSUME edges.
    • Queries: Example Cypher for roles trusting *, roles trusting identity providers, and cross-account assume paths.
    • Limits: Accounts IAMSpy cannot load are skipped (e.g. managed policies used only as permission boundaries); large graphs overwhelm the Neo4j browser.

    Takeaway: Run it across an AWS Organization to spot unexpected cross-account trust, especially wildcard principals and third-party roles.

  • Using Tailscale for Persistence
    summary

    TL;DR: Rory McCune (raesene, March 2024) demonstrates how an attacker with brief cluster-admin access can use Tailscale for stealthy persistence on Kubernetes nodes, forming a small controllable “botnet”.

    • Tailnet design: ACL tags so controllers reach bots but bots cannot reach controllers or each other; tags must exist in the ACL policy before use.
    • Enrollment: Reusable auth key that auto-applies the bots tag.
    • Egress: Falls back to DERP over 443/TCP, so it works anywhere outbound 443 is open.
    • Hiding: containerd ctr runs the container in namespace sys_net_mon with --net-host and host root mounted read-only at /host; binaries renamed systemd_net_mon_server / systemd_net_mon_client; client run with --ssh.
    • Alternative: Static pod manifest in /etc/kubernetes/manifests so kubelet keeps it running.
    • Limits: ctr needs direct node access (e.g. SSH); post does not cover detection.

    Takeaway: Watch for unexpected containerd namespaces, static pod manifests, renamed binaries and outbound Tailscale/DERP traffic from nodes.

  • cleanowners: GitHub Action to Remove Non-Organization Members from CODEOWNERS
    summary

    TL;DR: cleanowners is an MIT-licensed GitHub Action from GitHub’s OSPO that opens PRs removing users who are no longer organization members from CODEOWNERS files.

    • Behavior: Also opens a PR adding a placeholder if CODEOWNERS is missing or empty.
    • Auth: GitHub App (GH_APP_ID, GH_APP_INSTALLATION_ID, GH_APP_PRIVATE_KEY) preferred over GH_TOKEN; classic PAT needs repo and read:org.
    • App permissions: Contents and Pull requests read/write, Metadata read, Organization Members read.
    • Settings: ORGANIZATION or REPOSITORY, EXEMPT_REPOS, DRY_RUN, ISSUE_REPORT, GH_ENTERPRISE_URL.
    • Workflow: github-community-projects/cleanowners@v2 on a cron (example "3 2 1 * *", monthly).
    • Limits: Community support only, no GitHub SLA; App must be installed on each scanned repo.

    Takeaway: Stale CODEOWNERS silently break required-review rules; run this monthly with DRY_RUN first.

  • Small Language Models for Application Security: Beyond ChatGPT
    summary

    (Could not fetch full text.)

    TL;DR: Conference talk by Louis Barrett on using small language models, rather than large hosted models like ChatGPT, for application security tasks.

    • Topic: Applying small, self-hostable language models to AppSec work as an alternative to general-purpose chatbots.
    • Likely themes: A related Loco Moco Security Conference session (“Small Language Models for Application Security II”, July 2024) describes using small off-the-shelf models, training them, scoping projects, and keeping company data inside the organization. It is not confirmed to be the same talk or speaker.
    • Context: Related public work (e.g. Wiz fine-tuning a small model for secret detection) argues small models give privacy and latency benefits when run on-premises.
    • Source caveat: The YouTube page returned no description or transcript; summary is based on the video title and web search results only, so specifics of the talk are unknown.

    Takeaway: Watch it if you are weighing self-hosted small models for code review or secret detection where sending source code to a third-party LLM is not acceptable.

  • Ultimate Guide to Secrets in Lambda
    summary

    TL;DR: AJ Stuyvenberg (March 2024) compares four ways to give AWS Lambda functions secrets, environment variables, SSM Parameter Store, Secrets Manager and KMS, on cost, latency, auditability, rotation and size.

    • Env vars: Encrypted at rest, exposed via GetFunctionConfiguration; 4 KB total limit; about 25 ms added to cold start; poor per-secret auditing.
    • Parameter Store: Standard params free, 4 KB, 10,000 per region; advanced $0.05/month, 8 KB, TTL policies; above 40 RPS costs $0.05 per 10,000. About 217 ms cold, 39.3 ms warm.
    • Secrets Manager: $0.40/secret/month, 65 KB, rotation and cross-region replication. About 177 ms cold, 29.4 ms warm.
    • KMS: $1/key/month, $0.03 per 10,000 requests, 4 KB per encrypt; decrypt about 64.4 ms cold, 6.45 ms warm. Envelope encryption suits about 100 KB of secrets.
    • Extension: Criticizes the closed-source AWS Parameters and Secrets Lambda Extension; prefers SDK calls or Powertools.
    • Recommendations: Env vars for low-blast-radius keys, SecureString parameters for larger secrets, Secrets Manager when compliance (PCI-DSS, HIPAA) requires rotation.

    Takeaway: Whatever you pick, lock down lambda:GetFunctionConfiguration and kms:Decrypt, since anyone with the former can read env-var secrets in plaintext.

  • Access: Discord’s Centralized Portal to Discover, Request and Manage Internal Access
    summary

    TL;DR: Access is Discord’s Apache 2.0 open-source portal where employees discover, request and manage access to internal systems, built on top of Okta groups.

    • Stack: React/TypeScript SPA with a FastAPI backend; PostgreSQL 14+ in production, SQLite for development; OIDC or Cloudflare Access for login.
    • Okta token: Needs Group Admin and Application Admin; managing groups that grant Okta admin needs Super Admin.
    • Jobs: access sync, access notify, access sync-app-groups, plus repair commands with --dry-run.
    • Expiry: Pending requests expire after one week by default (MAX_ACCESS_REQUEST_AGE_SECONDS=604800), or never.
    • Plugins: pluggy-based hooks (async) for notifications, conditional access, metrics and app-group lifecycle.
    • MCP: Optional ENABLE_MCP=true lets LLM clients browse and file requests but not approve them.
    • Limits: Okta is the source of truth and authoritative sync can push changes back; lifecycle hook delivery is not guaranteed.

    Takeaway: A self-hosted alternative to commercial access-request tools if you already run Okta; treat its Okta token as highly privileged.

  • AzurEnum: Enumerate Microsoft Entra ID (Azure AD) Fast
    summary

    TL;DR: AzurEnum, from SySS Research (Enrique Hernandez, Domenik Jockers), is an MIT-licensed Python tool for fast enumeration of a Microsoft Entra ID (Azure AD) tenant’s security-relevant configuration.

    • Tenant info: User, group and app counts, Entra ID license, tenant ID.
    • Settings: Group creation, consent policy, guest access, named locations, conditional access policies and their enforcement.
    • Privilege: Admin roles, PIM assignments (including group-based), administrative units, dynamic groups, sync and MFA status of admins.
    • Secrets: Flags credentials stored in object attributes.
    • Setup: Python 3 and pipx; Linux recommended; username/password auth, tenant ID, text or JSON output.
